lessons.title: What Machine Learning Is
lessons.content:
Think about how a small child learns what a cat is. Nobody hands the child a rulebook saying 'four legs, pointed ears, whiskers, length between 30 and 50 centimetres'. Instead, the child sees many cats in the lane, on the roof, in picture books, and an adult says 'cat!' each time. After a while the child can spot a cat they have never seen before, even a strange orange one sleeping on a rickshaw seat. Machine learning (ML) is the same trick done by a computer: instead of a programmer writing every rule, we show the computer many examples and let it work out the pattern by itself.

The old way, writing rules: For most of computing history, a program was a list of exact instructions written by a person. Want to calculate a salary? Write salary = basic + house rent + medical. This works beautifully when the rules are known and simple. But try writing rules to recognise handwritten Bangla digits, or to decide whether an email is spam, or to predict tomorrow's electricity demand in Dhaka. The rules are too many, too fuzzy, and they keep changing. Programmers ended up writing thousands of if-else lines that still broke on new cases. This is the problem ML was built to solve.

The new way, learning from data: In ML we flip the process. In traditional programming, you give the computer rules plus data and it gives you answers. In machine learning, you give the computer data plus the answers for that data, and it gives you back the rules, in the form of a model. Then you use that model on new data to get new answers. A model is simply a function with adjustable knobs. The knobs are called parameters (or weights), and 'learning' means turning the knobs until the model's answers match the known answers as closely as possible.

A precise definition: Tom Mitchell gave a famous definition in 1997: a computer program is said to learn from experience E with respect to some task T and performance measure P, if its performance on T, as measured by P, improves with experience E. Let's apply it to a spam filter. Task T: label each email as spam or not spam. Performance P: the percentage of emails labelled correctly. Experience E: a collection of past emails that users marked as spam or not spam. If the filter gets more accurate as it sees more marked emails, it is learning. Whenever you meet a new ML problem, try to name T, P and E first. It forces you to be clear about what you actually want.

A tiny example of a model: Suppose you want to predict the monthly rent of a flat from its size. You collect data: a 500 square foot flat rents for 10 thousand taka, a 1000 square foot flat for 19 thousand, and so on. A simple model is rent = w times size + b. Here w and b are the parameters. If learning finds w = 0.018 and b = 1 (rent in thousand taka, size in square feet), then for a 800 square foot flat the model predicts 0.018 times 800 + 1 = 15.4 thousand taka. The computer did not know the word 'rent'; it only found numbers that make the line fit the examples. We will learn exactly how it finds them in lessons 05 and 06.

Some vocabulary: Each row of data (one flat, one email, one patient) is called an example, sample or instance. The input values describing it (size, number of rooms, area) are features, usually written as x. The answer we want to predict (rent, spam or not) is the label or target, written as y. Training is the process of fitting the parameters on known examples; inference or prediction is using the trained model on new inputs. The collection used for training is the training set.

Supervised learning: This is the most common type. Every training example comes with its correct label, like a teacher supervising with an answer key. There are two flavours. In classification, the label is a category: spam or not spam, which of the 10 digits, whether a mango is ripe, raw or rotten. In regression, the label is a number: house rent, tomorrow's temperature, the price of rice next month. A quick test: if you could sensibly ask 'how far off was the prediction?' in units like taka or degrees, it is regression; if the answer is simply right or wrong, it is classification.

Unsupervised learning: Here there are no labels at all. The computer receives only the inputs and must find structure by itself. The classic task is clustering: grouping similar items. A supershop chain could group its customers by buying habits and discover, without being told, a group that buys baby products and another that buys mostly snacks. Other unsupervised tasks are dimensionality reduction (squeezing many features into a few while keeping the important information) and anomaly detection (finding unusual transactions). Lessons 21 to 23 cover these.

Reinforcement learning: In reinforcement learning (RL), an agent acts in an environment, receives rewards or penalties, and learns which actions lead to the most reward over time. No one tells it the right move for each situation; it discovers good strategies by trial and error. Game-playing programs and some robot controllers use RL. It needs its own ideas (states, policies, value functions), so this course only names it; the full story is in the Reinforcement Learning course (cse-8-4).

In-between types: Labels are often expensive, because someone has to sit and tag each image or email. Semi-supervised learning uses a small labelled set plus a large unlabelled set. Self-supervised learning creates labels automatically from the data itself, for example hiding a word in a sentence and asking the model to guess it. Large language models are pre-trained in a self-supervised way. You only need the idea for now.

When ML is a good idea: ML shines when the pattern is real but hard to write down, when you have enough examples, and when some errors are acceptable. Face unlock on a phone, recommending videos, reading number plates, detecting fraudulent bKash transactions, forecasting demand for a shop, and reading X-ray images are all good fits. The model does not need to be perfect; it needs to be useful and better than the alternative.

When ML is a bad idea: If the rule is simple and known, just write the rule. Calculating VAT, sorting a list or converting taka to dollars does not need ML. If you have very little data, or the data does not contain the information needed (predicting a lottery number), ML cannot help. If every single mistake is unacceptable and must be explained in law, a learned model may be risky without extra care. A good engineer asks 'do I even need ML here?' before starting.

How learning actually happens, in one paragraph: Almost every method in this course follows the same recipe. First, choose a family of models (straight lines, decision trees, neural networks). Second, choose a loss function that measures how wrong the model is on the training examples. Third, use an optimisation method to adjust the parameters to make the loss small. Fourth, check the model on data it has never seen to make sure it generalises, meaning it works on new cases, not just the ones it memorised. Model, loss, optimisation, evaluation: keep these four words in mind and every later lesson will feel familiar.

Generalisation is the real goal: A model that scores 100 percent on its training examples may still be useless. Imagine a student who memorises the answers to last year's question paper. If the same questions come, full marks; if the teacher changes a single number, failure. In ML this is called overfitting, and fighting it is a big part of the job. That is why we always keep some data aside to test the model honestly. Lessons 04, 08, 09 and 10 are all about this.

Real example 1, Bangla digit recognition: Suppose the Election Commission wants to read handwritten digits on forms. Writing rules for every person's handwriting is hopeless. Instead, collect thousands of scanned digits, each labelled 0 to 9 by a person. Task T: classify a digit image. Performance P: percent correct on new forms. Experience E: the labelled images. This is supervised classification. Bangladeshi researchers have published handwritten Bangla digit datasets for exactly this kind of work, and models trained on them can read digits they have never seen.

Real example 2, grouping customers for a mobile operator: A mobile operator has usage data for millions of SIMs: call minutes, data used, recharge amounts, time of day. There is no label saying what type of customer each is. Running a clustering method might reveal groups such as night-time data users, heavy callers, and low-usage SIMs kept as backups. Marketing can then design different packages for each group. This is unsupervised learning: the groups were discovered, not given.

Where ML sits among related fields: Artificial intelligence (AI) is the big field of making machines act intelligently; ML is one approach inside AI, the one that learns from data. Deep learning is a part of ML that uses neural networks with many layers. Data science uses ML as one of its tools, together with statistics, data cleaning and visualisation. Statistics and ML overlap a lot; roughly, statistics cares more about understanding and inference, ML cares more about accurate prediction, but the boundary is blurry.

What this course covers: We start with data and the workflow (lessons 02 to 04), then regression, gradient descent, loss functions, overfitting and regularisation (05 to 10). Then classification with logistic regression and how to evaluate classifiers properly (11 to 14). Next come classic algorithms: k-nearest neighbours, naive Bayes, decision trees, ensembles, support vector machines and a first look at neural networks (15 to 20). Then unsupervised learning: k-means, hierarchical clustering and PCA (21 to 23). We finish with tools, production, ethics and a capstone project (24 to 26).

Common mistakes and exam questions: Students often mix up classification and regression; remember category versus number. Another confusion is thinking unsupervised means 'no human involved'; humans still choose the method and interpret the groups. Exams commonly ask: define ML (Mitchell's definition with T, P, E), give examples of each learning type, explain the difference between traditional programming and ML, and say whether a given problem is classification, regression or clustering. Practise by taking any app on your phone and asking which parts might use ML and of which type.

Recap: Machine learning lets computers learn patterns from examples instead of following hand-written rules. A model is a function with parameters; training adjusts the parameters to reduce a loss on known examples; the true test is performance on new data. Supervised learning uses labelled data for classification or regression, unsupervised learning finds structure without labels, and reinforcement learning learns from rewards. Next lesson, we walk through the full workflow of an ML project from the first question to a working system.
key_points: Machine learning means learning patterns from data and answers, instead of a programmer writing every rule.
Mitchell's definition: a program learns from experience E on task T with performance measure P if P on T improves with E.
A model is a function with adjustable parameters; training tunes them to fit known examples.
Supervised learning uses labelled data: classification predicts a category, regression predicts a number.
Unsupervised learning finds structure without labels, such as clusters; reinforcement learning learns from rewards.
Nearly every method follows the recipe: model, loss, optimisation, evaluation on unseen data.
The real goal is generalisation to new data, not a perfect score on training data.
Use ML when the pattern is real but hard to write as rules and enough data exists; otherwise just write the rule.
lessons.tip: For every ML problem you meet in this course, write one line naming T (task), P (performance measure) and E (experience). It takes ten seconds and makes the rest of the problem much clearer.
lessons.task: Open five apps on your phone (for example Facebook, YouTube, Google Maps, bKash and your camera). For each, find one feature that probably uses machine learning, and write whether it is classification, regression, clustering or something else, plus a guess at T, P and E.

quiz.q: Predicting tomorrow's maximum temperature in Rajshahi in degrees Celsius is which kind of task?
quiz.explain: The output is a number on a continuous scale, so it is regression.

quiz.q: In Mitchell's definition of learning, what does E stand for?
quiz.explain: A program learns from experience E with respect to task T and performance measure P.

quiz.q: A supershop groups its customers by buying habits with no labels given. This is:
quiz.explain: There are no labels; the algorithm discovers the groups itself, which is clustering, an unsupervised task.

quiz.q: Which problem is the WORST candidate for machine learning?
options: Calculating 15 percent VAT on a bill
quiz.explain: The VAT rule is simple and exactly known, so a plain formula is better than a learned model.

quiz.q: What does 'training' a model mean?
options: Running the model on new data
Adjusting its parameters so its outputs fit known examples
quiz.explain: Training tunes the parameters to reduce the error on the training examples; using it on new data is inference.

lessons.title: The Machine Learning Workflow
lessons.content:
Cooking biryani for a wedding is not just 'put rice in a pot'. You decide how many guests are coming, buy the right ingredients, wash and cut them, marinate the meat, cook, taste, adjust the salt, serve, and then watch whether people come back for a second plate. Skip a step and the whole thing can fail, no matter how good your pot is. A machine learning project is exactly like that. The algorithm is only the pot. Most of the real work, and most of the failures, happen in the steps around it. This lesson walks through the full workflow so that every later lesson has a place on the map.

Why a workflow matters: Beginners often think ML means 'pick a fancy algorithm and press run'. In practice, surveys of working data scientists repeatedly report that a large share of their time goes into finding, cleaning and understanding data, not into choosing algorithms. A project with clean, relevant data and a simple model usually beats a project with messy data and a complex model. A clear workflow also helps a team: everyone knows what stage the project is at and what 'done' means.

The steps in one line: Frame the problem, collect data, explore the data, prepare features, set a baseline, train models, evaluate honestly, deploy, monitor, and repeat. These steps are not a straight line; you will loop back many times. A poor evaluation result might send you back to collect more data or to rethink the problem itself.

Step 1, framing the problem: Start with the business or real-world question, not with the algorithm. 'We want to use AI' is not a problem. 'We want to know, each morning, how many cups of tea our stall will sell today, so we buy the right amount of milk' is a problem. From it, decide: what exactly is predicted (cups sold today), what type of task this is (regression, because it is a number), what inputs will be available at prediction time (day of the week, weather forecast, whether there is a cricket match), and how success will be measured (for example, average error in cups). Also ask what a wrong prediction costs. Buying too much milk wastes money; too little loses sales. These costs shape which metric you choose.

Step 2, collecting data: Where will the examples come from? Sales records, sensors, forms, public datasets, or labels made by people. Check three things. Is there enough data? Is it relevant, meaning does it contain the information needed to predict the target? Is it representative, meaning does it look like the situations where the model will actually be used? A model trained only on Dhaka city data may fail in rural Sunamganj. Also check whether you are allowed to use the data: personal data needs consent and care, which lesson 25 discusses.

Step 3, exploring the data: Before training anything, look at the data. Count rows and columns. Check the type of each column (number, category, date, text). Compute simple statistics: minimum, maximum, mean, median. Draw histograms and scatter plots. Look for missing values, impossible values (a person aged 230), duplicates and strange spikes. This step is called exploratory data analysis (EDA). It often reveals bugs early, for example a column where some prices are in taka and some in thousand taka.

Step 4, preparing features: Models need numbers in a sensible form. You fill or remove missing values, turn categories like 'Dhaka', 'Khulna' into numbers, scale features to similar ranges, and create new useful features, such as 'is it a weekend?' from a date. This is called data preprocessing and feature engineering, and lesson 03 does it with worked numbers. Good features often matter more than the choice of algorithm.

Step 5, splitting the data: Before training, set aside data that the model will never see during training, so you can test it honestly later. Typically you make a training set, a validation set for choosing settings, and a test set for the final check. Lesson 04 covers this, including the sneaky problem of data leakage.

Step 6, the baseline: A baseline is the simplest reasonable prediction method, used as a yardstick. For regression, a common baseline is 'always predict the average of the training targets'. For classification, it is 'always predict the most common class'. If your fancy model cannot beat the baseline, something is wrong. Worked example: a tea stall sold 120, 150, 130, 160 and 140 cups on five training days. The mean is (120 + 150 + 130 + 160 + 140) / 5 = 700 / 5 = 140. So the baseline always predicts 140 cups. On two new test days the stall actually sold 135 and 155 cups. The baseline errors are |135 - 140| = 5 and |155 - 140| = 15, so the mean absolute error (MAE) is (5 + 15) / 2 = 10 cups. Now if a model using day of week and weather gets an MAE of 6 cups on the same days, we know it really adds value: it cut the error from 10 to 6.

Why baselines save you from embarrassment: Suppose 95 out of 100 loan applicants in your data repaid their loans. A model that always says 'will repay' gets 95 percent accuracy while being completely useless for spotting risky applicants. If you had not computed the baseline, 96 percent accuracy might look impressive. With the baseline in mind, you see it is only 1 point better than doing nothing clever at all.

Step 7, training models: Now you choose model families and train them. Start simple: linear or logistic regression, a small decision tree. Then try stronger models such as random forests or gradient boosting. Each model has hyperparameters, settings you choose before training (like the depth of a tree), which you tune using the validation set or cross-validation (lesson 13). Keep a record of every experiment: what data, what features, what settings, what score. Otherwise you will forget which run was the good one.

Step 8, evaluating honestly: Pick metrics that match the real goal. For the tea stall, MAE in cups is easy to understand. For a disease test, recall (catching sick people) may matter more than accuracy. Lessons 07, 12 and 14 explore this. Look beyond a single number: where does the model fail? Does it fail more on rainy days, on certain districts, on certain groups of people? Use the test set only at the very end, once, to get an unbiased estimate.

Step 9, deploying: A model in a notebook helps nobody. Deployment means putting it where it is used: inside a mobile app, behind a web service, or as a nightly job that writes predictions into a database. You must make sure that the features computed in production are calculated exactly the same way as in training. Lesson 24 gives an overview.

Step 10, monitoring and maintenance: The world changes. Prices rise, customer habits shift, a new road opens. When the data the model sees in production drifts away from the training data, accuracy slowly falls. Monitoring means tracking inputs, predictions and, when the true answers arrive, the real error. When performance drops, you retrain with fresh data. A model is more like a garden than a building; it needs care after launch.

The loop: Real projects cycle. You train, evaluate, find that the model fails on Fridays, discover that the Friday data had a recording bug, fix the data, retrain, and so on. Industry process models such as CRISP-DM (Cross-Industry Standard Process for Data Mining) draw these steps as a circle for this reason: business understanding, data understanding, data preparation, modelling, evaluation and deployment, with arrows going back.

Who does what: In a company, these steps are rarely done by one person. A domain expert (the shop owner, a doctor, an agronomist) explains what matters and what the data really means. A data engineer builds the pipelines that collect and store data reliably. A data scientist or ML engineer explores, builds features and trains models. A software engineer helps put the model inside the product. In a small startup or a student project, you may wear all these hats yourself, which is exactly why knowing the full workflow matters. Talking to the domain expert early saves weeks: the tea stall owner can tell you in one minute that sales drop during Ramadan afternoons, something you might take days to discover from the numbers.

Keeping it reproducible: Six weeks into a project someone will ask, 'which data and settings gave that 6 cup error?'. If you cannot answer, the result is worthless. Good habits are simple: save the exact version of the dataset used, fix the random seed when splitting data so the split can be repeated, write preprocessing as code rather than manual spreadsheet edits, and log every experiment with its score. Version control tools like Git help for code; for data, even a dated folder and a short notes file are far better than nothing. Reproducibility is not bureaucracy; it is what lets you trust and improve your own work.

Real example 1, a tea stall near a university: Framing: predict tomorrow's cups to buy the right amount of milk and sugar. Data: a notebook where the owner wrote daily sales for six months, plus dates of exams, holidays and cricket matches. EDA reveals that sales collapse during Eid holidays and jump on match days. Features: day of week, holiday flag, match flag, rain forecast. Baseline MAE: 10 cups. A simple linear model: MAE 6 cups. Deployment: each evening a phone app shows the forecast. Monitoring: if errors grow, maybe a new competitor opened next door.

Real example 2, an e-commerce return predictor: A Bangladeshi online shop loses money when cash-on-delivery parcels are refused at the door. Framing: before shipping, estimate the probability that an order will be returned, so risky orders get a confirmation call. Task type: classification with probabilities. Data: past orders with a returned or not label. Baseline: always predict 'not returned', which might be right most of the time but catches no returns. Metric: recall on returned orders at a manageable number of calls per day. Deployment: the score appears next to each order in the dashboard. Monitoring: festival seasons may change the pattern.

Common mistakes: Jumping to algorithms before understanding the problem. Not computing a baseline. Testing on training data. Using features that will not be available at prediction time (for example, using 'delivery outcome' to predict returns). Tuning endlessly on the test set until it looks good, which makes the final score a lie. Forgetting that the model will need maintenance. Exams often ask you to list and explain the stages of an ML pipeline, to explain why a baseline is needed, or to identify which stage a described problem belongs to.

Recap: An ML project is a cycle: frame, collect, explore, prepare, split, baseline, train, evaluate, deploy, monitor, repeat. The algorithm is one step among many. Always start with a clear question and a baseline, judge models on data they have never seen, and plan for change after deployment. In the next lesson we zoom into the data preparation step and do cleaning, encoding and scaling with real numbers.
key_points: An ML project is a loop: frame, collect, explore, prepare, split, baseline, train, evaluate, deploy, monitor.
Start from a real question: what is predicted, which task type, what inputs exist at prediction time, how success is measured.
Exploratory data analysis finds missing, impossible and duplicate values before they ruin a model.
A baseline (mean for regression, majority class for classification) is the yardstick every model must beat.
Worked: training mean 140 cups gives baseline MAE 10 on test days; a model with MAE 6 adds real value.
Use the test set once at the end; tune with validation data or cross-validation.
Deployed models need monitoring because the world and the data drift over time.
lessons.tip: Before any modelling, write a one-paragraph project card: the question, the target, the inputs available at prediction time, the metric, and the baseline score. If you cannot fill it in, you are not ready to train.
lessons.task: Pick a small prediction problem from your own life, such as how many minutes your bus ride takes tomorrow. Write each of the ten workflow steps for it in one or two lines, including a baseline and how you would measure error.

quiz.q: What should be the FIRST step of an ML project?
options: Frame the problem: what to predict and how success is measured
quiz.explain: Everything else depends on a clear problem definition and success measure.

quiz.q: Training targets are 10, 20 and 30. A regression baseline that always predicts the training mean will predict:
95 percent of loan applicants repaid. A model reports 95 percent accuracy. What is the best conclusion?
options: It may be no better than always predicting 'repay'
quiz.explain: The majority-class baseline already gets 95 percent, so this model may add nothing.

quiz.q: Why is monitoring needed after deployment?
options: Models forget their weights over time
Real-world data can drift away from the training data, lowering accuracy
quiz.explain: Changing habits, prices and conditions make production data differ from training data.

quiz.q: Which feature is a problem for predicting whether an order will be returned, at the time of shipping?
quiz.explain: The delivery outcome is not known when the prediction is made; using it leaks the answer.

lessons.title: Data and Features: Cleaning, Encoding and Scaling
lessons.content:
Before you cook fish curry, you clean the fish: remove scales, cut it into pieces of similar size, wash out the mud. Nobody throws a whole muddy fish straight into the pot. Data is the same. Raw data straight from forms, sensors or spreadsheets is full of gaps, typing mistakes, words where numbers should be and columns on wildly different scales. Most ML algorithms only understand clean numbers. This lesson shows how to turn messy raw data into a clean table of features, with small worked examples you can check by hand.

The shape of ML data: Most classic ML works on a table. Each row is one example (a student, a flat, a day). Each column is a feature describing it (age, area, rainfall), plus one target column we want to predict. We usually call the feature table X, with n rows and d columns, and the target vector y with n values. For example, a table of 1000 flats with 5 features each gives X of size 1000 by 5 and y of length 1000. Images, sound and text can also be turned into tables of numbers, but the ideas in this lesson apply everywhere.

Types of features: Numerical features are numbers where arithmetic makes sense: area in square feet, temperature, income. They can be continuous (any value, like 23.7 degrees) or discrete (counts, like number of rooms). Categorical features are labels from a fixed set: division (Dhaka, Chattogram, Sylhet), blood group, payment method. Some categorical features have a natural order, called ordinal: education level (SSC, HSC, Bachelor, Master) or T-shirt size (S, M, L). Others have no order, called nominal: colour or district. There are also dates, free text and IDs. An ID like a student roll number is usually not a useful feature at all, because it carries no real meaning about the student.

Why cleaning matters: The saying 'garbage in, garbage out' is very true in ML. A model learns whatever patterns exist in the data, including errors. If some ages are typed as 250 instead of 25, a linear model will twist itself trying to fit those impossible points. If half the rainfall values are missing and you silently treat missing as zero, the model will believe many days were completely dry. Cleaning is not glamorous, but it often improves results more than switching algorithms.

Missing values, what to do: Values go missing because a sensor failed, a person skipped a question, or a record was lost. There are three main options. First, drop rows with missing values, which is fine if very few rows are affected and they are missing at random. Second, drop the column, if most of its values are missing. Third, impute, meaning fill in a sensible value. Simple imputation uses the mean or median of the column (for numbers) or the most frequent value (for categories). It also often helps to add a new yes/no feature 'was this value missing?', because sometimes missingness itself carries information.

Worked example, imputation: The ages of five survey respondents are 22, 25, missing, 30 and 28. Using the four known values, the mean is (22 + 25 + 30 + 28) / 4 = 105 / 4 = 26.25. The median is the middle of the sorted values 22, 25, 28, 30; with four values it is the average of the two middle ones, (25 + 28) / 2 = 26.5. So mean imputation fills 26.25, median imputation fills 26.5. Here they are close. But imagine the 25 had been mistyped as 250. The mean becomes (22 + 250 + 30 + 28) / 4 = 82.5, a silly age to fill in, while the median of 22, 28, 30, 250 is (28 + 30) / 2 = 29, which is still reasonable. That is why the median is often preferred when there might be outliers.

Duplicates and inconsistent values: The same row can appear twice because a form was submitted twice. Duplicates make the model over-weight those examples and can leak between training and test sets. Remove exact duplicates after checking they are truly errors. Inconsistent spelling is another classic: 'Dhaka', 'dhaka', 'DHAKA' and 'Dhaka ' with a trailing space are four different categories to a computer. Normalise text by trimming spaces and fixing case. Also check units: one column mixing kilograms and grams, or taka and thousand taka, will confuse any model.

Outliers: An outlier is a value far from the others. Some are errors (an age of 250), some are real but rare (a flat rent of 3 lakh taka in Gulshan). Fix or remove errors. For real extreme values, think about the goal: they may be important, as in fraud detection, or you may limit their effect by capping values at a chosen percentile or by using a model and loss that are less sensitive to them (lesson 07). A common quick check is the z-score, which we compute below: values more than about 3 standard deviations from the mean deserve a look.

Encoding categories: Most algorithms need numbers, so text categories must be encoded. For ordinal features, label encoding with numbers in the natural order works: SSC = 1, HSC = 2, Bachelor = 3, Master = 4. The order of the numbers matches a real order. But for nominal features, label encoding is dangerous. If you code Dhaka = 1, Chattogram = 2, Sylhet = 3, a linear model will think Sylhet is 'three times' Dhaka and that Chattogram sits halfway between them. That is nonsense.

Worked example, one-hot encoding: For a nominal feature, create one new column per category, with a 1 in the matching column and 0 elsewhere. With three divisions, the column 'division' becomes three columns: is_Dhaka, is_Chattogram, is_Sylhet. A flat in Dhaka becomes (1, 0, 0), one in Chattogram (0, 1, 0), one in Sylhet (0, 0, 1). No fake ordering appears, and the model can learn a separate effect for each division. The cost is more columns: a feature with 64 districts becomes 64 columns. For linear models people often drop one of the columns, because the last one can be inferred from the others (if it is not Dhaka and not Chattogram, it must be Sylhet); this avoids redundant columns.

Why scaling matters: Imagine features 'age' (around 20 to 60) and 'monthly income' (around 20000 to 80000 taka). Any method that uses distances, such as k-nearest neighbours (lesson 15) or k-means (lesson 21), will be dominated by income simply because its numbers are bigger. A difference of 1000 taka would count as much as a difference of 1000 years of age. Gradient descent (lesson 06) also converges much more slowly when features have very different scales. Scaling puts features on comparable ranges. Tree-based models (lesson 17) are an exception; they only compare values within one feature, so scaling does not change them.

Worked example, min-max scaling: Min-max scaling maps each value into the range 0 to 1 with x' = (x - min) / (max - min). Monthly incomes are 20000, 35000, 50000 and 80000 taka. Min = 20000, max = 80000, so max - min = 60000. Then 20000 becomes 0 / 60000 = 0, 35000 becomes 15000 / 60000 = 0.25, 50000 becomes 30000 / 60000 = 0.5, and 80000 becomes 60000 / 60000 = 1. Min-max is easy to understand, but a single extreme value squashes all the others towards 0.

Worked example, standardization: Standardization (also called z-score scaling) uses z = (x - mean) / standard deviation, giving a column with mean 0 and standard deviation 1. Take the values 2, 4, 4, 4, 5, 5, 7, 9. Their sum is 40, so the mean is 40 / 8 = 5. The squared deviations from 5 are 9, 1, 1, 1, 0, 0, 4, 16, which add up to 32; divided by 8 gives a variance of 4, so the (population) standard deviation is 2. The z-scores are then (2 - 5) / 2 = -1.5, (4 - 5) / 2 = -0.5 three times, 0 twice, (7 - 5) / 2 = 1 and (9 - 5) / 2 = 2. The value 9 is 2 standard deviations above the mean: unusual but not extreme.

The golden rule of scaling: Compute the mean, standard deviation, min, max, median for imputation, and every other preprocessing statistic using only the training data. Then apply those same numbers to the validation and test data and later to live data. If you compute the mean on the whole dataset including test rows, information from the test set leaks into training, and your test score becomes too optimistic. Lesson 04 discusses this leakage in detail.

Feature engineering: Often the best improvement comes from creating new features that expose the pattern more clearly. From a date you can extract day of week, month, whether it is a holiday, or days until Eid. From a flat's area and number of rooms you can compute area per room. From GPS coordinates you can compute distance to the nearest metro station. From a timestamp of bKash transactions you can compute 'number of transactions in the last hour'. Domain knowledge is the key ingredient: someone who knows the business can suggest features that no algorithm would invent alone.

Real example 1, cleaning hospital admission data: A district hospital wants to predict how long patients will stay. The raw spreadsheet has blood pressure missing for 8 percent of patients, 'gender' written as M, Male, m and male, ages including 0 for 'unknown', and a few duplicate admissions. Cleaning steps: normalise gender to two consistent values, treat age 0 as missing, impute missing ages and blood pressure with medians from the training set plus 'was missing' flags, remove duplicates, one-hot encode the ward, and standardise numeric columns. Only then is the data ready for a model.

Real example 2, features for rice price prediction: To forecast next month's coarse rice price in a local bazar, raw data includes past prices, rainfall, flood reports and import news. Useful engineered features: last month's price, the change over the last three months, the month of the year (prices often behave differently around harvest seasons), and a flag for major floods. One-hot encoding the month avoids pretending December is 'twelve times' January.

Common mistakes and exam questions: Label-encoding nominal categories, which invents a fake order. Fitting the scaler on the full dataset, which leaks test information. Forgetting to apply the same transformation to new data at prediction time. Using mean imputation when there are big outliers. Scaling the target in regression and forgetting to scale predictions back. Exams love: compute min-max and z-scores for a small list, explain when to use one-hot versus label encoding, list ways to handle missing values, and explain why distance-based algorithms need scaling.

Recap: Data must be cleaned before learning: handle missing values (drop or impute, median is robust), remove duplicates, fix inconsistent categories and units, and deal with outliers thoughtfully. Encode ordinal categories with ordered numbers and nominal ones with one-hot vectors. Scale numeric features with min-max or standardization, using statistics from the training set only. Good feature engineering, guided by domain knowledge, often beats a fancier algorithm. Next, we learn how to split data so our evaluation stays honest.
key_points: ML data is usually a table X (rows are examples, columns are features) plus a target y.
Missing values can be dropped or imputed; median imputation resists outliers (ages 22, 25, 30, 28 give mean 26.25, median 26.5).
Remove duplicates, fix inconsistent spellings and units, and handle outliers based on whether they are errors or rare truths.
Ordinal categories can use ordered numbers; nominal categories should be one-hot encoded to avoid a fake order.
Min-max scaling: x' = (x - min) / (max - min), mapping incomes 20000..80000 to 0..1.
Standardization: z = (x - mean) / sd; for 2, 4, 4, 4, 5, 5, 7, 9 the mean is 5 and sd is 2.
Fit all preprocessing statistics on training data only, then apply them to validation, test and live data.
Feature engineering with domain knowledge often improves results more than changing the algorithm.
lessons.tip: Keep a 'data diary' for each dataset: every cleaning decision, with the reason, in one line each. When the model behaves strangely later, this diary is the first place to look.
lessons.task: Write down the heights (in cm) of six friends or family members, pretending one value is missing. Impute it with the mean and the median, then compute min-max scaled values and z-scores for the full list by hand or with a phone calculator.

quiz.q: Why is one-hot encoding preferred over label encoding for a feature like 'division'?
options: Label encoding would invent a fake numeric order between divisions
quiz.explain: Numbers 1, 2, 3 suggest an order and distances that do not exist between divisions.

quiz.q: Incomes are 20000, 35000, 50000 and 80000. What is the min-max scaled value of 35000?
A column has mean 5 and standard deviation 2. What is the z-score of 9?
When should the mean used for scaling be computed?
options: On the whole dataset including the test set
Separately on each of train and test
On the training set only, then reused for validation and test
quiz.explain: Using test data to compute it leaks information and makes the evaluation too optimistic.

quiz.q: Which model type is generally NOT affected by feature scaling?
options: Linear regression trained by gradient descent
quiz.explain: Trees split on thresholds within one feature at a time, so rescaling a feature does not change the splits.

lessons.title: Splitting Data: Training, Validation and Test Sets
lessons.content:
Imagine a teacher who gives students a practice sheet of 20 maths problems, and then uses exactly the same 20 problems in the final exam. Everyone who memorised the answers gets full marks, and the teacher learns nothing about who can actually solve problems. A good teacher keeps the exam questions secret until exam day. Machine learning needs the same discipline. If we judge a model on the same examples it learned from, we only measure its memory, not its understanding. This lesson is about how to divide data so that our scores tell the truth.

Generalisation, the thing we actually want: A model is useful only if it performs well on new data it has never seen: next month's customers, tomorrow's weather, a new patient. This ability is called generalisation. The error a model makes on its own training data is called training error. The error it would make on new data from the same source is called generalisation error or test error. Training error is almost always lower, sometimes by a lot. To estimate generalisation error, we need data the model did not train on.

The simplest split, train and test: Take your labelled data, shuffle it randomly, and split it into two parts, for example 80 percent for training and 20 percent for testing. Train the model only on the training part. Then measure its performance on the test part once. Because the model never saw those examples, the test score is an honest estimate of how it will do on new data, provided the new data comes from a similar distribution.

Why we also need a validation set: In practice you do not train just one model. You try several algorithms and many settings: tree depth 3, 5 or 10, learning rate 0.1 or 0.01, which features to include. If you pick the best setting by looking at the test score, you have quietly used the test set to make decisions. After trying 50 settings, the winner might simply be the one that got lucky on those particular test examples. The test score is now biased upwards. The fix is a third part, the validation set (also called the development or dev set), used for all choices during development. The test set stays locked until the very end.

The three roles: The training set is used to learn the parameters, the numbers inside the model, such as weights. The validation set is used to choose hyperparameters, the settings outside the model, and to compare models and features. The test set is used once, at the end, to report final performance. A useful mental picture: training set is the textbook, validation set is the mock test you take many times, test set is the board exam you sit once.

Worked example, a 70/15/15 split: You have 1000 labelled loan applications. A common split is 70 percent training, 15 percent validation, 15 percent test. That gives 0.70 times 1000 = 700 training rows, 0.15 times 1000 = 150 validation rows and 150 test rows. Other common splits are 60/20/20 and 80/10/10. With millions of rows, even 1 percent for test may be enough (that is still 10000 or more examples), so very large datasets often use 98/1/1. The question to ask is: is the validation and test set large enough to measure the differences I care about?

How big should the test set be?: A test set of 20 examples gives a very noisy estimate. If a model gets 18 out of 20 right, the accuracy is 90 percent, but a single extra mistake changes it to 85 percent. With 1000 test examples, one mistake changes accuracy by only 0.1 percentage points. So small test sets make it impossible to tell apart models that differ by a few percent. When data is small, k-fold cross-validation (lesson 13) uses the data more efficiently by rotating which part is held out.

Random split and the random seed: Usually the rows are shuffled before splitting, so each part is a fair sample. Shuffling uses a random number generator; if you fix its starting value, called the seed, you get the same split every time you rerun the code. That makes experiments reproducible and comparable. Without a fixed seed, two teammates may get different splits and argue about results that differ only because of luck.

Stratified split: Suppose only 10 percent of the 1000 loan applicants defaulted, so 100 defaults and 900 non-defaults. A purely random 15 percent test set should contain about 15 defaults, but by chance it might contain 8 or 22. With so few positives, that changes results a lot. A stratified split keeps the class proportions the same in each part: exactly 10 percent defaults in each. So the training set of 700 gets 70 defaults, the validation set of 150 gets 15, and the test set of 150 gets 15. Stratification is especially important for imbalanced classes (lesson 14).

Time-based split: When data has a time order, such as daily sales, electricity demand or stock prices, a random split cheats. If you randomly mix days, the model might train on 12 March and 14 March and then be tested on 13 March, effectively peeking at the future around it. In real use you always predict the future from the past. So for time series, train on older data and test on newer data: for example, train on January 2023 to June 2024, validate on July to September 2024, test on October to December 2024. This gives a realistic and usually less flattering score.

Group split: Sometimes several rows belong to the same person or object: many X-ray images from the same patient, many transactions from the same customer, many photos of the same cow. If the same patient appears in both training and test sets, the model can recognise the patient rather than the disease, and the test score looks too good. A group split puts all rows from one patient into the same part. Ask yourself: in real use, will the model meet completely new patients, customers or places? If yes, split by group.

Data leakage, the silent killer: Leakage happens when information that would not be available at prediction time, or information from the test set, sneaks into training. The model then looks brilliant in testing and fails in the real world. Leakage is one of the most common reasons why ML projects disappoint after launch. There are two big families: target leakage and train-test contamination.

Target leakage: A feature that is a consequence of the target, or recorded after it, gives the answer away. Example: predicting whether a patient has pneumonia using a feature 'took antibiotics', where antibiotics were given after diagnosis. The model learns 'antibiotics means pneumonia', which is useless for diagnosis. Another example: predicting loan default using 'number of reminder calls made', when the calls only happen after a missed payment. A good check: for every feature, ask 'when exactly is this value known?'. If the answer is after the moment of prediction, drop it.

Train-test contamination: This happens when preprocessing uses the whole dataset before splitting. If you compute the mean for scaling, the median for imputation, or select the 'best' features using all rows, the test rows have influenced training. The fix is simple: split first, then fit every preprocessing step on the training set only, and apply the fitted steps to validation and test. Libraries such as scikit-learn offer pipelines that bundle preprocessing with the model so this happens automatically (lesson 24). Duplicates that land in both sets are another form of contamination.

When the test set is used up: If you look at the test score, go back, change the model and test again many times, the test set slowly turns into a validation set. Its score is no longer an honest estimate. In serious projects and competitions, the final test set is kept by someone else or hidden behind a server so you cannot peek. If you have to iterate after seeing the test score, it is better to collect a fresh test set later.

Distribution shift: All splitting assumes that future data looks like past data. If a model trained on data from before a pandemic is used during one, or a crop model trained on normal years is used in a flood year, even a perfect split cannot protect you. Keep this in mind when reporting results: 'accuracy 92 percent on held-out 2024 data from Dhaka division' is more honest than just '92 percent'.

A complete recipe in pseudo-code: Putting it all together, a safe workflow looks like this. data = load(); train, temp = split(data, 70 percent, stratify by label, seed 42); val, test = split(temp, 50 percent, stratify, seed 42); scaler = fit_scaler(train); model = train_model(scaler(train)); for each setting: score on scaler(val), keep the best; finally, report score of best model on scaler(test), once. Notice the order: the split happens first, every 'fit' touches only the training rows, and the test rows are used in exactly one line at the very end. If you ever see the test set appearing inside a loop, alarm bells should ring.

Real example 1, a crop disease classifier: An agriculture startup collects leaf photos from farms in Rangpur and Dinajpur, labelled healthy or diseased. Several photos come from each field. A random split puts photos of the same field in both training and test, and accuracy looks like 98 percent. A group split by field drops it to 88 percent, a more realistic number for new farms. Testing separately on photos from Jashore, a district not in training at all, reveals another drop, telling the team they need more varied data.

Real example 2, forecasting electricity demand: A power distribution company predicts tomorrow's demand for a city. The team uses data from 2021 to 2023 for training, the first half of 2024 for validation (choosing features and model settings), and the second half of 2024 as the test set. A random split would have reported a much smaller error, because the model could interpolate between neighbouring days instead of truly forecasting.

Common mistakes and exam questions: Tuning on the test set. Splitting after scaling or imputing. Random splitting of time series. Letting the same person or object appear in both training and test. Forgetting stratification with rare classes. Reporting only training accuracy. Typical exam questions: explain the roles of training, validation and test sets; compute the sizes of a split; define data leakage with an example; explain why time series must be split by time.

Recap: Split data before doing anything else. Use the training set to learn parameters, the validation set to choose hyperparameters and models, and the test set once at the end. Stratify for imbalanced classes, split by time for time series and by group when rows share an entity. Fit preprocessing on training data only, and hunt for features that would not be known at prediction time. An honest split is what makes every number in the rest of this course meaningful. Next lesson, we train our first real model: linear regression.
key_points: Generalisation means performing well on unseen data; training error alone hides overfitting.
Training set learns parameters, validation set chooses hyperparameters and models, test set is used once at the end.
A 70/15/15 split of 1000 rows gives 700 / 150 / 150; huge datasets can use tiny test fractions.
Stratified splits keep class proportions equal in every part (10 percent positives everywhere).
Time series must be split by time (past for training, future for testing); shared entities need a group split.
Data leakage: target leakage uses features known only after the outcome; contamination comes from preprocessing on all data.
Split first, then fit scaling, imputation and feature selection on the training set only.
lessons.tip: For every feature in your table, write down the exact moment its value becomes known. Any feature known after the moment of prediction is leakage and must go.
lessons.task: You have 2000 rows of daily rickshaw fare data for five years, with 8 percent of rows marked as 'festival days'. Write a split plan: sizes for training, validation and test, whether to split randomly, stratified or by time, and one possible leakage risk.

quiz.q: Which set should be used to choose the depth of a decision tree?
quiz.explain: Hyperparameters are chosen on validation data; the test set must stay untouched until the end.

quiz.q: 1000 rows are split 70/15/15. How many rows are in the validation set?
quiz.explain: 15 percent of 1000 is 150.

quiz.q: Why is a random split a bad idea for daily electricity demand data?
options: The model can use nearby future days during training, which is not possible in real forecasting
Random splits are always too small
quiz.explain: Forecasting means predicting the future from the past, so the split must respect time order.

quiz.q: Computing the scaling mean on the full dataset before splitting causes:
quiz.explain: Test rows influence the preprocessing, so the test score becomes optimistic.

quiz.q: A dataset has 100 positives out of 1000. With a stratified 150-row test set, how many positives does it contain?
quiz.explain: Stratification keeps 10 percent positives: 10 percent of 150 is 15.

lessons.title: Linear Regression and Least Squares
lessons.content:
Walk around Mirpur looking for a flat and you quickly get a feeling: bigger flats cost more rent, roughly in proportion. If a 500 square foot flat is 10 thousand taka and a 1100 square foot flat is 20 thousand, you can guess that 800 square feet will be somewhere around 15 thousand. Without realising it, you have drawn a straight line through the data in your head. Linear regression is that idea made precise: find the best straight line through the data and use it to predict. It is the oldest and simplest ML model, and it teaches the core ideas that every bigger model uses.

What regression means: Regression is supervised learning where the target is a number: rent, temperature, yield, price. We have training pairs (x, y) and want a function that, given a new x, predicts y. Linear regression assumes the relationship is (approximately) a straight line. In statistics you may have met the least squares line in the Probability and Statistics course; here we look at it as a machine learning model, with an eye on how it is trained and evaluated.

The model: For one input feature, the hypothesis is y_hat = w x + b. The hat on y_hat means 'predicted value'. w is the weight or slope: how much y changes when x increases by 1. b is the bias or intercept: the predicted y when x = 0. Learning means choosing w and b. With many features x1, x2, ..., xd, the model becomes y_hat = w1 x1 + w2 x2 + ... + wd xd + b, a flat plane or hyperplane instead of a line. Each weight tells the effect of its feature while the others are held fixed.

Residuals, how wrong a line is: For each training example, the residual (error) is e = y - y_hat, the vertical gap between the real point and the line. A good line has small residuals. But we need one number to compare lines. Simply adding the residuals does not work, because positive and negative errors cancel: a terrible line could have residuals +10 and -10 summing to zero. So we square them. The sum of squared errors is SSE = sum of (y - y_hat) squared. Dividing by the number of examples n gives the mean squared error, MSE. The least squares line is the line with the smallest possible SSE.

Why squares?: Squaring makes every error positive, punishes big errors much more than small ones (an error of 4 counts as 16, four times worse than an error of 2), and gives a smooth function whose minimum we can find with calculus. Under the assumption that the noise in y is bell-shaped (Gaussian), least squares also matches the most likely line in a statistical sense. The downside: a single wild outlier, squared, can pull the line a lot. Lesson 07 compares alternatives.

The formulas: Setting the derivatives of SSE with respect to w and b to zero gives the closed-form solution. Let x_bar and y_bar be the means of x and y. Then w = sum of (x - x_bar)(y - y_bar) divided by sum of (x - x_bar) squared, and b = y_bar - w x_bar. The second formula says the best line always passes through the point (x_bar, y_bar), the centre of the data. The numerator measures how x and y move together (it is n - 1 times the sample covariance) and the denominator measures how spread out x is.

Worked example, the data: Five flats, with x = size in hundreds of square feet and y = rent in thousand taka: (5, 10), (6, 12), (8, 15), (10, 19), (11, 20). These are invented but realistic-looking numbers. The means are x_bar = (5 + 6 + 8 + 10 + 11) / 5 = 40 / 5 = 8 and y_bar = (10 + 12 + 15 + 19 + 20) / 5 = 76 / 5 = 15.2.

Worked example, the slope: Deviations of x from 8 are -3, -2, 0, 2, 3. Deviations of y from 15.2 are -5.2, -3.2, -0.2, 3.8, 4.8. Multiply pairwise: (-3)(-5.2) = 15.6, (-2)(-3.2) = 6.4, (0)(-0.2) = 0, (2)(3.8) = 7.6, (3)(4.8) = 14.4. The sum is 44. The squared x deviations are 9, 4, 0, 4, 9, summing to 26. So w = 44 / 26 = 1.692 (to three decimals). Each extra 100 square feet adds about 1.69 thousand taka of rent.

Worked example, the intercept and a prediction: b = y_bar - w x_bar = 15.2 - 1.692 times 8 = 15.2 - 13.538 = 1.662. The fitted line is rent = 1.692 times size + 1.662. For a 900 square foot flat, size = 9, so predicted rent = 1.692 times 9 + 1.662 = 15.23 + 1.66 = 16.89 thousand taka, about 16900 taka. Notice that the intercept should not be read literally as 'a flat of zero size costs 1662 taka'; size 0 is far outside the data. Predicting far outside the range of training x values, called extrapolation, is risky for every model.

Worked example, residuals and error: The predictions for the five flats are 10.123, 11.815, 15.2, 18.585 and 20.277. The residuals y - y_hat are -0.123, 0.185, -0.2, 0.415 and -0.277. Their squares add up to SSE = 0.338, and MSE = 0.338 / 5 = 0.068. The root mean squared error RMSE is the square root of MSE, about 0.26 thousand taka, roughly 260 taka, in the same units as rent, which makes it easy to explain. A nice property to check: the residuals of a least squares line with an intercept always sum to zero (here -0.123 + 0.185 - 0.2 + 0.415 - 0.277 = 0).

R squared, how much is explained: Compare our line with the simplest baseline, always predicting y_bar. The baseline's total squared error is SST = sum of (y - y_bar) squared = 27.04 + 10.24 + 0.04 + 14.44 + 23.04 = 74.8. Our line leaves SSE = 0.338. So R squared = 1 - SSE / SST = 1 - 0.338 / 74.8 = 0.9955. The line explains about 99.5 percent of the variation in rent in this data. R squared is 1 for a perfect fit, 0 for a model no better than the mean, and it can even be negative on new data for a model worse than the mean. A high R squared on training data does not prove the model will generalise, and it does not prove that x causes y.

Multiple linear regression: Real rent depends on more than size: number of rooms, floor, distance to the main road, whether there is a lift. With d features, we stack the training inputs into a matrix X (n rows, d + 1 columns including a column of 1s for the bias) and the targets into a vector y. The least squares solution can be written as w = (X transpose X) inverse X transpose y, the normal equation. You do not need to memorise matrix calculus now; the point is that there is an exact formula. In practice libraries solve it with numerically stable methods rather than computing an inverse directly.

When the exact formula is not enough: The normal equation needs to work with a d by d matrix, which becomes slow when d is very large (tens of thousands of features), and it fails if features are perfectly redundant (for example, area in square feet and the same area in square metres), because X transpose X then has no inverse. Also, for most other models (logistic regression, neural networks) no closed-form formula exists at all. That is why the next lesson introduces gradient descent, a general method that improves parameters step by step.

Interpreting weights: In y_hat = 1.692 x + 1.662, the weight 1.692 has a clear meaning: thousand taka per hundred square feet. With multiple features, a weight means the change in prediction for a one-unit change in that feature with all other features fixed. Be careful comparing weights of features on different scales; a weight on 'size in square feet' looks tiny next to a weight on 'number of lifts' just because of units. Standardising features first makes weights more comparable. And again, weights show association in this data, not proof of cause.

Assumptions and limits: Linear regression works best when the relationship is roughly linear, errors are independent, their spread is similar across x, and there are no extreme outliers dominating. If the pattern is curved, a straight line underfits; lesson 08 adds polynomial features to bend it. If features are strongly correlated with each other (multicollinearity), individual weights become unstable even if predictions are fine; regularisation (lesson 10) helps.

Real example 1, predicting electricity bills: A housing society in Uttara collects monthly data: units consumed and number of air conditioners in each flat. A linear model bill = w1 times units + w2 times ACs + b would mostly rediscover the tariff, but adding a feature for month (summer versus winter) can help predict next month's bill from usage so far. The residuals show which flats are surprisingly expensive, maybe because of a faulty meter.

Real example 2, rice yield and fertiliser: An agriculture officer records urea used (kg per hectare) and Boro yield (tonnes per hectare) on demonstration plots. A fitted line shows the average yield increase per extra 10 kg of urea within the tested range. But extrapolating beyond the tested range is dangerous: too much fertiliser does not keep increasing yield forever, and the real curve bends. This is a reminder that a linear model is a local approximation.

Common mistakes and exam questions: Mixing up which variable is x and which is y. Forgetting that b = y_bar - w x_bar. Summing residuals instead of squared residuals. Reading the intercept literally far outside the data. Believing high R squared means causation. Typical exam questions: compute the least squares line for 4 to 6 points, predict a value, compute residuals, SSE, MSE and R squared, and explain what the normal equation is and when gradient descent is preferred.

Recap: Linear regression predicts a number with y_hat = w x + b (or a weighted sum of many features). Least squares chooses w and b to minimise the sum of squared residuals, with w = sum((x - x_bar)(y - y_bar)) / sum((x - x_bar) squared) and b = y_bar - w x_bar. In our flat example, w = 1.692, b = 1.662, MSE = 0.068 and R squared = 0.9955. With many features, the normal equation gives an exact answer, but for big problems and other models we need an iterative method. That method, gradient descent, is the next lesson. Keep the flat data handy: we will reuse the same idea of minimising squared error, but this time we will walk downhill towards the answer instead of jumping straight to it with a formula.
key_points: Linear regression predicts a number with y_hat = w x + b, or a weighted sum of several features.
Residual e = y - y_hat; least squares minimises SSE, the sum of squared residuals (MSE = SSE / n).
Closed form: w = sum((x - x_bar)(y - y_bar)) / sum((x - x_bar)^2), b = y_bar - w x_bar.
Worked flats example: w = 44 / 26 = 1.692, b = 1.662, prediction for size 9 is about 16.89 thousand taka.
R squared = 1 - SSE / SST compares the model with always predicting the mean (here 0.9955).
The normal equation w = (X^T X)^(-1) X^T y solves multiple regression exactly, but is slow or fails for huge or redundant features.
Weights show association, not causation; extrapolation far outside the data is risky.
lessons.tip: Always sanity-check a fitted line: the residuals should sum to (nearly) zero and the line should pass through (x_bar, y_bar). If either fails, there is an arithmetic slip.
lessons.task: Collect five pairs from daily life, such as distance in km and CNG or bus fare in taka for five trips. Compute the least squares slope and intercept by hand, predict the fare for a new distance, and compute the residuals and R squared.

quiz.q: For the least squares line, which point is the line guaranteed to pass through?
quiz.explain: b = y_bar - w x_bar means y_hat at x_bar equals y_bar.

quiz.q: Why does least squares square the residuals instead of just adding them?
options: So that positive and negative errors do not cancel, and big errors are punished more
So that outliers have less effect
quiz.explain: Squaring makes every error positive and weights large errors heavily (which also makes outliers influential).

quiz.q: With x_bar = 8, y_bar = 15.2 and w = 1.692, what is b (approximately)?
A model has SSE = 20 and SST = 80 on its data. What is R squared?
When is gradient descent preferred over the normal equation for linear regression?
options: When there are a very large number of features
When there are only two data points
When the data is perfectly linear
Never; the normal equation is always better
quiz.explain: The normal equation works with a d by d matrix, which becomes expensive for huge d; iterative methods scale better.

lessons.title: Gradient Descent: Learning Step by Step
lessons.content:
Imagine you are standing somewhere on the hills of Bandarban at night, in thick fog, and you want to reach the lowest point of the valley. You cannot see the valley. But you can feel the ground under your feet: which direction slopes down most steeply. So you take a step in that direction, feel again, take another step, and keep going until the ground feels flat. That is gradient descent, the most important optimisation method in machine learning. It trains linear regression on huge datasets, logistic regression, and almost every neural network in use today.

The problem it solves: Training a model means finding parameters that make a cost function small. For linear regression the cost is the mean squared error. In lesson 05 we found the best parameters with an exact formula. But for most models no such formula exists, and even for linear regression the formula becomes slow with very many features. We need a general method that only requires two things: the ability to compute the cost, and the ability to compute its slope with respect to each parameter.

The cost surface: Think of the cost J as a landscape over the parameters. With one parameter w, J(w) is a curve; with two parameters, a surface like a bowl or a hilly field; with a million parameters, a landscape in a million dimensions that we cannot picture but can still compute. For linear regression with MSE, the landscape is a nice smooth bowl with exactly one bottom, called convex. Neural network landscapes are bumpier, with many valleys, but gradient descent still works well in practice.

The slope tells the way: From calculus, the derivative dJ/dw tells how J changes when w increases a little. If the derivative is positive, increasing w increases the cost, so we should decrease w. If it is negative, we should increase w. With many parameters, the vector of all partial derivatives is called the gradient. It points in the direction of steepest increase of J. So to go downhill, we move in the opposite direction of the gradient.

The update rule: Repeat: w_new = w_old - alpha times dJ/dw, for every parameter at the same time. Here alpha is the learning rate, a small positive number that controls the step size. The minus sign is what makes it descent. Near the bottom the slope becomes small, so steps automatically become smaller, and at the exact bottom the slope is zero and w stops changing. In pseudo-code: initialise w; repeat many times: compute gradient g; w = w - alpha * g.

Worked example, the setup: Take three points (1, 2), (2, 4) and (3, 6), and the simple model y_hat = w x with no bias. Clearly the perfect answer is w = 2, but let gradient descent find it. The cost is J(w) = (1/3) times the sum of (w x - y) squared. Its derivative is dJ/dw = (2/3) times the sum of (w x - y) times x. Start from w = 0.

Worked example, the first step: At w = 0, every prediction is 0, so the errors w x - y are -2, -4 and -6. The cost is (4 + 16 + 36) / 3 = 56 / 3 = 18.67. The gradient is (2/3) times ((-2)(1) + (-4)(2) + (-6)(3)) = (2/3) times (-2 - 8 - 18) = (2/3) times (-28) = -18.67. The gradient is negative, so we should increase w. With learning rate alpha = 0.05, the new w = 0 - 0.05 times (-18.67) = 0 + 0.933 = 0.933.

Worked example, the next steps: At w = 0.933, the cost has dropped to 5.31. Repeating the update gives w = 1.431, then 1.697, then 1.838, with costs 1.51, 0.43 and 0.12. Each step closes about 47 percent of the remaining gap to 2: the gap goes 2, 1.067, 0.569, 0.303, 0.162. After about 20 steps w is extremely close to 2. This is exactly how training looks in practice: the cost falls quickly at first and then more slowly as you approach the bottom.

Worked example, a learning rate that is too big: Now try alpha = 0.2 from w = 0. The first step gives w = 0 - 0.2 times (-18.67) = 3.733, overshooting past 2 to the other side of the valley. The next steps go 0.498, 3.302, 0.872: bouncing back and forth across the bottom. The cost still falls slowly (18.67, 14.02, 10.53, 7.91, 5.94) because each bounce is a little shorter. With alpha = 0.25, things explode: w goes 4.667, -1.556, 6.741, -4.321, and the cost rises 33.2, 59.0, 104.9, 186.5. Training has diverged. For this cost, any alpha above about 0.214 diverges.

Why that limit?: The gradient here simplifies to (28/3)(w - 2). So each update multiplies the gap (w - 2) by (1 - alpha times 28/3). With alpha = 0.05 the factor is 0.533, so the gap shrinks steadily. With alpha = 0.2 the factor is -0.867: the sign flips (overshoot) but the size still shrinks. With alpha = 0.25 the factor is -1.333, so the gap grows every step. The factor's size is below 1 only when alpha is below 2 divided by 28/3, which is 0.214. Real models have no such tidy formula, but the lesson holds: too small is slow, too large bounces or explodes.

Choosing the learning rate in practice: Try values on a log scale such as 1, 0.1, 0.01, 0.001 and plot the training cost against the number of steps for each. A good rate makes the cost fall smoothly and fairly fast. If the cost goes up or turns into NaN (not a number), the rate is too high. If it creeps down painfully slowly, it is too low. Many practitioners also reduce the learning rate during training (a schedule), taking bigger steps early and smaller steps near the bottom. Adaptive methods such as Adam adjust step sizes per parameter automatically; you will meet them properly in Deep Learning (cse-8-1).

Gradient descent with a bias: For the full model y_hat = w x + b and MSE cost, the two partial derivatives are dJ/dw = (2/n) sum of (y_hat - y) x and dJ/db = (2/n) sum of (y_hat - y). Both are computed using the current w and b, and both parameters are updated together. Notice the pattern: error times input for the weight, just error for the bias. This same pattern reappears in logistic regression (lesson 11) and in the output layer of neural networks (lesson 20).

Batch, stochastic and mini-batch: Batch gradient descent computes the gradient using all n training examples for every step. It is accurate but slow when n is millions. Stochastic gradient descent (SGD) uses just one random example per step: very cheap, very noisy, but the noise averages out over many steps and can even help escape poor regions. Mini-batch gradient descent uses a small batch, such as 32 or 256 examples, per step, combining efficiency on modern hardware with reasonably smooth progress. It is the standard choice for large datasets. One pass over the whole training set is called an epoch.

When to stop: Common stopping rules are a fixed number of epochs, the cost changing by less than a tiny amount between steps, the gradient becoming very small, or, very importantly, the validation error starting to rise (early stopping, lesson 10). Without some rule, you either stop too early with an undertrained model or waste time.

Why scaling helps: If one feature ranges 0 to 1 and another 0 to 100000, the cost landscape becomes a long, narrow valley. The gradient points mostly across the valley, not along it, so gradient descent zigzags and needs a tiny learning rate to stay stable. After standardising features (lesson 03), the valley becomes rounder and gradient descent walks almost straight to the bottom. This is one of the most practical reasons for scaling.

Local minima and saddle points: In a convex bowl, like the MSE cost of linear regression, there is only one bottom, so gradient descent with a sensible learning rate always reaches the best answer. Other models have landscapes with several valleys. Gradient descent may settle in a local minimum, a valley that is lowest only in its neighbourhood, or slow down on a flat area or saddle point, where the ground slopes down in one direction and up in another. Starting from different random initial values, using the noise of stochastic or mini-batch updates, and momentum (which keeps some of the previous step's direction, like a ball rolling downhill) all help. For large neural networks, researchers have found that many local minima give similarly good results, so this problem is less scary than it sounds.

Checking your gradient by hand: If you write gradient code yourself, a classic bug check is the numerical gradient. Pick a tiny number h, such as 0.0001, and compute (J(w + h) - J(w - h)) / (2h). This should almost exactly equal your formula's derivative. In our example at w = 0, J(0.0001) - J(-0.0001) is about -0.0037, and dividing by 0.0002 gives about -18.67, matching the formula. If they disagree, your derivative code has a bug. This trick is slow, so it is only used for testing, never for actual training.

Real example 1, an online shop's rating predictor: A Bangladeshi e-commerce site with millions of past orders wants to predict a customer's product rating. Solving a giant normal equation is impractical, so the team trains a linear model with mini-batch gradient descent: batches of 512 orders, standardised features, learning rate 0.01 found by trying a few values, and early stopping on validation error. Each epoch takes minutes instead of the hours an exact solve might need.

Real example 2, your phone keyboard: Next-word suggestions are produced by neural network models trained with variants of mini-batch gradient descent on huge text collections. The same 'compute gradient, take a small step' loop, repeated a very large number of times, is what turns random initial weights into a model that suggests 'kemon acho' after you type 'Hi'.

Common mistakes and exam questions: Forgetting the minus sign (that is gradient ascent). Updating w and then using the new w to compute the gradient for b in the same step, instead of updating both together. Learning rate too large, causing divergence. Not scaling features. Confusing an epoch with a step. Exam favourites: write the update rule, perform one or two steps by hand for a tiny dataset, explain the effect of the learning rate with a sketch, and compare batch, stochastic and mini-batch versions.

Recap: Gradient descent minimises a cost by repeatedly stepping opposite to the gradient: w = w - alpha times dJ/dw. In our worked example on (1, 2), (2, 4), (3, 6), alpha = 0.05 moved w from 0 to 0.933 to 1.431 and on towards 2, alpha = 0.2 bounced, and alpha = 0.25 diverged. Choose the learning rate by experiment, scale features, use mini-batches for big data, and stop with a sensible rule. Next lesson asks a question we have been skipping: which cost should we be minimising in the first place?
key_points: Gradient descent minimises a cost by stepping opposite to the gradient: w = w - alpha times dJ/dw.
The gradient points uphill; its negative points to the steepest descent; at the minimum it is zero.
Worked: on (1,2),(2,4),(3,6) with y_hat = w x, the first gradient at w = 0 is -18.67, so alpha = 0.05 gives w = 0.933.
Too small a learning rate is slow; too large overshoots (alpha = 0.2 bounces) or diverges (alpha = 0.25).
For MSE with a bias: dJ/dw = (2/n) sum(error times x), dJ/db = (2/n) sum(error); update both together.
Batch uses all data per step, stochastic uses one example, mini-batch uses a small batch; one pass over data is an epoch.
Feature scaling turns a narrow valley into a round bowl, so gradient descent converges much faster.
lessons.tip: When training any model, always plot the cost against the step number. That one plot instantly tells you if the learning rate is too high (rising or jumping), too low (crawling) or about right (smooth, fast drop that levels off).
lessons.task: Using the points (1, 3), (2, 6) and (3, 9) and the model y_hat = w x starting from w = 0, do three gradient descent steps by hand with alpha = 0.05. Then repeat with alpha = 0.3 and describe what happens.

quiz.q: In the update w = w - alpha times dJ/dw, what is alpha?
quiz.explain: Alpha is the learning rate: it scales the size of each step.

quiz.q: If dJ/dw is negative at the current w, what does gradient descent do?
quiz.explain: w - alpha times (a negative number) is larger than w, so w increases, which lowers the cost.

quiz.q: Training cost goes 10, 25, 70, 300 over the first steps. The most likely cause is:
options: The learning rate is too high
The model has too few parameters
quiz.explain: A rising, exploding cost is the classic sign of divergence from a too-large learning rate.

quiz.q: Which version of gradient descent uses a small group of examples, such as 32, per step?
options: Stochastic gradient descent with one example
quiz.explain: Mini-batch uses small batches, balancing speed and stability; it is the standard for large data.

quiz.q: Why does feature scaling help gradient descent?
options: It reduces the number of features
It turns a long narrow valley into a rounder bowl so steps head more directly to the minimum
It removes the need for a learning rate
It guarantees the global minimum for any model
quiz.explain: With similar feature scales, the gradient points more directly at the minimum, avoiding zigzags.

lessons.title: Loss Functions: Measuring How Wrong a Model Is
lessons.content:
When a cricket coach gives feedback, how they score mistakes shapes how the player trains. If every dropped catch costs one point no matter what, the fielder treats all chances equally. If dropping a catch off the final over costs ten points, the fielder will focus hard on pressure moments. Machine learning models are the same. The loss function is the coach's scoring rule. Gradient descent will do whatever it takes to make the loss small, so the loss you choose quietly decides what the model cares about. Choose it badly and you get a model that is excellent at the wrong thing.

Loss, cost and metric: Three words that are often mixed up. A loss function measures the error on a single example, for example (y - y_hat) squared. A cost function (also called the objective) combines the losses over the training set, usually by averaging, and may add extra terms such as a regularisation penalty (lesson 10). A metric is what humans use to judge the model, such as accuracy or MAE in taka. Sometimes the metric and the loss are the same; often they are not, because the metric might not be smooth enough for gradient descent. For example, accuracy jumps in steps, so we train with a smooth loss and report accuracy.

What makes a good loss: It should measure what we actually care about, be small when predictions are good, and for gradient-based training it should be smooth enough to have useful slopes almost everywhere. It also helps if it is convex for simple models, so there is a single best answer. Different problems call for different losses, and some losses are more sensitive to outliers than others.

Mean squared error (MSE): The loss for one example is (y - y_hat) squared; the cost is the average over all examples. We used it for linear regression.
