It is smooth and convex for linear models, and its gradient is simple: proportional to the error. Its key personality trait: because errors are squared, big errors dominate. An error of 10 contributes 100, as much as a hundred errors of 1. This is good when large errors are truly much worse, for example when predicting a bridge's load. It is bad when the data contains outliers you do not trust.

Mean absolute error (MAE): The loss is |y - y_hat|, the absolute error, averaged over examples. Every taka of error counts the same, whether it is part of a small or a big miss. So MAE is far less pulled by outliers. It is also easy to explain: 'on average we are off by 6 cups of tea'. Its drawback for training is the sharp corner at zero error, where the slope suddenly jumps from -1 to +1, which can make gradient-based optimisation less smooth near the solution. In practice this is usually manageable.

Worked example, outlier sensitivity: A model makes these errors on five test days: 1, -2, 1, 0 and 10. The last one is a strange day, maybe a data entry mistake. MSE = (1 + 4 + 1 + 0 + 100) / 5 = 106 / 5 = 21.2. MAE = (1 + 2 + 1 + 0 + 10) / 5 = 14 / 5 = 2.8. Now suppose the strange day is corrected and its error becomes 2. MSE = (1 + 4 + 1 + 0 + 4) / 5 = 10 / 5 = 2, and MAE = (1 + 2 + 1 + 0 + 2) / 5 = 6 / 5 = 1.2. One bad point made MSE more than ten times bigger, but MAE only a bit more than double. A model trained on MSE would work very hard to reduce that one error, possibly at the cost of all the others.

Mean versus median, a deeper link: Suppose a model can only predict one constant number for everybody. Which constant minimises MSE? The mean of the targets. Which minimises MAE? The median. For targets 2, 3, 4, 5 and 36 (one rich outlier), the mean is 50 / 5 = 10, while the median is 4. MSE-trained models chase the mean and get dragged by outliers; MAE-trained models behave like the median. This one fact explains a lot about how the two losses behave.

Huber loss, the best of both: Huber loss acts like squared error for small errors and like absolute error for large ones. With a threshold delta: if |e| is at most delta, the loss is 0.5 e squared; otherwise it is delta times (|e| - 0.5 delta). With delta = 1 and our errors 1, -2, 1, 0, 10: the losses are 0.5, 1 times (2 - 0.5) = 1.5, 0.5, 0, and 1 times (10 - 0.5) = 9.5. The average is 12 / 5 = 2.4. The outlier now adds 9.5 instead of 100. Huber is smooth near zero like MSE and robust to outliers like MAE. You choose delta to say what counts as 'large'.

RMSE and reporting: The root mean squared error, RMSE, is the square root of MSE. It has the same unit as the target, so an RMSE of 0.26 thousand taka is easy to read. RMSE is always at least as big as MAE; a big gap between them is a hint that a few large errors exist. When you report regression results, give MAE or RMSE in real units and compare with the baseline from lesson 02.

Losses for classification, the 0-1 loss: For classification the most natural loss is the 0-1 loss: 0 if the predicted class is right, 1 if it is wrong. Its average is the error rate, 1 minus accuracy. The trouble is that it is flat almost everywhere and jumps at the decision boundary, so its gradient is zero or undefined. Gradient descent gets no hint about which direction improves things. So we train classifiers with smooth stand-ins, called surrogate losses, and still report accuracy and related metrics.

Log loss (cross-entropy), a preview: Many classifiers output a probability p that the example belongs to class 1. Log loss for one example is -log(p) if the true label is 1 and -log(1 - p) if it is 0 (natural logarithm). If the true label is 1 and the model says p = 0.9, the loss is -log(0.9) = 0.105, small. If it says p = 0.1, the loss is -log(0.1) = 2.303, much bigger. If it says p = 0.5, a shrug, the loss is 0.693. Confident wrong answers are punished very heavily, which pushes the model to be honest about its uncertainty. Lesson 11 uses this loss to train logistic regression.

Why not just use MSE for classification?: You could code the classes as 0 and 1 and fit a regression with squared error, and people sometimes try. But squared error punishes a prediction of 3 for a true label of 1 as badly as a prediction of -1, even though 3 is 'very confidently correct'. Such points pull the boundary in strange directions. Paired with a sigmoid output, squared error also gives weak gradients when the model is confidently wrong, so learning stalls exactly when it should be fastest. Log loss does not have these problems, which is why it is the standard choice for probabilistic classifiers.

Hinge loss, a preview: Support vector machines use the hinge loss. With labels written as +1 and -1 and a raw score s from the model, the loss is max(0, 1 - y times s). If the true label is +1 and the score is 2, the loss is max(0, 1 - 2) = 0: correct with a comfortable margin, so no penalty. If the score is 0.3, the loss is 0.7: correct side but too close to the boundary. If the score is -1, the loss is 2: wrong side. Hinge loss rewards not just being right but being right with a safety margin, as lesson 19 explains.

Asymmetric costs: Sometimes over-prediction and under-prediction are not equally bad. A pharmacy forecasting medicine demand might lose more from running out (patients go without) than from overstocking a little. You can then use an asymmetric loss that charges more for under-predicting. A family of such losses, called quantile or pinball loss, lets a model predict a chosen percentile instead of the average, for example 'a demand level we will exceed only 10 percent of the time'. For classification, the same idea becomes class weights (lesson 14).

Matching the loss to the business: Ask what a mistake costs in the real world. For a ride-sharing app estimating arrival time, being 5 minutes late may annoy users more than being 5 minutes early, and a 30 minute miss destroys trust, so you might use Huber or a mild asymmetric loss. For estimating the number of flood shelter places, under-estimation is dangerous. For predicting a probability that will be used for decisions, log loss keeps probabilities well calibrated. The loss is a design decision, not a default.

Real example 1, delivery time prediction: A food delivery app in Dhaka predicts delivery times. Its historical data includes a few orders that took four hours due to a rider's phone dying. Training with MSE, the model inflates estimates for everyone to partly cover these freak cases, and customers see pessimistic times. Switching to Huber loss (or MAE) makes typical estimates more accurate while ignoring most of the freak cases' pull. The team reports MAE in minutes, plus the share of orders that arrived more than 15 minutes late.

Real example 2, flood probability: A district disaster office uses a model to estimate the probability that a union will flood in the next three days, to plan boat and shelter allocation. The model is trained with log loss so that a predicted 70 percent really means about 70 percent in practice. A model trained only to maximise accuracy might say 'no flood' everywhere in a dry year and look accurate, yet give useless probabilities when it matters.

Common mistakes and exam questions: Confusing loss (one example) with cost (average plus penalties) and metric (what you report). Using MSE with untrusted outliers. Trying to train directly on accuracy. Forgetting that log loss uses the natural logarithm and that it explodes for confident wrong answers. Reporting MSE in squared units and confusing readers. Exams ask: compute MSE, MAE and RMSE for a list of errors; explain why MSE is sensitive to outliers; compute log loss for given probabilities; explain why the 0-1 loss is not used for gradient-based training.

Recap: The loss decides what the model cares about. MSE punishes large errors heavily and follows the mean; MAE treats all errors equally and follows the median; Huber blends them. With errors 1, -2, 1, 0, 10, MSE is 21.2 while MAE is 2.8 and Huber (delta 1) is 2.4. For classification, the 0-1 loss is what we care about but cannot train on directly, so we use surrogates such as log loss and hinge loss. Next, we bend our straight lines into curves with polynomial regression and meet the twin dangers of underfitting and overfitting.
key_points: A loss scores one example, a cost averages losses (plus penalties), and a metric is what you report to people.
MSE squares errors, so large errors and outliers dominate; MAE counts every unit of error equally.
Worked: errors 1, -2, 1, 0, 10 give MSE 21.2 and MAE 2.8; fixing the outlier gives MSE 2 and MAE 1.2.
The best constant prediction is the mean under MSE and the median under MAE.
Huber loss is quadratic for small errors and linear for large ones (here average 2.4 with delta 1).
The 0-1 loss has no useful gradient, so classifiers train on surrogates such as log loss and hinge loss.
Log loss: -log(0.9) = 0.105 for a confident right answer, -log(0.1) = 2.303 for a confident wrong one.
Choose the loss from the real cost of mistakes, including asymmetric costs.
lessons.tip: Whenever you report a regression model, write MAE and RMSE side by side. If RMSE is much larger than MAE, look for a handful of huge errors before trusting the model.
lessons.task: Write down how many minutes late your bus or class started on seven different days (use 0 for on time). Treat these as errors and compute MSE, MAE, RMSE and Huber loss with delta = 2. Which number best describes your experience?

quiz.q: Errors on four examples are 2, -2, 2 and -2. What is the MSE?
quiz.explain: Each squared error is 4, so the average is 16 / 4 = 4.

quiz.q: Which loss is LEAST affected by a single huge outlier?
quiz.explain: MAE grows linearly with each error, so one large error cannot dominate the way it does when squared.

quiz.q: If a model must predict one constant value for all examples, which constant minimises MAE?
quiz.explain: The median minimises the sum of absolute deviations; the mean minimises squared deviations.

quiz.q: True label is 1 and the model predicts p = 0.1. The log loss (natural log) is about:
quiz.explain: -log(0.1) = 2.303, a large penalty for a confident wrong prediction.

quiz.q: Why are classifiers not usually trained directly on the 0-1 loss?
options: It is too slow to compute
It gives probabilities instead of classes
It is flat with jumps, so it gives no useful gradient
quiz.explain: Gradient descent needs slopes; the 0-1 loss is piecewise constant, so we use smooth surrogates.

lessons.title: Polynomial Regression, Underfitting and Overfitting
lessons.content:
Three students prepare for a maths exam. The first reads only the chapter titles and answers every question with the same formula; he fails because his understanding is too simple. The second practises problems, understands the patterns and does well on new questions. The third memorises every practice answer including the typing mistakes in the solution book; she gets full marks on the practice sheet but stumbles on new questions. In machine learning these are underfitting, a good fit and overfitting. This lesson shows all three with real numbers, using a tool that lets us control how complex a model is: polynomial regression.

When a straight line is not enough: Many relationships curve. Crop yield rises with fertiliser and then levels off. The distance a car needs to stop grows faster than its speed. Electricity demand dips at moderate temperatures and rises at both cold and hot extremes. A straight line cannot follow these shapes, no matter how well it is trained. Its errors will show a pattern, for example positive at both ends and negative in the middle, a clear sign that the model family is too simple.

The trick, new features: Polynomial regression keeps linear regression's machinery but adds new features made from powers of x. Instead of y_hat = w1 x + b, we use y_hat = w1 x + w2 x squared + b for degree 2, or add x cubed for degree 3, and so on. The model is still linear in its weights, so least squares and gradient descent work exactly as before; we have only changed the features. The curve comes from the features, not from a new algorithm. This is a powerful general idea: feature engineering can give a simple model a complex shape.

Degree as a complexity dial: Degree 1 is a line, degree 2 a parabola that can bend once, degree 3 can bend twice, and in general a degree d polynomial can bend d - 1 times. A higher degree means more parameters and more flexibility. With n training points, a polynomial of degree n - 1 can pass exactly through every one of them. That sounds wonderful but, as we will see, it is usually a disaster.

Worked example, the data: Four training points, invented for this example: (0, 1), (1, 2.5), (2, 4.5) and (3, 10.5). Secretly, they were made from the true pattern y = x squared + 1 with a bit of noise added, so the true values would be 1, 2, 5 and 10. We keep one extra point for validation: (4, 17), which lies exactly on the true pattern. Let us fit degrees 1, 2 and 3 by least squares and compare.

Worked example, degree 1 (a line): The best line is y_hat = 3.05 x + 0.05. Its predictions at x = 0, 1, 2, 3 are 0.05, 3.1, 6.15 and 9.2. The training MSE is about 1.42. At the validation point x = 4 it predicts 3.05 times 4 + 0.05 = 12.25, while the truth is 17. The squared error is (17 - 12.25) squared = 22.56. The line is too stiff to follow the upward curve: high training error and high validation error. This is underfitting.

Worked example, degree 2 (a parabola): The least squares parabola is y_hat = 1.175 - 0.325 x + 1.125 x squared. Its training MSE drops to about 0.15. At x = 4 it predicts 1.175 - 1.3 + 18 = 17.875, close to the true 17, with a squared error of only 0.77. This model has the right amount of flexibility: it captures the curve but does not chase every bump of noise. This is a good fit.

Worked example, degree 3 (a cubic): With four points and four parameters, the cubic y_hat = 1 + 2.417 x - 1.5 x squared + 0.583 x cubed passes exactly through all four training points. Training MSE is exactly 0, a perfect score. But at x = 4 it predicts 1 + 9.667 - 24 + 37.333 = 24, far above the true 17, with a squared error of 49, even worse than the line. At x = 5 it would predict 48.5 against a true 26. The cubic has memorised the noise, and the twisting needed to hit every noisy point sends it flying off outside the data. This is overfitting.

Reading the table: Training MSE goes 1.42, 0.15, 0 as the degree rises: it always falls or stays the same, because a more flexible model can always fit training data at least as well. Validation squared error goes 22.6, 0.8, 49: it falls and then rises. This U-shape is the most important picture in machine learning. Training error alone would have chosen the cubic, the worst model here. The validation set chose the parabola, the right one. That is why lesson 04 insisted on holding data out.

Underfitting in general: An underfit model is too simple for the pattern. Symptoms: training error is high, and validation error is similarly high. Adding more data does not help much, because the model cannot use it. Remedies: use a more flexible model (higher degree, deeper tree, bigger network), add better features, or reduce regularisation. In everyday terms: the student needs to learn more concepts, not do more of the same practice.

Overfitting in general: An overfit model is too flexible for the amount of data and fits the noise. Symptoms: very low training error but much higher validation error, a large gap between the two. Remedies: get more training data, use a simpler model (lower degree, shallower tree), add regularisation (lesson 10), use early stopping, or remove useless features. Overfitting is especially likely when the number of parameters is large compared to the number of examples.

Why noise causes overfitting: Every real dataset contains noise: measurement errors, random variation, typing slips. Noise has no pattern, so it cannot be predicted on new data. A model flexible enough to fit the noise exactly is forced to put strange wiggles between and beyond the training points, and those wiggles are pure error on new data. A good model learns the signal and ignores the noise. The art is choosing a level of flexibility that captures the signal but not much noise.

Learning curves: Another diagnostic tool is to plot training and validation error against the number of training examples. For an underfit model, both curves quickly flatten at a high error, close to each other; more data will not help. For an overfit model, training error is low and validation error is high with a big gap, but the gap shrinks as data grows; more data will help. Drawing these curves before collecting more data can save a lot of money and effort.

Model complexity curve: Plotting training and validation error against complexity (here, polynomial degree) gives the classic picture: training error keeps falling, validation error falls, reaches a minimum, then rises. The best model sits at the bottom of the validation curve. Left of it is the underfitting zone, right of it the overfitting zone. You will see the same shape when the dial is tree depth, number of neighbours in k-NN (in reverse), or training epochs for a neural network.

Choosing the degree in practice: The recipe is a small loop. For d in 1, 2, 3, ..., 10: build polynomial features of degree d from the scaled training x; fit least squares on the training set; compute the error on the validation set; remember it. Then pick the d with the lowest validation error, refit on training (or training plus validation) data, and check the test set once. With only a little data, replace the single validation set by k-fold cross-validation (lesson 13), so the choice does not depend on one lucky split. In our tiny example the loop would pick d = 2.

Interpolation versus extrapolation: Look again at the cubic. Between the training points it is not crazy; the damage appears at x = 4 and beyond, outside the training range. Overfit models are often most dangerous exactly where we have no data. Even the good parabola should be used with care far outside x = 0 to 3. Whenever a model is asked about inputs unlike anything in its training data, a far-away district, an unusually large flat, a record-breaking temperature, treat its answer with suspicion.

Occam's razor: An old principle says that among explanations that fit the facts equally well, prefer the simplest. In ML terms: if a degree 2 and a degree 5 model have similar validation error, choose degree 2. Simpler models are easier to explain, faster, and usually more robust when the world changes a little. Simplicity is not a law of nature, but it is a very good default bet.

Practical cautions with polynomials: High-degree polynomial features take huge values: if x is 100, x to the power 5 is ten billion. Always scale x first, or the numbers become unstable. With several input features, polynomial features also include cross terms such as x1 times x2, and their count explodes as the degree grows. In practice, degree 2 or 3 is common, and for complex shapes people turn to trees, splines or neural networks instead.

Real example 1, rice yield versus urea: An agricultural research station measures Boro yield on plots with different urea doses. A straight line suggests 'always more urea, always more rice', which is wrong and wasteful. A degree 2 curve rises, levels off and gently falls at very high doses, matching agronomic experience. A degree 6 curve fits each plot's random variation and recommends an oddly precise dose that changes wildly if one plot is removed. The station picks degree 2 using validation plots.

Real example 2, a student's mock test model: A coaching centre in Chattogram builds a model to predict HSC results from 40 different mock test scores, attendance and other columns, using data from only 60 past students. The model scores almost perfectly on those 60 students but predicts poorly for this year's batch. With more features than the data can support, the model memorised the past batch. Using fewer, meaningful features and more years of data gives a weaker-looking but more honest model.

Common mistakes and exam questions: Picking the model with the lowest training error. Assuming more complex always means better. Forgetting that polynomial regression is still linear regression on new features. Not scaling before creating powers. Collecting more data to cure underfitting, which rarely helps. Exams ask: define underfitting and overfitting with symptoms and remedies, interpret a table or plot of training and validation error versus complexity, explain why training error never increases with degree, and describe learning curves.

Recap: Polynomial regression adds powers of x as features, letting a linear model draw curves, with the degree acting as a complexity dial. In our example, the line underfit (validation squared error 22.6), the parabola fit well (0.8), and the cubic overfit (training error 0, validation 49). Training error always falls with complexity; validation error falls then rises, and its minimum is where we want to be. Next lesson gives this trade-off its proper name and a formula: bias and variance.
key_points: Polynomial regression adds features x squared, x cubed, ... so a model that is linear in its weights can draw curves.
The degree is a complexity dial; with n points, degree n - 1 can pass through all of them.
Worked: on (0,1),(1,2.5),(2,4.5),(3,10.5), degree 1 predicts 12.25 at x = 4, degree 2 predicts 17.875, degree 3 predicts 24 (truth 17).
Underfitting: training and validation error both high; fix with more flexible models or better features.
Overfitting: training error very low, validation error much higher; fix with more data, simpler models or regularisation.
Training error never rises with complexity; validation error is U-shaped, and its minimum picks the model.
Learning curves show whether more data will help (overfitting) or not (underfitting).
lessons.tip: Never trust a model whose training error is much better than its validation error. Write both numbers side by side in every experiment log; the gap is your overfitting alarm.
lessons.task: Plot the four points (0, 1), (1, 2.5), (2, 4.5), (3, 10.5) on graph paper. Draw the line y = 3.05x + 0.05, the parabola y = 1.175 - 0.325x + 1.125x^2 and mark the cubic's value 24 at x = 4. Mark the true point (4, 17) and explain in two sentences which curve you would trust and why.

quiz.q: A model has training MSE 0.1 and validation MSE 45. What is most likely happening?
quiz.explain: Very low training error with much higher validation error is the classic sign of overfitting.

quiz.q: Why is polynomial regression still called linear regression?
options: Because the curve is always a straight line
Because it uses only one feature
Because the model is linear in its weights; only the features are powers of x
Because gradient descent cannot be used
quiz.explain: y_hat = w1 x + w2 x^2 + b is a weighted sum of features, so least squares still applies.

quiz.q: As polynomial degree increases, what happens to TRAINING error?
quiz.explain: A more flexible model can always fit the training data at least as well as a simpler one.

quiz.q: Both training and validation errors are high and close to each other. What is the best next step?
options: Collect much more data of the same kind
Use a more flexible model or better features
quiz.explain: This is underfitting; the model is too simple, so more flexibility or features help.

quiz.q: In the worked example, which degree gave the lowest validation error at x = 4?
quiz.explain: Degree 2 predicted 17.875 against the true 17, squared error about 0.77.

lessons.title: The Bias-Variance Trade-off
lessons.content:
Picture four archers shooting at a target at a village fair. The first archer's arrows land in a tight group, but all in the top-left corner, far from the bullseye: consistent but consistently wrong. The second archer's arrows are scattered everywhere around the bullseye: right on average, but wildly inconsistent. The third is both scattered and off-centre, the worst. The fourth lands a tight group right on the bullseye, the dream. These four pictures are the clearest way to understand bias and variance, the two hidden sources of error behind underfitting and overfitting that we met in lesson 08.

The key thought experiment: Imagine you could collect many different training sets from the same source: the same kind of flats, the same kind of fields, just a different random sample each time. Train the same type of model on each training set. You now have many slightly different models. Ask all of them to predict the same new point. Their answers will differ. Two questions describe them: on average, are they centred on the truth? And how much do they spread out? The first is about bias, the second about variance.

Bias: Bias is the gap between the average prediction (over all those possible training sets) and the true value. High bias means the model family is systematically wrong, usually because it is too simple to represent the real pattern. A straight line fitted to a curved relationship will be off in the same way no matter which sample you draw. Bias is the first archer: consistent, but aiming at the wrong spot. High bias causes underfitting.

Variance: Variance measures how much the predictions change from one training set to another. High variance means the model is very sensitive to the particular sample it saw, usually because it is so flexible that it fits the noise. A degree 10 polynomial trained on two different samples of 12 points can produce wildly different curves. Variance is the second archer: centred on average, but each shot lands somewhere different. High variance causes overfitting.

Noise: Even a perfect model cannot predict the random part of the data: measurement error, unrecorded factors, pure chance. This is called irreducible error or noise. If two identical flats on the same street rent for slightly different amounts because of the landlords' moods, no model can predict that difference. Noise sets a floor below which no model's error can go.

The decomposition: For squared error, there is a famous identity. At a given input, the expected squared error of the model (averaged over training sets and over noise) equals bias squared plus variance plus noise variance. Written compactly: expected error = bias^2 + variance + noise. You cannot reduce noise with a better algorithm; you can only trade bias against variance. This formula is exact for squared error; for other losses the same intuition holds, even though the formula looks different.

Worked example, a simple model: Suppose the true value at some input is 12. We train a simple model on four different training sets, and at that input the four models predict 8, 9, 11 and 12. The average prediction is (8 + 9 + 11 + 12) / 4 = 40 / 4 = 10. So the bias is 10 - 12 = -2, and bias squared is 4. The variance is the average squared distance from the average prediction: ((8 - 10)^2 + (9 - 10)^2 + (11 - 10)^2 + (12 - 10)^2) / 4 = (4 + 1 + 1 + 4) / 4 = 10 / 4 = 2.5.

Worked example, checking the identity: Now compute the average squared error directly: ((8 - 12)^2 + (9 - 12)^2 + (11 - 12)^2 + (12 - 12)^2) / 4 = (16 + 9 + 1 + 0) / 4 = 26 / 4 = 6.5. And bias squared plus variance is 4 + 2.5 = 6.5. They match exactly. If the observed targets also carried noise with variance 1, the expected error against observed values would be 4 + 2.5 + 1 = 7.5.

Worked example, a complex model: A very flexible model trained on the same four sets predicts 7, 15, 10 and 16 at that input. The average is 48 / 4 = 12, so the bias is 0, perfect on average. But the variance is ((7 - 12)^2 + (15 - 12)^2 + (10 - 12)^2 + (16 - 12)^2) / 4 = (25 + 9 + 4 + 16) / 4 = 54 / 4 = 13.5. So its expected squared error is 0 + 13.5 = 13.5, about double the simple model's 6.5. Zero bias did not save it; the instability cost more than the simple model's systematic miss. This is exactly the polynomial story of lesson 08 seen through a different lens.

The trade-off: As model complexity increases, bias usually falls (the model can represent more patterns) and variance usually rises (it can also fit more noise). Total error, the sum, typically falls and then rises: the same U-shape as validation error. The best complexity balances the two. That is why it is called a trade-off: pushing one down tends to push the other up.

Diagnosing which problem you have: You cannot see bias and variance directly on a real project, but training and validation errors give strong hints. High training error means high bias (the model cannot even fit what it has seen). Low training error but much higher validation error means high variance. Both high with a big gap means both problems. Compare with a target level, such as human-level performance or the error you need for the product to be useful.

Worked example, an error budget: Suppose a team building a Bangla handwritten digit reader believes a careful human makes about 2 percent errors, so they treat 2 percent as the best achievable. Case A: training error 12 percent, validation error 13 percent. The gap from 2 to 12 is large (10 points) while the train-validation gap is small (1 point), so bias is the main problem. Case B: training error 3 percent, validation error 11 percent. Now the gap from 2 to 3 is tiny but the train-validation gap is 8 points, so variance is the main problem. Case C: training 10 percent, validation 18 percent: both problems at once, so fix bias first and then attack variance. This small calculation stops teams from wasting months on the wrong remedy.

Why the decomposition makes sense: Think about where an error can come from. Part of it is that even the average model aims at the wrong spot (bias). Part is that your particular model, trained on your particular sample, wobbles away from that average (variance). And part is that the real answer itself contains a random wobble that nobody could predict (noise). When you expand the squared error and average over training sets and noise, the mixed cross terms average out to zero, so the three squared sizes simply add up, much like the sides of a right-angled triangle add up as squares in Pythagoras' theorem.

Remedies for high bias: Use a more flexible model (higher polynomial degree, deeper tree, more neurons), add more informative features, reduce regularisation, or train longer if the optimiser has not converged. More data alone does not fix high bias: the first archer will keep missing in the same way no matter how many arrows you give him.

Remedies for high variance: Get more training data (this directly reduces variance), use a simpler model, add regularisation (lesson 10), select fewer features, use early stopping, or average many models together. Averaging is powerful: if you average several models whose errors are not perfectly correlated, the variance of the average is smaller. Bagging and random forests (lesson 18) are built on this idea.

How different algorithms sit on the scale: Linear regression and logistic regression with few features tend to have high bias and low variance. A fully grown decision tree has low bias and high variance: change a few training rows and the tree can change completely. k-NN with k = 1 has low bias and high variance; with large k it becomes smoother, with higher bias and lower variance. Neural networks can be very flexible, so they rely on lots of data and regularisation to keep variance in check.

A modern twist: In very large neural networks, researchers have observed that test error can sometimes fall again as models grow far beyond the point where they fit the training data perfectly, a phenomenon called double descent. This does not cancel the basic trade-off for the models in this course, but it shows that the story is richer for huge models. You will meet such ideas in Deep Learning (cse-8-1). For classic models and moderate data, the U-shaped trade-off is the right mental model.

Real example 1, predicting flat rents with little data: A small proptech startup in Sylhet has only 80 listings. A deep tree fits them almost perfectly but predicts new listings badly, and retraining on a slightly different 80 listings gives very different predictions: high variance. A linear model with size, rooms and area predicts more steadily. The team chooses the linear model now, and plans to revisit tree ensembles once they have several thousand listings, when the extra flexibility can be afforded.

Real example 2, a crowd forecasting Eid traffic: A transport authority asks ten analysts to forecast the number of people leaving Dhaka before Eid. Each analyst alone is noisy, some high and some low. Their average is usually closer to the truth than most individuals, because their random errors partly cancel: variance falls when you average. But if all of them used the same outdated survey, they will all be wrong in the same direction: averaging does not fix shared bias. Ensembles in ML behave exactly like this.

Common mistakes and exam questions: Thinking bias here means unfairness (that is a different meaning, discussed in lesson 25). Believing that zero bias is always good. Expecting more data to cure underfitting. Forgetting the noise term. Exam questions: define bias and variance, write the decomposition, compute bias, variance and expected error from a small table of predictions, match high bias and high variance with underfitting and overfitting, and list remedies for each.

Recap: Expected squared error equals bias squared plus variance plus irreducible noise. Bias is systematic error from a too-simple model; variance is instability from a too-flexible one. Our simple model had bias squared 4 and variance 2.5 (error 6.5), while the flexible model had zero bias but variance 13.5. Use training and validation errors to diagnose, and pick remedies accordingly. Next lesson introduces regularisation, the most common tool for reducing variance without throwing away a flexible model. Keep the archer picture in mind: regularisation is like asking the wild second archer to steady his hands, accepting a slight drift from the bullseye in exchange for a much tighter group.
key_points: Imagine training the same model on many random training sets: bias is how far the average prediction is from the truth, variance is how much predictions spread.
Expected squared error = bias^2 + variance + irreducible noise.
Worked: predictions 8, 9, 11, 12 with truth 12 give bias -2, bias^2 4, variance 2.5, error 6.5.
A flexible model with predictions 7, 15, 10, 16 has zero bias but variance 13.5, so it is worse overall.
High bias means underfitting (high training error); high variance means overfitting (large train-validation gap).
More data and averaging reduce variance; more flexibility and better features reduce bias.
Noise sets a floor that no algorithm can beat.
lessons.tip: When stuck on a model, write two numbers: training error and validation error, and a third: the error you need. Whether the big gap is between need and training (bias) or between training and validation (variance) tells you what to try next.
lessons.task: Ask five friends to guess the number of seats in your classroom or a local bus without counting. Count the true number. Compute the average guess, the bias, the variance of the guesses and the average squared error, and check that bias^2 + variance equals the average squared error.

quiz.q: A model's training error is high and its validation error is about the same. This mainly indicates:
quiz.explain: The model cannot even fit the training data, which is high bias (underfitting).

quiz.q: Predictions from four training sets at a point are 4, 6, 6, 8. What is their variance (average squared deviation)?
quiz.explain: Mean is 6; squared deviations are 4, 0, 0, 4; average is 8 / 4 = 2.

quiz.q: Which action mainly reduces VARIANCE?
quiz.explain: More data makes the fitted model less sensitive to the particular sample, lowering variance.

quiz.q: The decomposition of expected squared error is:
quiz.explain: Expected squared error = bias squared + variance + irreducible noise.

quiz.q: Ten analysts all use the same outdated survey. Averaging their forecasts will:
options: Not remove the shared bias, though it may reduce random variation
quiz.explain: Averaging cancels independent random errors (variance) but not a common systematic error (bias).

lessons.title: Regularisation: L1, L2 and Keeping Models Simple
lessons.content:
A tailor in Dhaka's New Market can make a shirt that fits you perfectly while you stand still, wrinkle-free and skin-tight. The moment you lift your arms, it tears. A sensible tailor leaves a little room, accepting a slightly less perfect fit at rest so the shirt works when you actually move. Regularisation is that sensible tailor. It deliberately stops a model from fitting the training data too perfectly, accepting a little more training error to gain much better performance on new data. It is the most common cure for the high variance we met in lesson 09.

The idea in one line: Change what we minimise. Instead of minimising only the training loss, minimise training loss plus lambda times a penalty on the size of the weights. Large weights let a model make sharp, wiggly predictions that chase noise; penalising them pushes the model towards smoother, simpler functions. The number lambda (written as alpha in some libraries) is the regularisation strength, a hyperparameter you choose. With lambda = 0 you get the ordinary model; with a huge lambda the weights are crushed towards zero.

Why large weights mean overfitting: Look back at the overfit cubic in lesson 08: y_hat = 1 + 2.417 x - 1.5 x^2 + 0.583 x^3. The weights fight each other: a big positive x term, a negative x^2 term, a positive x^3 term, balancing carefully to pass through every noisy point. Small changes in the data change them a lot. A model whose weights must be large and finely balanced is fragile. Penalising weight size discourages exactly this kind of fragile balancing.

L2 regularisation (ridge): The L2 penalty is the sum of the squared weights: w1^2 + w2^2 + ... + wd^2. Linear regression with this penalty is called ridge regression. The cost becomes J = sum of squared errors + lambda times sum of squared weights. The bias term b is usually not penalised, because shifting the whole prediction up or down does not make the model more wiggly. L2 shrinks all weights smoothly towards zero but rarely makes any exactly zero.

Worked example, the penalty value: Suppose a model has weights (3, -2, 0.5). The L2 penalty is 3^2 + (-2)^2 + 0.5^2 = 9 + 4 + 0.25 = 13.25. The L1 penalty, which we meet next, is |3| + |-2| + |0.5| = 3 + 2 + 0.5 = 5.5. Notice how L2 punishes the big weight 3 heavily (it contributes 9 out of 13.25), while the small weight 0.5 barely counts (0.25). L2 especially hates large weights.

Worked example, ridge with one weight: Take our gradient descent data from lesson 06: (1, 2), (2, 4), (3, 6), with model y_hat = w x. The ridge cost is J(w) = sum of (w x - y)^2 + lambda w^2. Setting the derivative to zero gives w = (sum of x y) / (sum of x^2 + lambda). Here sum of x y = 1 times 2 + 2 times 4 + 3 times 6 = 28 and sum of x^2 = 1 + 4 + 9 = 14. With lambda = 0, w = 28 / 14 = 2, the ordinary least squares answer. With lambda = 7, w = 28 / 21 = 1.333. With lambda = 14, w = 28 / 28 = 1. The bigger lambda, the more the weight shrinks towards zero.

Reading that example: On this clean data, shrinking is a loss: the true slope is 2 and ridge pulls it down. That is the bias side of the trade-off: regularisation always adds some bias. It pays off when the data is noisy and the model is flexible, because the reduction in variance is bigger than the added bias. On a tiny, perfect dataset there is no variance to reduce, so regularisation only hurts. That is why lambda must be chosen with validation data, not set blindly.

Gradient descent with L2, weight decay: The gradient of lambda w^2 is 2 lambda w. So each gradient descent step becomes w = w - alpha (gradient of loss + 2 lambda w), which can be rewritten as w = (1 - 2 alpha lambda) w - alpha times gradient of loss. Each step first shrinks the weight by a small fixed fraction, then applies the usual update. This is why L2 regularisation in neural networks is often called weight decay: weights gently decay towards zero unless the data keeps pushing them up.

A bonus, ridge repairs the normal equation: In lesson 05 we saw that the normal equation fails when features are perfectly redundant, because X transpose X has no inverse. Ridge regression's exact solution is w = (X transpose X + lambda I) inverse X transpose y, where I is the identity matrix. Adding lambda to the diagonal makes the matrix invertible for any positive lambda, so ridge always has a unique answer. This is one reason ridge is a safe default when features are correlated, such as area in square feet and number of rooms.

A probabilistic view: There is another way to see these penalties. If, before seeing any data, you believe weights are probably small and bell-shaped around zero, then finding the most probable weights given the data turns out to be exactly ridge regression. If you use a sharper, pointed belief centred on zero (the Laplace distribution), which favours many tiny weights and a few large ones, you get lasso. So regularisation is a way of telling the model your prior belief: simple explanations are more likely than complicated ones. You will meet this Bayesian view again in Pattern Recognition (cse-6-12).

L1 regularisation (lasso): The L1 penalty is the sum of absolute weights: |w1| + |w2| + ... + |wd|. Linear regression with it is called lasso (least absolute shrinkage and selection operator). Its special power: it tends to set some weights exactly to zero. A weight of zero means the feature is ignored completely. So lasso performs automatic feature selection, which is very handy when you have many features and suspect most are useless.

Why L1 produces zeros: Compare the pushes. L2's push on a weight is proportional to the weight itself (2 lambda w), so as w gets small, the push gets small too, and w approaches zero but never quite reaches it. L1's push has constant size lambda (its slope is +lambda or -lambda), no matter how small the weight is. So a weight whose usefulness to the loss is smaller than lambda gets pushed all the way to zero and stays there. A geometric picture says the same: the region of allowed weights for L1 is a diamond with sharp corners on the axes, and the best point often lands on a corner where some weights are zero; the L2 region is a round circle with no corners.

Elastic net: Elastic net combines both penalties: lambda1 times the L1 sum plus lambda2 times the L2 sum. It keeps lasso's ability to zero out useless features while behaving more stably when features are strongly correlated with each other (lasso tends to pick one of a correlated group almost at random; elastic net shares weight among them). It costs one extra hyperparameter to tune.

Scale before you regularise: The penalty treats all weights equally, but a weight's size depends on its feature's units. If flat size is in square feet, its weight is small (about 0.017 per square foot); if in hundreds of square feet, the same effect needs a weight 100 times larger, which L2 would punish 10000 times harder. To make the penalty fair, standardise the features first (lesson 03). Forgetting this is one of the most common practical mistakes with ridge and lasso.

Choosing lambda: Try a range of values on a log scale, such as 0.001, 0.01, 0.1, 1, 10, 100. For each, train on the training set and measure the validation error (or use cross-validation, lesson 13). Too small a lambda leaves overfitting; too large causes underfitting, as all weights shrink to almost nothing and the model predicts close to the mean. The validation error versus lambda curve is again U-shaped, mirrored: complexity goes down as lambda goes up.

Regularisation beyond linear models: The same idea appears everywhere. Logistic regression uses L1 or L2 penalties. Neural networks use weight decay, plus other regularisers such as dropout (randomly switching off neurons during training) and data augmentation (training on flipped or slightly changed copies of images). Decision trees are regularised by limiting depth or requiring a minimum number of samples per leaf. SVMs have a parameter C that controls how strictly the training data must be fitted (lesson 19). Different tools, same purpose: limit effective complexity.

Early stopping: When training with gradient descent, the validation error often falls for a while and then starts rising as the model begins to fit noise. Early stopping simply keeps the weights from the step where validation error was lowest. Weights start small, so stopping early keeps them from growing too large; its effect is similar to L2 regularisation. It is cheap and very widely used, especially for neural networks and boosted trees.

Real example 1, house price model with many features: A real-estate portal in Chattogram has 2000 listings and 300 features, including many one-hot columns for neighbourhoods and amenities. Ordinary least squares overfits badly: training error tiny, validation error huge. Ridge with lambda chosen by cross-validation cuts validation error substantially. Lasso performs about as well while setting most of the 300 weights to exactly zero, leaving a short list of features that the sales team can actually understand, such as size, floor, nearness to the main road and parking.

Real example 2, a spam filter's vocabulary: A Bangla-English SMS spam filter uses one feature per word, tens of thousands in total. Many words appear only once or twice. Without regularisation, a logistic regression might give a huge weight to a rare word that happened to appear in one spam message. L2 regularisation keeps such weights modest, so one rare word cannot dominate, and the filter generalises better to new messages.

Common mistakes and exam questions: Penalising the bias term. Forgetting to scale features. Choosing lambda on the test set. Believing regularisation always improves training error (it never does; it improves validation error when variance is the problem). Mixing up which penalty gives zeros (L1 does). Exam questions: write the ridge and lasso cost functions, compute L1 and L2 penalties for given weights, compute a shrunken weight with the one-feature ridge formula, explain why L1 produces sparse models, and explain what happens as lambda grows.

Recap: Regularisation adds a penalty on weight size to the training loss: L2 (ridge) uses squared weights and shrinks smoothly; L1 (lasso) uses absolute weights and can zero out features; elastic net mixes both. In our example, ridge shrank w from 2 to 1.333 at lambda = 7 and to 1 at lambda = 14. Scale features first, choose lambda by validation, and remember early stopping and other regularisers. With the regression toolkit complete, the next lesson turns to classification with logistic regression.
key_points: Regularisation minimises training loss + lambda times a penalty on weight size, trading a little bias for less variance.
L2 (ridge) penalty: sum of squared weights; it shrinks all weights smoothly (weight decay in gradient descent).
L1 (lasso) penalty: sum of absolute weights; it can set weights exactly to zero, giving automatic feature selection.
Worked: weights (3, -2, 0.5) give L2 = 13.25 and L1 = 5.5.
One-feature ridge: w = sum(xy) / (sum(x^2) + lambda); on (1,2),(2,4),(3,6) w goes 2, 1.333, 1 for lambda 0, 7, 14.
Do not penalise the bias; standardise features before regularising; choose lambda on validation data.
Elastic net mixes L1 and L2; early stopping, dropout and tree depth limits are other regularisers.
lessons.tip: Whenever you fit a linear or logistic model with more than a handful of features, make ridge your default and tune lambda with cross-validation. Try lasso when you want to know which features truly matter.
lessons.task: For the points (1, 3), (2, 5) and (3, 7) and the model y_hat = w x (no bias), compute the ridge weight w = sum(xy) / (sum(x^2) + lambda) for lambda = 0, 2, 7 and 20. Plot w against lambda and describe the trend in one sentence.

quiz.q: What is the L2 penalty for weights (2, -1, 3)?
Which regularisation tends to make some weights exactly zero?
quiz.explain: L1's constant-size push drives weak weights all the way to zero, giving sparse models.

quiz.q: As lambda becomes very large in ridge regression, the model tends to:
options: Underfit, predicting close to the mean
quiz.explain: A huge penalty crushes weights towards zero, leaving only the bias, which is close to the mean.

quiz.q: Why should features be standardised before ridge or lasso?
options: Because lasso only works on binary features
Because the penalty depends on weight size, which depends on each feature's units
quiz.explain: Without scaling, features in small units need big weights and get punished unfairly.

quiz.q: On data (1,2),(2,4),(3,6) with y_hat = w x, what ridge weight does lambda = 14 give?

lessons.title: Logistic Regression: Classification with Probabilities
lessons.content:
A doctor in a Rajshahi clinic looks at a patient's test results and says, 'I am about 80 percent sure this is dengue, let's do one more test.' She does not just say yes or no; she gives a degree of belief, and the decision depends on how confident she is. Logistic regression is the machine learning version of that doctor for two-class problems. Despite its name, it is a classification method. It takes a weighted sum of features, exactly like linear regression, and squeezes it into a probability between 0 and 1. It is simple, fast, explainable, and still one of the most used models in banks, hospitals and tech companies.

Why not use linear regression for classes?: Suppose we code 'pass' as 1 and 'fail' as 0 and fit a straight line to hours studied. The line will predict values like 1.4 or -0.3 for some students, which make no sense as probabilities. Worse, a few students who studied a huge number of hours pull the line and shift the point where predictions cross 0.5, misclassifying ordinary students. We need an output that always stays between 0 and 1 and a loss suited to yes/no labels.

The sigmoid function: The sigmoid (also called the logistic function) is sigma(z) = 1 / (1 + e^(-z)). It takes any real number z and returns a value between 0 and 1. Some values worth remembering: sigma(0) = 0.5; sigma(1) = 0.731; sigma(2) = 0.881; sigma(4) = 0.982; and by symmetry sigma(-1) = 0.269, sigma(-2) = 0.119, sigma(-4) = 0.018. In general sigma(-z) = 1 - sigma(z). Large positive z gives almost 1, large negative z almost 0, and the curve is a smooth S shape in between.

The model: Logistic regression computes z = w1 x1 + w2 x2 + ... + wd xd + b, the same linear score as linear regression, and then outputs p = sigma(z), interpreted as the probability that the example belongs to class 1. The score z is sometimes called the logit or log-odds, because z = log(p / (1 - p)). So each weight says how much one unit of its feature changes the log-odds of class 1. Positive weights push towards class 1, negative weights towards class 0.

Worked example, one feature: A model for passing an exam from hours studied h has z = -4 + 0.5 h. A student who studied 4 hours gets z = -4 + 2 = -2, so p = sigma(-2) = 0.119, about 12 percent chance of passing. At 8 hours, z = 0, p = 0.5. At 10 hours, z = 1, p = 0.731. At 12 hours, z = 2, p = 0.881. The probability rises smoothly with study time but never exceeds 1.

From probability to decision: To output a class, compare p with a threshold, usually 0.5: predict class 1 if p is at least 0.5, otherwise class 0. Since sigma(z) is at least 0.5 exactly when z is at least 0, this is the same as predicting class 1 when z is at least 0. The threshold does not have to be 0.5; for disease screening you might predict 'positive' at p = 0.2 to catch more cases. Lesson 12 explores this trade-off.

The decision boundary: The decision boundary is the set of points where z = 0, where the model is exactly undecided. In the hours example, -4 + 0.5 h = 0 gives h = 8 hours: below 8 the model predicts fail, above it pass. With two features, the boundary is a line. For example, with z = -6 + x1 + x2, the boundary is x1 + x2 = 6. The point (2, 3) has z = -1, so p = 0.269 and it is predicted class 0. The point (4, 5) has z = 3, so p = 0.953, class 1. With more features, the boundary is a flat plane or hyperplane. That is why logistic regression is called a linear classifier: its boundary is straight.

Curved boundaries: If the classes are separated by a circle or a curve, a plain logistic regression cannot follow it. As in lesson 08, the trick is feature engineering: adding features like x1 squared, x2 squared and x1 times x2 lets the boundary bend, while the model remains linear in its weights. For very complex shapes, other models such as trees, kernel SVMs or neural networks are usually more convenient.

The loss, log loss: For training we use the log loss (binary cross-entropy) previewed in lesson 07. For one example with true label y (0 or 1) and predicted probability p, the loss is -(y log(p) + (1 - y) log(1 - p)). When y = 1, only -log(p) remains; when y = 0, only -log(1 - p). With natural logs: if y = 1 and p = 0.9, the loss is 0.105; if p = 0.5, it is 0.693; if p = 0.1, it is 2.303. The cost is the average over training examples. For logistic regression this cost is convex, so gradient descent finds the single best answer.

Why log loss and not squared error: Log loss comes naturally from asking 'which weights make the observed labels most probable?', the principle of maximum likelihood. It also gives clean gradients: confidently wrong predictions get large gradients and are corrected quickly. With squared error on a sigmoid output, the cost is not convex, and learning can stall when the model is confidently wrong, because the sigmoid is flat there.

The gradient, a beautiful result: For log loss with a sigmoid output, the gradient for one example is remarkably simple: dLoss/dwj = (p - y) times xj, and dLoss/db = (p - y). It has the same 'error times input' shape as linear regression's gradient, with the error now being predicted probability minus true label. Averaged over the training set, these drive the gradient descent update w = w - alpha times gradient.

Worked example, one gradient step: Start with w = 0 and b = 0. Take one training example: x = 2 hours, y = 1 (passed). Then z = 0, p = 0.5, and the loss is -log(0.5) = 0.693. The gradients are dLoss/dw = (0.5 - 1) times 2 = -1 and dLoss/db = 0.5 - 1 = -0.5. With learning rate 0.1: w = 0 - 0.1 times (-1) = 0.1, and b = 0 - 0.1 times (-0.5) = 0.05. Now z = 0.1 times 2 + 0.05 = 0.25, p = sigma(0.25) = 0.562, and the loss falls to -log(0.562) = 0.576. One step moved the model in the right direction.

The full training loop in pseudo-code: initialise w = 0 and b = 0; repeat for many epochs: for each mini-batch, compute z = X w + b and p = sigmoid(z); compute errors e = p - y; gradient_w = average of e times x; gradient_b = average of e; w = w - alpha * gradient_w; b = b - alpha * gradient_b; track the validation log loss and stop when it stops improving. Compare this with linear regression's loop in lesson 06: the only real change is the sigmoid and the loss. That is why learning linear regression well first pays off.

Calibration, can we trust the probabilities?: A model is well calibrated if, among all cases where it says 70 percent, about 70 percent really are class 1. Logistic regression trained with log loss is often reasonably well calibrated, which is a big advantage when the probability itself drives a decision, such as how many boats to send. You can check calibration by grouping validation predictions into bins (0 to 0.1, 0.1 to 0.2, and so on) and comparing the average prediction with the actual fraction of positives in each bin.

More than two classes, softmax: For K classes, such as classifying a news headline as politics, sports or entertainment, multinomial logistic regression (softmax regression) computes one score per class and turns them into probabilities with the softmax function: p_k = e^(z_k) / sum over j of e^(z_j). For scores (2, 1, 0), the exponentials are 7.389, 2.718 and 1, summing to 11.107, so the probabilities are 0.665, 0.245 and 0.090. They are positive and add up to 1. The loss is cross-entropy: -log of the probability given to the true class. Another simple approach is one-versus-rest: train one binary classifier per class.

Regularisation and scaling: Logistic regression overfits when features are many, so L2 (or L1) penalties from lesson 10 are standard; many libraries apply L2 by default. If the training data is perfectly separable, the unregularised weights grow without limit as the model tries to become infinitely confident; regularisation keeps them finite. As always, standardise features for gradient descent and fair penalties.

Interpreting the model: Because z is the log-odds, e^(wj) is the odds ratio: how much the odds of class 1 multiply when feature j increases by 1. If the weight on 'previous late payments' is 0.7, each extra late payment multiplies the odds of default by e^0.7, about 2.01, roughly doubling them. This interpretability is why logistic regression remains popular for credit scoring and medical risk scores, where decisions must be explained.

Real example 1, mobile loan approval: A digital lending service in Bangladesh decides whether to approve small loans using features such as months of mobile wallet history, average monthly balance, regularity of income and past repayment behaviour. A logistic regression outputs the probability of repayment. The lender approves when p exceeds a threshold chosen from the cost of defaults versus lost customers, and can explain to a rejected applicant which factors mattered most.

Real example 2, flood warning by union: A disaster office estimates the probability that a union floods within three days from upstream river level, rainfall forecast and soil wetness. A logistic regression with standardised features is trained on past seasons. Its probabilities are shown on a map; unions above 0.3 get early warnings and boats pre-positioned, a deliberately low threshold because missing a flood is far worse than a false alarm.

Common mistakes and exam questions: Thinking logistic regression does regression (it classifies). Forgetting that the boundary is where z = 0, not where p = 1. Treating p = 0.5 as the only possible threshold. Using squared error to train it. Forgetting regularisation with many features. Exams ask: compute sigma for given z, compute p for given weights and features, find the decision boundary, compute log loss, perform one gradient descent step, and compute softmax probabilities for three scores.

Recap: Logistic regression computes a linear score z = w x + b and turns it into a probability with the sigmoid, p = 1 / (1 + e^(-z)). It predicts class 1 when p is at least the threshold (z at least 0 for 0.5), giving a straight decision boundary such as h = 8 hours or x1 + x2 = 6. It is trained with log loss, whose gradient is simply (p - y) times x. Softmax extends it to many classes. Next lesson asks the crucial follow-up: once a classifier makes predictions, how do we measure whether it is good?
key_points: Logistic regression is a classifier: p = sigma(w x + b), with sigma(z) = 1 / (1 + e^(-z)).
Key values: sigma(0) = 0.5, sigma(2) = 0.881, sigma(-2) = 0.119, and sigma(-z) = 1 - sigma(z).
With threshold 0.5, predict class 1 when z >= 0; the decision boundary z = 0 is a straight line or hyperplane.
Worked: z = -4 + 0.5h gives boundary h = 8 hours; z = -6 + x1 + x2 gives boundary x1 + x2 = 6.
Training uses log loss -(y log p + (1 - y) log(1 - p)), which is convex for logistic regression.
Gradient per example: (p - y) times x for weights, (p - y) for the bias; one step from w = 0 moved p from 0.5 to 0.562.
Softmax handles many classes: scores (2, 1, 0) give probabilities 0.665, 0.245, 0.090.
Weights are log-odds effects; e^w is an odds ratio, which makes the model explainable.
lessons.tip: Memorise a few sigmoid values (0 gives 0.5, 1 gives about 0.73, 2 about 0.88, 4 about 0.98). With them you can sanity-check any logistic regression output in your head.
lessons.task: A model predicts whether a mango is ripe with z = -10 + 2 times softness (on a 0-10 scale). By hand or calculator, compute p for softness 3, 5, 6 and 8, find the decision boundary, and compute the log loss for a ripe mango with softness 6.

quiz.q: What is sigma(0) for the sigmoid function?
For z = -4 + 0.5h, where is the decision boundary with threshold 0.5?
quiz.explain: The boundary is z = 0: -4 + 0.5h = 0 gives h = 8.

quiz.q: Which loss is normally used to train logistic regression?
quiz.explain: Log loss follows from maximum likelihood and gives a convex cost with simple gradients.

quiz.q: For one example with p = 0.8, y = 1 and feature x = 3, what is the log loss gradient for the weight?
quiz.explain: (p - y) times x = (0.8 - 1) times 3 = -0.6.

quiz.q: Why is logistic regression called a linear classifier?
options: Its output is a straight line
It cannot use more than one feature
Its decision boundary is a straight line or flat hyperplane in feature space
quiz.explain: The boundary w x + b = 0 is linear in the features, even though the probability curve is S-shaped.

lessons.title: Evaluating Classifiers: Confusion Matrix, Precision, Recall, F1, ROC and AUC
lessons.content:
Imagine a security guard at a shopping mall in Dhaka whose job is to stop shoplifters at the door. A lazy guard who never stops anyone is 'right' for almost every customer, because almost everyone is honest, yet he catches zero thieves. An over-eager guard who stops everybody catches every thief but insults hundreds of honest shoppers. Neither is good, and a single 'percentage correct' number cannot tell you why. Evaluating a classifier means asking several separate questions: how many real cases did we catch, how many alarms were false, and what trade-off do we want? This lesson gives you the standard tools, with worked numbers.

The four outcomes: For a two-class problem, call one class positive (the thing we are looking for: spam, fraud, disease, flood) and the other negative. Every prediction falls into one of four boxes. True positive (TP): actually positive, predicted positive, a correct catch. True negative (TN): actually negative, predicted negative, correctly left alone. False positive (FP): actually negative but predicted positive, a false alarm, also called a type I error. False negative (FN): actually positive but predicted negative, a miss, also called a type II error. The words are easy to decode: the second word is what the model said, the first word says whether that was right.

The confusion matrix: Arranging these four counts in a 2 by 2 table gives the confusion matrix, with rows for the actual class and columns for the predicted class (some books swap rows and columns, so always read the labels). It shows exactly where the model gets confused. For more than two classes, the matrix becomes K by K, and off-diagonal cells show which classes are mixed up, for example a digit reader confusing 1 with 7.

Worked example, a spam filter: A filter is tested on 1000 messages, of which 60 are really spam and 940 are not. It flags 50 messages as spam; 40 of them really are spam. So TP = 40, FP = 50 - 40 = 10, FN = 60 - 40 = 20 (spam it missed), and TN = 940 - 10 = 930. Check: 40 + 10 + 20 + 930 = 1000. We will compute every metric from these four numbers.

Accuracy: Accuracy = (TP + TN) / total = (40 + 930) / 1000 = 0.97, so 97 percent. Sounds great. But a lazy filter that never flags anything gets TN = 940 and TP = 0, an accuracy of 94 percent, without catching a single spam. Our filter is only 3 points better than doing nothing. Accuracy is fine when classes are balanced and errors cost the same, but misleading when the positive class is rare. This is the accuracy paradox, explored further in lesson 14.

Precision: Precision = TP / (TP + FP) = 40 / 50 = 0.8. It answers: of the messages we flagged, how many really were spam? Precision is about trust in an alarm. High precision means few false alarms. It matters when false positives are costly: sending a real job offer email to the spam folder, or wrongly blocking a customer's bKash account.

Recall (sensitivity): Recall = TP / (TP + FN) = 40 / 60 = 0.667. It answers: of all the real spam, how much did we catch? Recall is about coverage. High recall means few misses. It matters when false negatives are costly: missing a cancer in screening, missing a fraudulent transaction, or failing to warn a village about a flood. Recall is also called sensitivity or true positive rate (TPR).

Specificity and false positive rate: Specificity = TN / (TN + FP) = 930 / 940 = 0.989. It is the recall of the negative class: of all genuine messages, how many did we correctly leave alone? The false positive rate is FPR = FP / (FP + TN) = 10 / 940 = 0.011, which equals 1 minus specificity. Medical tests often report sensitivity and specificity; ML papers more often report precision and recall.

The F1 score: Precision and recall pull in opposite directions, so we often want one number that balances them. F1 is their harmonic mean: F1 = 2 times P times R / (P + R) = 2 times 0.8 times 0.667 / (0.8 + 0.667) = 1.067 / 1.467 = 0.727. The harmonic mean is pulled towards the smaller value: if precision is 1.0 and recall is 0.1, the plain average is 0.55, but F1 is only about 0.18. So F1 is high only when both are reasonably high. A general version, F-beta, weights recall beta times as much as precision; F2, for example, is used when recall matters more.

The threshold trade-off: A logistic regression outputs probabilities; the class depends on the threshold. Raise the threshold from 0.5 to 0.8 and the model flags only messages it is very sure about: precision usually goes up, recall goes down. Lower it to 0.2 and it flags more: recall up, precision down. There is no free lunch; you choose the operating point from the costs. A cancer screening test might run at high recall and accept many false alarms, followed by a more precise second test; a spam filter might prefer high precision so that real mail is rarely lost.

The ROC curve: To see all thresholds at once, plot the true positive rate (recall) on the y-axis against the false positive rate on the x-axis, for every possible threshold. This is the ROC curve (receiver operating characteristic, a name from radar engineering). A threshold above every score gives the point (0, 0): nothing flagged. A threshold below every score gives (1, 1): everything flagged. A perfect classifier passes through (0, 1), catching all positives with no false alarms. Random guessing lies along the diagonal from (0, 0) to (1, 1).

Worked example, building a tiny ROC: Six test messages get spam scores. Three are really spam, with scores 0.9, 0.8 and 0.4; three are genuine, with scores 0.7, 0.3 and 0.2. Sort all scores and move the threshold down. At threshold 0.85 only 0.9 is flagged: TPR = 1/3, FPR = 0. At 0.75, both 0.9 and 0.8: TPR = 2/3, FPR = 0. At 0.5, the genuine 0.7 is also flagged: TPR = 2/3, FPR = 1/3. At 0.35, the spam 0.4 joins: TPR = 1, FPR = 1/3. At 0.25: TPR = 1, FPR = 2/3. At 0.1: TPR = 1, FPR = 1. Joining (0, 0), (0, 1/3), (0, 2/3), (1/3, 2/3), (1/3, 1), (2/3, 1), (1, 1) gives a staircase ROC curve.

AUC: The area under the ROC curve (AUC) summarises it in one number between 0 and 1. AUC = 1 is perfect, 0.5 is no better than random. It has a lovely meaning: AUC equals the probability that a randomly chosen positive example gets a higher score than a randomly chosen negative one. In our example there are 3 times 3 = 9 positive-negative pairs. The spam 0.9 beats all three genuine scores (3 pairs), 0.8 beats all three (3 pairs), and 0.4 beats 0.3 and 0.2 but not 0.7 (2 pairs). That is 8 out of 9, so AUC = 0.889. Computing the area of the staircase gives the same answer. AUC does not depend on any single threshold, which makes it useful for comparing models before choosing an operating point.

Precision-recall curve: When positives are very rare, the ROC curve can look excellent even if precision is poor, because the false positive rate divides by a huge number of negatives. In such cases, plotting precision against recall for all thresholds, and summarising with the area under that curve, gives a more honest picture. Lesson 14 returns to this.

Putting costs on the matrix: When you know what each error costs, you can compare models in money. Suppose a missed spam (FN) costs a user 500 taka on average through scams, and a genuine message wrongly hidden (FP) costs 20 taka of inconvenience. Our filter's cost is 20 times 500 + 10 times 20 = 10000 + 200 = 10200 taka per 1000 messages. The do-nothing filter misses all 60 spam: 60 times 500 = 30000 taka. Now the difference between 97 and 94 percent accuracy looks much bigger: the model saves about two thirds of the cost. You can also try several thresholds and pick the one with the lowest total cost on validation data.

More than two classes: For K classes, compute precision, recall and F1 for each class by treating it as positive and the rest as negative. Then average. The macro average gives each class equal weight, so a rare class counts as much as a common one. The micro average pools all the TP, FP and FN counts first, so common classes dominate; in single-label multiclass problems, micro-averaged precision, recall and F1 all equal plain accuracy. Choose macro when doing well on rare classes matters.

Real example 1, a dengue rapid screening model: A hospital tests a model that flags likely dengue cases from symptoms and basic blood counts. Missing a real case is dangerous, so the team sets the threshold for recall of at least 0.95, accepting a precision of maybe 0.5: half the flagged patients do not have dengue but get a confirmatory lab test. They report sensitivity, specificity, precision and the confusion matrix, not just accuracy.

Real example 2, a fraud detector for mobile payments: Only a tiny fraction of transactions are fraudulent. Investigators can review a limited number of alerts per day. The company picks the threshold so that the alerts per day fit the team's capacity, then measures precision (how many alerts are real fraud) and recall (what share of fraud was caught). Comparing two candidate models, they use the area under the precision-recall curve, since ROC AUC was close to 0.99 for both and did not separate them.

Common mistakes and exam questions: Reporting only accuracy on imbalanced data. Mixing up precision (denominator: predicted positives) and recall (denominator: actual positives). Forgetting that FPR uses actual negatives. Reading a confusion matrix with rows and columns swapped. Treating AUC as accuracy. Exam questions: fill in a confusion matrix from a story, compute accuracy, precision, recall, specificity and F1, explain the effect of raising the threshold, sketch an ROC curve and interpret AUC, and choose between precision and recall for a given application.

Recap: Every binary prediction is a TP, TN, FP or FN, laid out in the confusion matrix. From TP = 40, FP = 10, FN = 20, TN = 930 we got accuracy 0.97, precision 0.8, recall 0.667, specificity 0.989 and F1 0.727, while a do-nothing model already had accuracy 0.94. Thresholds trade precision against recall; the ROC curve shows all thresholds, and AUC (0.889 in our six-message example) is the chance a positive outranks a negative. Next lesson makes our evaluation more reliable with cross-validation and uses it to tune hyperparameters.
key_points: TP, TN, FP (false alarm, type I) and FN (miss, type II) form the confusion matrix.
Accuracy = (TP + TN) / total; misleading with rare positives (97 percent vs a 94 percent do-nothing baseline).
Precision = TP / (TP + FP) = 40 / 50 = 0.8: how trustworthy an alarm is.
Recall = TP / (TP + FN) = 40 / 60 = 0.667: how many real positives are caught; specificity = TN / (TN + FP).
F1 = 2PR / (P + R) = 0.727, the harmonic mean, high only when both are high.
Raising the threshold usually raises precision and lowers recall; choose it from the costs.
ROC plots TPR against FPR over all thresholds; AUC is the chance a random positive outscores a random negative (8/9 = 0.889 in the example).
Use precision-recall curves for rare positives, and macro averages when small classes matter.
lessons.tip: Always write the confusion matrix first, with clear row and column labels, before computing any metric. Every formula then becomes a matter of picking the right cells, and you will never mix up precision and recall.
lessons.task: Imagine a model that predicts whether it will rain in your area each day. Over 30 days it predicted rain on 12 days; it actually rained on 10 days, and on 8 of those the model had predicted rain. Build the confusion matrix and compute accuracy, precision, recall, specificity and F1.

quiz.q: A model has TP = 30, FP = 20, FN = 10, TN = 940. What is its precision?
Using the same counts (TP = 30, FN = 10), what is the recall?
For cancer screening where missing a case is very dangerous, which metric should be kept high?
quiz.explain: Recall measures how many real cases are caught; misses (FN) are the costly error here.

quiz.q: What usually happens when you raise the classification threshold from 0.5 to 0.9?
quiz.explain: Fewer, more confident positive predictions mean fewer false alarms but more misses.

quiz.q: An AUC of 0.5 means the model:
options: Is right half the time at threshold 0.5
Ranks positives above negatives no better than random
quiz.explain: AUC is the probability a random positive outscores a random negative; 0.5 is chance level.

lessons.title: Cross-Validation and Hyperparameter Tuning
lessons.content:
Suppose you want to know how good a new batsman really is. You watch one match and he scores 90. Is he a star? Maybe the bowling was weak that day. If you watch five matches against different teams and he scores 90, 15, 60, 40 and 70, you get a much more reliable picture: an average of 55 with a lot of ups and downs. A single validation split is like judging from one match. Cross-validation watches several matches: it evaluates a model on several different held-out parts of the data and averages the results. And once we can measure models reliably, we can tune their settings systematically. That is this lesson.

The problem with one split: In lesson 04 we split data into training, validation and test sets. With plenty of data this works well. With a few hundred or a few thousand rows, the validation set is small and its score depends heavily on which rows happened to land in it. Two models whose true quality differs by 1 percent can swap places just because of a lucky or unlucky split. Also, the rows in the validation set never get used for training, which wastes precious data.

k-fold cross-validation: Shuffle the data and divide it into k equal parts, called folds. Then repeat k times: hold out one fold as the validation fold, train the model on the other k - 1 folds, and score it on the held-out fold. Each row is used for validation exactly once and for training k - 1 times. Finally, average the k scores. Common choices are k = 5 and k = 10. In pseudo-code: folds = split(data, k); for i in 1..k: model = train(all folds except i); scores[i] = evaluate(model, fold i); report mean(scores) and spread.

Worked example, 5-fold on 1000 rows: With 1000 training rows and k = 5, each fold has 1000 / 5 = 200 rows. In each round, the model trains on 800 rows and is validated on 200. Suppose the five validation accuracies are 0.82, 0.85, 0.80, 0.84 and 0.84. The mean is (0.82 + 0.85 + 0.80 + 0.84 + 0.84) / 5 = 4.15 / 5 = 0.83. The deviations from 0.83 are -0.01, 0.02, -0.03, 0.01 and 0.01; their squares sum to 0.0001 + 0.0004 + 0.0009 + 0.0001 + 0.0001 = 0.0016. Dividing by k - 1 = 4 gives 0.0004, whose square root is 0.02. So we report accuracy 0.83 plus or minus 0.02 (sample standard deviation).

Why report the spread: The spread tells you how stable the estimate is. If model A scores 0.83 plus or minus 0.02 and model B scores 0.84 plus or minus 0.03, the difference of 0.01 is smaller than the fold-to-fold wobble, so you cannot confidently say B is better. A cleaner comparison uses the same folds for both models and looks at the per-fold differences: if B beats A in all five folds, that is more convincing than the averages alone.

Choosing k: Larger k means each training set is closer to the full data (with k = 10, each model sees 90 percent), so the estimate is less pessimistic, but it costs k trainings. Smaller k is cheaper. k = 5 or 10 is a good default. The extreme case, k = n, is leave-one-out cross-validation (LOOCV): train on all rows but one, test on that one, repeat n times. With 1000 rows that means 1000 trainings. It uses data maximally and is useful for tiny datasets or for models that can be updated cheaply, but it is usually too expensive and its estimate can be noisy.

Stratified k-fold: For classification, especially with imbalanced classes, make each fold keep the same class proportions as the whole dataset, just as in a stratified split (lesson 04). If 10 percent of rows are positive, each fold gets about 10 percent positives. Otherwise one fold might contain almost no positives and give a meaningless recall. Most libraries offer stratified k-fold and use it by default for classifiers.

Group and time-series cross-validation: The same warnings as lesson 04 apply. If several rows belong to one patient or one field, use group k-fold so all of an entity's rows stay in the same fold. For time series, never shuffle. Use forward-chaining (also called rolling or expanding window) validation: train on months 1 to 6, validate on month 7; then train on 1 to 7, validate on 8; and so on. Each validation period is always in the future of its training data.

Parameters versus hyperparameters: Parameters are learned from data during training: the weights of linear and logistic regression, the split thresholds of a tree. Hyperparameters are chosen before training and control how learning happens: the regularisation strength lambda, the polynomial degree, the learning rate, the number of neighbours k in k-NN, the maximum depth of a tree, the number of trees in a forest. Hyperparameters cannot be learned by minimising training error, because the most flexible setting always wins on training data. They must be chosen by validation or cross-validation.

Grid search: List a few candidate values for each hyperparameter and try every combination. For k-NN, you might try k in {1, 3, 5, 7, 9}, weighting in {uniform, distance} and distance metric in {Euclidean, Manhattan}. That is 5 times 2 times 2 = 20 combinations. With 5-fold cross-validation, each combination needs 5 trainings, so 20 times 5 = 100 model fits. Pick the combination with the best mean cross-validation score. Grid search is simple and thorough, but the number of combinations multiplies quickly: 6 hyperparameters with 5 values each is 5^6 = 15625 combinations.

Random search: Instead of trying every grid point, sample, say, 30 random combinations from ranges or distributions (for example, lambda from 0.0001 to 100 on a log scale). Research and practical experience show that random search often finds good settings faster than grid search, because usually only a few hyperparameters really matter.
