A grid wastes many trials varying unimportant ones, while random sampling tries many different values of the important ones. More advanced methods, such as Bayesian optimisation, use earlier results to choose promising next trials; you only need to know they exist.

Coarse to fine: A practical strategy is to start with a wide, coarse search on a log scale (lambda in 0.001, 0.01, 0.1, 1, 10, 100), find the best region, then search more finely around it (lambda in 0.3, 0.5, 1, 2, 3). Always check that the best value is not at the edge of your range; if lambda = 100 wins, try 1000 too.

Repeated cross-validation: Even 5-fold results depend a little on how the rows were shuffled into folds. Repeated k-fold runs the whole procedure several times with different shuffles, for example 5-fold repeated 3 times, giving 15 scores. The average becomes steadier and the spread more trustworthy, at three times the cost. It is worth it when datasets are small and decisions are close.

You can overfit the validation data too: Every time you try another setting and keep the winner, you squeeze a little information out of the validation folds. Try a thousand random settings on a small dataset and the best one will partly be lucky. Signs of this are a winning score that looks surprisingly high and a much lower score on the final test set. Remedies: keep the search modest, prefer simpler settings when scores are within the spread, and always confirm on an untouched test set. This is the same overfitting story from lesson 08, one level higher.

Nested cross-validation: If you choose hyperparameters with cross-validation and then report that same best cross-validation score as your model's performance, the number is slightly optimistic: you picked the best of many tries on the same data. The clean solution is nested cross-validation: an outer loop splits data into folds for evaluation; inside each outer training part, an inner cross-validation chooses hyperparameters. It is expensive, so many projects instead keep a separate untouched test set for the final number, which serves the same purpose.

Pipelines prevent leakage: If scaling, imputation or feature selection are fitted on the full training data before cross-validation, every fold's validation part has leaked into preprocessing. The fix is to put preprocessing and the model together in a pipeline and run the pipeline inside each fold, so the scaler is fitted only on that fold's training part. Libraries like scikit-learn make this easy (lesson 24). This is one of the most common hidden bugs in student projects.

After tuning, the final model: Once the best hyperparameters are found, retrain the model on all the training data (all folds together) with those settings, then evaluate once on the test set. The cross-validation models themselves are usually thrown away; they were only measuring instruments.

Real example 1, tuning a crop disease classifier: A team in Rangpur has 2400 labelled leaf images represented by simple colour and texture features, and tries an SVM. They use stratified 5-fold cross-validation, grouped by farm, inside a pipeline with scaling, and random search over C and the kernel width with 40 trials (200 fits). The best setting scores a mean F1 of 0.86 plus or minus 0.03 across folds. Retrained on all 2400 images, it scores 0.84 on a separate test set from new farms, a believable result.

Real example 2, forecasting monthly sales: A pharmacy chain wants to choose the regularisation strength for a demand forecasting model. With 36 months of data, they use forward-chaining validation with the last 12 months: train on months 1 to 24 and validate on 25, train on 1 to 25 and validate on 26, and so on. Shuffled k-fold would have let the model peek at the future and picked a setting that looks better than it is.

Common mistakes and exam questions: Tuning hyperparameters on the test set. Fitting preprocessing outside the cross-validation loop. Shuffling time series. Reporting only the mean without the spread. Forgetting to retrain on all training data at the end. Confusing parameters and hyperparameters. Exams ask: describe k-fold cross-validation, compute fold sizes and the mean and standard deviation of fold scores, count model fits for a grid search, compare grid and random search, and explain LOOCV and nested cross-validation.

Recap: k-fold cross-validation rotates which fold is held out, so every row is used for both training and validation, giving a mean score and a spread (0.83 plus or minus 0.02 in our example). Stratify for classes, group for shared entities, and roll forward in time for time series. Hyperparameters are tuned by searching with cross-validation: grid search tries all combinations (20 combinations times 5 folds = 100 fits), random search samples them and is often more efficient. Keep preprocessing inside the loop and the test set outside it. Next lesson tackles a problem that breaks many naive models: imbalanced data.
key_points: k-fold cross-validation splits data into k folds, trains on k - 1 and validates on the remaining one, k times, then averages.
Worked: 1000 rows with k = 5 gives folds of 200; scores 0.82, 0.85, 0.80, 0.84, 0.84 give mean 0.83 and standard deviation 0.02.
Report the spread; compare models on the same folds before declaring a winner.
Use stratified k-fold for classes, group k-fold for shared entities and forward-chaining for time series.
Parameters are learned in training; hyperparameters (lambda, k, depth, learning rate) are chosen by validation.
Grid search tries every combination (5 x 2 x 2 = 20 combos, 100 fits with 5 folds); random search samples and is often more efficient.
Put preprocessing in a pipeline inside each fold; retrain on all training data at the end and test once.
lessons.tip: Before running any search, compute how many model fits it will need (combinations times folds). If the number scares you, switch from grid to random search or shrink the ranges with a quick coarse search first.
lessons.task: Take 20 numbers (for example, your last 20 exam or quiz marks) and pretend they are a dataset. Split them into 5 folds of 4 by hand. For each fold, use the mean of the other 16 numbers as the 'prediction' and compute the mean absolute error on the held-out 4. Report the average and spread of the five errors.

quiz.q: With 1200 rows and 4-fold cross-validation, how many rows does each model train on?
quiz.explain: Each fold has 1200 / 4 = 300 rows; training uses the other 3 folds, 900 rows.

quiz.q: Which of these is a hyperparameter, not a learned parameter?
options: A split threshold chosen during tree training
quiz.explain: Lambda is set before training and chosen by validation; weights and thresholds are learned from data.

quiz.q: A grid search tries 4 values of C and 3 values of gamma with 5-fold CV. How many model fits are needed?
quiz.explain: 4 x 3 = 12 combinations, each trained 5 times: 60 fits.

quiz.q: For monthly sales data, which validation scheme is appropriate?
options: Forward-chaining (train on the past, validate on the next period)
quiz.explain: Time series must be validated on periods after the training data, never shuffled.

quiz.q: Why should scaling be fitted inside each cross-validation fold?
options: Scaling is only allowed on test data
It increases the number of folds
Otherwise the validation fold's data leaks into preprocessing and the score is optimistic
quiz.explain: Fitting the scaler on all rows lets validation information influence training, a form of leakage.

lessons.title: Imbalanced Data: When One Class Is Rare
lessons.content:
Imagine looking for counterfeit 1000 taka notes in a big bundle from a bank. Almost every note is real; perhaps one in a thousand is fake. If your job were simply to be 'right as often as possible', you would declare every note genuine and be right 99.9 percent of the time, while letting every fake through. Many of the most important ML problems look like this: fraud, rare diseases, machine failures, defaults on loans, floods in a given week. The thing we care about is rare. Standard training and standard metrics quietly fail on such data unless we handle it deliberately. This lesson shows how.

What imbalanced means: A dataset is imbalanced when one class is much more frequent than another. Mild imbalance, such as 70 to 30, usually causes no special trouble. Strong imbalance, such as 99 to 1 or 99.9 to 0.1, changes everything. We call the rare class the minority (usually the positive class, the one we want to find) and the common class the majority.

Why models struggle: Most learning algorithms minimise the average loss over all training examples. If 99 percent of examples are negative, the cheapest way to get a low average loss is to predict negative almost always. The few positives contribute so little to the total that the model may barely learn their pattern at all. A decision tree may never bother to split them off; a logistic regression may push all probabilities close to zero.

Worked example, the accuracy paradox: A payments company has 1000 transactions, of which 10 are fraud and 990 are normal. A useless model that always predicts 'normal' gets 990 correct out of 1000: accuracy 99 percent. Its recall on fraud is 0 / 10 = 0, and its precision is undefined because it never predicts fraud. A real model that catches 8 of the 10 frauds while flagging 30 normal transactions has TP = 8, FN = 2, FP = 30, TN = 960. Its accuracy is (8 + 960) / 1000 = 96.8 percent, lower than the useless model! Yet its recall is 0.8 and its precision is 8 / 38 = 0.21. Accuracy ranked the useless model higher. This is why accuracy alone must never be used on imbalanced data.

Better metrics: Report the confusion matrix, then precision, recall and F1 for the minority class (lesson 12). Use the precision-recall curve and its area (often called average precision) to compare models across thresholds. A useful reference: for a random classifier, precision equals the share of positives, so on this data a random model has precision of about 0.01, and our model's 0.21 is about 21 times better than chance. ROC AUC is still meaningful but can look flattering when negatives are overwhelming, because the false positive rate divides by a huge number. Many teams also report 'precision at k': of the top k alerts, how many are real.

The golden rule of resampling: All the techniques below change the training data only. Never resample the validation or test sets. Those must reflect the real-world class ratio, otherwise your evaluation describes a world that does not exist. And when using cross-validation, resample inside each training fold, never before splitting, or duplicated or synthetic minority examples will leak into the validation folds.

Random undersampling: Throw away some majority examples so the classes are closer to balanced. From our 990 normal and 10 fraud, you could keep all 10 frauds and a random 90 normals, a 10 percent minority, or even 10 and 10. Training becomes faster and the model pays more attention to fraud. The big cost is wasted information: you discarded hundreds of normal examples that described what normal behaviour looks like. It works best when the majority class is huge and fairly repetitive.

Random oversampling: Copy minority examples, perhaps many times, until the classes are more balanced. No information is thrown away. But the model sees the same few fraud examples again and again and may memorise them exactly, which is overfitting in a new disguise: high recall on training data, disappointing recall on new fraud.

SMOTE, synthetic minority examples: SMOTE (Synthetic Minority Over-sampling Technique) creates new, slightly different minority examples instead of exact copies. For a minority example x, pick one of its nearest minority neighbours n, and create a new point somewhere on the line between them: new = x + r times (n - x), where r is a random number between 0 and 1. Worked example: x = (2, 3), neighbour n = (4, 7), r = 0.5. Then n - x = (2, 4), half of it is (1, 2), and the new point is (2 + 1, 3 + 2) = (3, 5). This fills in the minority region more smoothly than duplicates. Caution: if minority and majority regions overlap, SMOTE can create unrealistic points in the wrong territory, and it does not apply directly to raw categorical features without variants designed for them.

Class weights: Instead of changing the data, change the loss. Give each minority example a larger weight, so a mistake on it costs more. A common 'balanced' formula sets the weight of class c to n / (K times n_c), where n is the total number of examples, K the number of classes and n_c the count of class c. For our data: normal weight = 1000 / (2 times 990) = 0.505, fraud weight = 1000 / (2 times 10) = 50. So misclassifying one fraud costs about 50 / 0.505 = 99 times as much as misclassifying one normal transaction, exactly cancelling the 99 to 1 imbalance. Most libraries accept class weights for logistic regression, SVMs, trees and neural networks. It is simple, wastes no data and is often the first thing to try.

Threshold moving: A probabilistic classifier trained on imbalanced data may give fraud probabilities like 0.15 even to suspicious cases. With the default threshold of 0.5, it flags almost nothing. Lowering the threshold, say to 0.1, raises recall at the cost of precision. Choose the threshold on validation data, using the business costs or the capacity of the team that handles alerts. Threshold moving is cheap and is often as effective as resampling.

Get more of the rare class: Sometimes the best solution is data. Ask investigators to label more confirmed fraud cases, combine data from several months or branches, or use domain knowledge to engineer features that separate the rare class clearly (for example, 'number of new devices used in the last day'). Better features often beat every sampling trick.

When the rare class is extremely rare: If positives are 1 in 100000 or have barely any examples, framing the problem as anomaly detection can help: model what normal looks like, using only normal data, and flag anything that does not fit. Such methods are covered more in Data Mining (cse-7-6). Ensembles that combine undersampling with bagging, training many models on different balanced subsets, are another practical option.

Calibrating after resampling: Oversampling, undersampling or class weights change the class balance the model believes in, so its predicted probabilities are no longer realistic: a model trained on a 50-50 sample will predict fraud far more often than 1 percent. If you need true probabilities, for example to estimate expected losses, recalibrate the outputs on validation data that has the real class ratio. If you only need a ranking or a yes/no decision with a tuned threshold, this matters less.

Worked example, choosing by cost: Suppose a missed fraud costs the company 20000 taka on average and checking a false alarm costs 200 taka of staff time. Model X catches 8 of 10 frauds with 30 false alarms: cost = 2 times 20000 + 30 times 200 = 40000 + 6000 = 46000 taka. Model Y catches 9 of 10 with 80 false alarms: cost = 1 times 20000 + 80 times 200 = 20000 + 16000 = 36000 taka. Y has lower precision (9 / 89, about 0.10, versus 0.21) but is cheaper overall. The do-nothing model costs 10 times 20000 = 200000 taka. Putting money on the confusion matrix turns a confusing metric debate into a clear business decision.

A sensible order of attack: First, pick the right metric and make sure the validation and test sets have the real ratio and enough positives (use stratified splits). Second, try class weights or threshold moving, which are cheap and keep all data. Third, if results are still weak, try SMOTE or undersampling inside cross-validation and compare. Throughout, look for better features and more labelled positives, which usually help more than any resampling trick. Keep a baseline of the plain model to show what each step really adds.

Real example 1, mobile financial fraud: A mobile financial service in Bangladesh has millions of daily transactions and only a small number of confirmed frauds. The team trains a gradient-boosted tree model with class weights, keeps validation data at the true ratio, and chooses the threshold so that the investigation team receives about 500 alerts a day. They track precision at 500 (how many of the daily alerts are real fraud) and the share of reported fraud that the model had flagged in advance.

Real example 2, predicting machine failures in a garments factory: Sewing machines fail rarely, maybe a few times a year each. Sensor data from vibration and motor current is collected every minute, so 'failure within the next day' is a tiny minority. The engineers combine undersampling of normal periods with features like rising vibration over the last 6 hours, evaluate with recall and precision on a later month (time-based split), and accept many false alarms because an unnecessary check is cheap compared with a line stopping during an export order.

Common mistakes and exam questions: Reporting accuracy on imbalanced data. Resampling before splitting, which leaks copies into the test set. Oversampling the test set. Forgetting that class weights or resampling distort predicted probabilities. Using SMOTE blindly on categorical data. Exam questions: explain the accuracy paradox with numbers, compare undersampling, oversampling and SMOTE, compute a SMOTE point, compute balanced class weights, and choose suitable metrics for a fraud or disease scenario.

Recap: When one class is rare, a model can score high accuracy while catching nothing: on 990 normal and 10 fraud, 'always normal' gets 99 percent. Judge such models with precision, recall, F1 and precision-recall curves. Fix training with undersampling, oversampling, SMOTE (between (2, 3) and (4, 7) with r = 0.5 we made (3, 5)), class weights (0.505 versus 50 here) or threshold moving, applied only to training data. Better data and features often help most. And whenever you can, translate errors into real costs, as in our 46000 versus 36000 taka comparison. Next lesson starts the tour of classic algorithms with the simplest of all: k-nearest neighbours.
key_points: Imbalanced data has a rare minority class; models minimising average loss tend to ignore it.
Accuracy paradox: with 990 normal and 10 fraud, 'always normal' scores 99 percent accuracy and 0 recall.
Use confusion matrix, precision, recall, F1, precision-recall curves and precision at k instead of accuracy.
Resample training data only, inside each fold; validation and test keep the real class ratio.
Undersampling discards majority data; oversampling duplicates minority data and risks overfitting.
SMOTE makes new points new = x + r(n - x); x = (2, 3), n = (4, 7), r = 0.5 gives (3, 5).
Balanced class weights n / (K n_c) give 0.505 for normal and 50 for fraud here; threshold moving is another cheap fix.
Resampling and weights distort probabilities; recalibrate if real probabilities are needed.
lessons.tip: On any classification project, first print the class counts. If the smallest class is under about 10 percent, write 'imbalanced: no accuracy' at the top of your notes and choose your metric before training anything.
lessons.task: A school's attendance system wants to predict which of 400 students will drop out this year; last year only 12 did. Write down the accuracy of a model that always predicts 'stays', compute balanced class weights, and suggest which metric and which threshold strategy you would use, with one sentence of reasoning each.

quiz.q: In a dataset with 995 negatives and 5 positives, what accuracy does a model get by always predicting negative?
quiz.explain: It is right on all 995 negatives: 995 / 1000 = 99.5 percent, while catching no positives.

quiz.q: Which data should resampling methods such as SMOTE be applied to?
options: Only the training data (inside each fold)
quiz.explain: Validation and test sets must reflect the real distribution; resampling before splitting leaks data.

quiz.q: SMOTE with x = (1, 1), neighbour n = (3, 5) and r = 0.25 creates which point?
With 900 class A and 100 class B examples, what is the balanced weight n / (K n_c) for class B?
What is a key risk of plain random oversampling of the minority class?
options: The model may memorise the repeated minority examples and overfit
It makes the test set imbalanced
quiz.explain: Seeing exact copies many times encourages memorisation rather than generalisation.

lessons.title: k-Nearest Neighbours: Learning by Looking Around
lessons.content:
When you move to a new area of Dhaka and want to guess whether a restaurant is any good, you might simply ask the people who live closest to it. If most of your nearest neighbours say it is good, you trust it. That is the entire idea of the k-nearest neighbours algorithm (k-NN): to classify a new example, find the k most similar examples in the training data and let them vote. There is no equation to fit, no weights to learn, no gradient descent. It is perhaps the simplest machine learning method, and a surprisingly useful one, and studying it teaches deep lessons about distance, scaling and high-dimensional data.

Lazy learning: Most models do their hard work during training and are quick at prediction. k-NN is the opposite. Training is just storing the data. All the work happens at prediction time, when it compares the new example with stored ones. That is why k-NN is called a lazy learner or instance-based learner, while logistic regression, which builds a compact model in advance, is an eager learner. Laziness has a price: prediction can be slow and memory-hungry when the training set is large.

The algorithm: Given a new point q, compute its distance to every training point. Sort by distance and take the k nearest. For classification, predict the most common label among them (majority vote). For regression, predict the average of their target values. In pseudo-code: distances = [dist(q, x) for x in training]; nearest = k smallest; return majority_label(nearest) or mean_target(nearest). That's all.

Euclidean distance: The usual measure is straight-line distance. For points p = (p1, p2) and q = (q1, q2), the Euclidean distance is the square root of (p1 - q1)^2 + (p2 - q2)^2, and the same pattern extends to any number of features: square each difference, add them, take the square root. It is Pythagoras' theorem.

Manhattan distance: The Manhattan (city block) distance adds absolute differences: |p1 - q1| + |p2 - q2|. It is the distance a rickshaw travels on a grid of streets, where it cannot cut diagonally through buildings. It is less influenced by one large difference than Euclidean distance, because nothing is squared. Both are special cases of the Minkowski distance; you can try both as a hyperparameter.

Worked example, the data: Six fruits are described by two scaled features, size score and roughness score. Mangoes: A = (1, 2), B = (2, 3), C = (3, 1). Jackfruits: D = (6, 5), E = (7, 7), F = (8, 6). A new fruit has q = (4, 3). Which is it?

Worked example, the distances: To A: differences (-3, 1), Euclidean square root of (9 + 1) = 3.162, Manhattan 3 + 1 = 4. To B: differences (-2, 0), Euclidean 2.0, Manhattan 2. To C: differences (-1, -2), Euclidean square root of 5 = 2.236, Manhattan 3. To D: differences (2, 2), Euclidean square root of 8 = 2.828, Manhattan 4. To E: differences (3, 4), Euclidean 5.0, Manhattan 7. To F: differences (4, 3), Euclidean 5.0, Manhattan 7. Sorted by Euclidean distance: B (2.0), C (2.236), D (2.828), A (3.162), then E and F (5.0).

Worked example, the votes: With k = 1, the nearest is B, a mango, so we predict mango. With k = 3, the nearest are B, C and D: two mangoes and one jackfruit, so mango wins 2 to 1. With k = 5 we take B, C, D, A and then one of E or F, which are tied at 5.0: three mangoes against two jackfruits, still mango. With Manhattan distance the order is B (2), C (3), then A and D tied at 4: ties like this must be broken by a rule, such as preferring the smaller index or the closer Euclidean distance, or by distance weighting.

Choosing k: k is the key hyperparameter. With k = 1, the model follows every single training point, including noisy and mislabelled ones: low bias, high variance, and a jagged decision boundary. With large k, the prediction averages over many neighbours: smoother boundaries, more bias, less variance. If k equals the whole training set, k-NN always predicts the majority class. Choose k by cross-validation (lesson 13), commonly trying odd values like 1, 3, 5, ..., 21 for two-class problems, since odd k avoids voting ties.

Distance-weighted voting: Plain voting treats the 1st and the kth neighbour equally. Distance weighting gives closer neighbours more say, for example weight = 1 / distance. In our example with k = 3: B gets 1 / 2.0 = 0.5, C gets 1 / 2.236 = 0.447 and D gets 1 / 2.828 = 0.354. Mango total 0.947 versus jackfruit 0.354. Weighting also naturally breaks most ties.

Why scaling is essential: Distances add up differences across features, so a feature measured in big numbers dominates. Take three customers described by (age, monthly income in taka): a = (25, 30000), b = (26, 50000), c = (60, 31000). Unscaled, the distance from a to b is about 20000 and from a to c about 1000.6, so c looks far more similar to a, purely because the income gap with b is large in taka. Intuitively, a 25-year-old is more like a 26-year-old than a 60-year-old. After min-max scaling (age from range 20 to 60, income from range 20000 to 80000), the distances become 0.334 to b and 0.875 to c. Now b is the closer one. Without scaling, k-NN silently becomes an 'income-only' model.

Other ways to measure similarity: For categorical features, the Hamming distance counts how many features differ. Customer (Dhaka, bKash, student) and customer (Dhaka, Nagad, job holder) differ in 2 of 3 features, so the distance is 2. For text and other data where direction matters more than size, cosine similarity compares the angle between vectors: cos = (p dot q) / (length of p times length of q). The vectors (1, 2) and (2, 4) point the same way, so their cosine similarity is 1 even though one is twice as long; (1, 0) and (0, 1) are at right angles, with similarity 0. Two news articles that use the same words in the same proportions are similar even if one is much longer. Choosing the right similarity is part of designing a k-NN model.

k-NN as a baseline and a sanity check: Because it needs no training, k-NN is a quick baseline. If a carefully tuned logistic regression or tree cannot beat a 5-NN model on the validation set, something is wrong with the features or the setup. k-NN is also useful for finding near-duplicate rows and mislabelled examples: a training point whose nearest neighbours all carry a different label deserves a second look.

k-NN for regression: To predict a flat's rent, find the k most similar flats (by scaled size, rooms and location) and average their rents. If the 3 nearest flats rent for 15, 17 and 16 thousand taka, the prediction is (15 + 17 + 16) / 3 = 16 thousand. Distance weighting can be used here too. k-NN regression can follow any curved shape, but it cannot extrapolate: for a flat larger than all training flats, it can only predict rents similar to the largest ones it has seen.

The curse of dimensionality: k-NN works beautifully in 2 or 3 dimensions but struggles with many features. In high dimensions, data becomes sparse and distances lose meaning. Imagine data spread evenly in a unit cube and you want a neighbourhood containing 10 percent of the points. In 1 dimension you need a segment of length 0.1. In 10 dimensions, a small cube containing 10 percent of the volume needs edge length 0.1^(1/10), about 0.79, so your 'neighbourhood' stretches across most of every feature's range. In 100 dimensions it needs about 0.98. Nearest neighbours are then not really near, and the nearest and farthest points end up at similar distances. Irrelevant features make this much worse, because they add noise to every distance. Feature selection and dimensionality reduction (lesson 23) help.

The cost of laziness: Predicting one point needs a distance to every training point: n times d operations for n points with d features. For 1 million training points and thousands of queries per second, that is too slow. Data structures such as k-d trees and ball trees speed up search in low dimensions, and approximate nearest neighbour methods trade a little accuracy for big speedups in high dimensions. These ideas power modern similarity search, such as finding similar products or images.

Strengths and weaknesses: Strengths: no training time, simple to explain ('these five similar customers did X'), naturally handles many classes, and can model very irregular boundaries. Weaknesses: slow and memory-heavy predictions, sensitive to scaling and irrelevant features, poor in high dimensions, and needs a meaningful distance. Categorical features need a suitable distance too, such as counting mismatches.

Real example 1, recommending similar products: An online grocery in Dhaka represents each product by scaled features such as price, category one-hot columns and how often it is bought with other items. When a customer views a brand of lentils, the site shows the 5 nearest products by distance, a simple k-NN recommendation that needs no complex training and is easy to update as new products are added.

Real example 2, estimating land prices: A land registry office wants a quick estimate for a plot's price per decimal. Using recent sales described by scaled distance to the main road, distance to the upazila centre and whether the plot floods, it takes the 7 most similar recent sales and averages their prices, weighting closer matches more. Officials like it because each estimate comes with the actual comparable sales, which they can inspect.

Common mistakes and exam questions: Forgetting to scale features. Using an even k in a two-class problem and getting ties. Choosing k by training accuracy (k = 1 always scores 100 percent on training data, since each point is its own nearest neighbour). Including irrelevant features. Expecting k-NN to be fast on huge datasets. Exams ask: compute Euclidean and Manhattan distances, classify a point for k = 1 and k = 3, explain the effect of k on bias and variance, explain why scaling matters with numbers, and describe the curse of dimensionality.

Recap: k-NN stores the training data and predicts by letting the k nearest examples vote (classification) or average (regression). In our fruit example, q = (4, 3) was nearest to B (distance 2.0), and k = 1, 3 and 5 all predicted mango. Small k means low bias and high variance; large k the reverse. Scale features first (the age-income example flipped the nearest neighbour), beware of high dimensions, and remember that prediction cost grows with the data. Next lesson revisits naive Bayes, a classifier built from probabilities instead of distances.
key_points: k-NN stores the training data and predicts by majority vote (classification) or average (regression) of the k nearest points.
Euclidean distance = sqrt(sum of squared differences); Manhattan = sum of absolute differences.
Worked: q = (4, 3) has nearest neighbours B (2.0), C (2.236), D (2.828); k = 1, 3 and 5 all predict mango.
Small k gives low bias and high variance; large k gives smoother boundaries; choose k by cross-validation, odd for two classes.
Distance weighting (for example 1 / d) gives closer neighbours more say and breaks ties.
Scaling is essential: unscaled age and income made a 60-year-old look closest; after scaling the 26-year-old was.
The curse of dimensionality: to cover 10 percent of a 10-dimensional cube needs edge 0.79, so 'near' stops meaning near.
Lazy learning: no training cost but expensive predictions; k-d trees and approximate search help.
lessons.tip: Before running k-NN, ask two questions: 'Are all features scaled to similar ranges?' and 'Is every feature actually relevant to similarity?'. Most k-NN failures come from a 'no' to one of these.
lessons.task: Write down five friends with two features each, such as height in cm and how many hours a day they use their phone, plus whether they like cricket (yes or no). Add yourself as a new point. Scale both features with min-max, compute the Euclidean distances to the five friends, and predict whether you like cricket with k = 1 and k = 3.

quiz.q: Why is k-NN called a lazy learner?
options: It does almost no work at training time and does the work at prediction time
It learns slowly with gradient descent
It cannot handle more than two classes
quiz.explain: Training just stores the data; distances are computed when a prediction is needed.

quiz.q: What is the Manhattan distance between (1, 2) and (4, 6)?
quiz.explain: |1 - 4| + |2 - 6| = 3 + 4 = 7 (the Euclidean distance would be 5).

quiz.q: What usually happens as k increases from 1 to a large value?
options: The model always becomes more accurate
The decision boundary becomes more jagged
The boundary becomes smoother: variance falls and bias rises
quiz.explain: Averaging over more neighbours smooths predictions, trading variance for bias.

quiz.q: Why must features be scaled before k-NN?
options: k-NN only accepts values between 0 and 1
Features with large numeric ranges would dominate the distance
It reduces the number of neighbours
quiz.explain: Distances add raw differences, so income in taka swamps age in years unless both are scaled.

quiz.q: Why does k-NN with k = 1 always get 100 percent TRAINING accuracy (with no duplicate points having different labels)?
options: Because k = 1 is always the best setting
Because each training point is its own nearest neighbour
quiz.explain: The distance from a point to itself is 0, so it predicts its own label; this says nothing about generalisation.

lessons.title: Naive Bayes and Probabilistic Classifiers
lessons.content:
Your phone buzzes with an SMS: 'Congratulations! You have won a free offer, click now'. Before reading to the end, you already feel it is spam. Why? Words like 'congratulations', 'free' and 'offer' are far more common in spam than in messages from your family. You are combining clues, each nudging your belief up or down. Naive Bayes is a classifier that does exactly this with probabilities. You met it briefly in the Artificial Intelligence course as a spam filter; here we treat it as a machine learning model, add the practical fixes that make it work, and compare it with the other classifiers in this course.

Bayes' rule, a quick recap: For a class C and evidence x, Bayes' rule says P(C | x) = P(x | C) times P(C) / P(x). P(C) is the prior: how common the class is before seeing the evidence. P(x | C) is the likelihood: how probable the evidence is if the class is C. P(C | x) is the posterior: our updated belief after seeing the evidence. P(x) is the same for every class, so to compare classes we only need the numerator: posterior is proportional to likelihood times prior. The details of Bayes' theorem were covered in Probability and Statistics (cse-2-6); here we use it.

The problem with many features: An email has thousands of possible words. To estimate P(x | spam) for the exact combination of words in one email, we would need many examples of that exact combination, which never exist. The number of possible combinations explodes with the number of features. We need a simplification.

The naive assumption: Naive Bayes assumes that, given the class, the features are independent of each other. Then the likelihood of all features factorises into a product: P(x1, x2, ..., xd | C) = P(x1 | C) times P(x2 | C) times ... times P(xd | C). Each factor can be estimated by simple counting. The assumption is called naive because it is usually false: in spam, 'free' and 'offer' tend to appear together. Surprisingly, naive Bayes often classifies well anyway, because to pick the right class it only needs the correct class to get the highest score, not exactly correct probabilities.

The classifier: For each class C, compute score(C) = P(C) times the product of P(xj | C) over all features, then predict the class with the highest score. To turn scores into probabilities, divide each score by the sum of all scores. Training is just counting: P(C) is the fraction of training examples in class C, and P(xj | C) is how often feature j takes its value among class C examples.

Worked example, the training counts: A tiny training set has 10 SMS messages: 4 spam and 6 not spam (ham). Our vocabulary has just two words. 'offer' appears in 3 of the 4 spam and 1 of the 6 ham. 'meeting' appears in 0 of the 4 spam and 4 of the 6 ham. So the priors are P(spam) = 4/10 = 0.4 and P(ham) = 0.6. The likelihoods are P(offer | spam) = 3/4 = 0.75, P(offer | ham) = 1/6, P(meeting | spam) = 0/4 = 0, P(meeting | ham) = 4/6.

Worked example, one word: A new message contains 'offer' (ignore 'meeting' for now). Score(spam) = 0.4 times 0.75 = 0.3. Score(ham) = 0.6 times 1/6 = 0.1. Normalising, P(spam | offer) = 0.3 / (0.3 + 0.1) = 0.75. One word moved the belief from the prior of 40 percent spam to 75 percent.

The zero-probability problem: Now a message contains both 'offer' and 'meeting'. Score(spam) = 0.4 times 0.75 times P(meeting | spam) = 0.4 times 0.75 times 0 = 0. A single word never seen in spam training data makes spam impossible, no matter how strong all the other evidence is. That is clearly too extreme; it just means our small sample happened not to contain it. With large vocabularies this happens constantly.

Laplace smoothing: The fix is to pretend we saw every outcome at least once more than we did. For a yes/no word feature, use P(word | C) = (count + 1) / (number of class C examples + 2), adding 1 to the count and 2 to the total because there are two outcomes (present, absent). This is Laplace (add-one) smoothing. It never gives zero and barely changes probabilities when counts are large. More generally, add alpha to each count and alpha times the number of possible values to the total.

Worked example, with smoothing: Now P(offer | spam) = (3 + 1) / (4 + 2) = 4/6 = 0.667, P(offer | ham) = (1 + 1) / (6 + 2) = 2/8 = 0.25, P(meeting | spam) = (0 + 1) / (4 + 2) = 1/6 = 0.167, P(meeting | ham) = (4 + 1) / (6 + 2) = 5/8 = 0.625. For the message with both words: score(spam) = 0.4 times 0.667 times 0.167 = 0.0444, score(ham) = 0.6 times 0.25 times 0.625 = 0.0938. So P(spam) = 0.0444 / (0.0444 + 0.0938) = 0.32. The message is predicted ham: 'meeting' is strong evidence for ham, but no longer an absolute veto.

Working with logarithms: Multiplying thousands of small probabilities quickly produces numbers too small for a computer to store (underflow): they become exactly 0. The standard trick is to add logarithms instead: log score(C) = log P(C) + sum of log P(xj | C). Since log is increasing, the class with the highest log score is the same as with the highest score. In our example, log score(spam) = log 0.4 + log 0.667 + log 0.167, about -0.92 - 0.41 - 1.79 = -3.11, and log score(ham) = log 0.6 + log 0.25 + log 0.625, about -0.51 - 1.39 - 0.47 = -2.37, so ham wins, as before.

A hidden linear classifier: Look at the log score again: log P(C) plus a sum of per-word terms. For two classes, the difference log score(spam) - log score(ham) works out to a constant plus a weighted sum of the word features (for the multinomial version, one fixed number added for each occurrence of a word). Predicting spam when this difference is positive is exactly a linear decision rule, the same shape as logistic regression's z = w x + b. The weights here are not tuned by gradient descent but read off from counts. This explains both why naive Bayes is so fast and why its boundary is as simple as logistic regression's.

Preparing text: For text, the features come from tokenisation, splitting text into words. For Bangla and mixed Bangla-English messages, decisions such as lower-casing English words, removing punctuation, handling both Bangla and English digits, and treating 'offer' and 'offers' as the same word all change the counts. Words never seen during training are usually ignored at prediction time, since they give no evidence either way. Very common words like 'and' or 'এবং' carry little information and are sometimes removed. These choices often matter more than the choice between naive Bayes variants.

Variants for different features: Bernoulli naive Bayes models each word as present or absent, like our example. Multinomial naive Bayes models word counts, so a word appearing five times counts more; it is the classic choice for text classification. Gaussian naive Bayes handles numeric features by assuming each feature within each class follows a bell curve, estimated by the class mean and standard deviation; the likelihood of a value is read from that bell curve. For example, to classify fish as rui or katla from length and weight, it learns a mean and spread of length for rui, another for katla, and so on.

Generative versus discriminative models: Naive Bayes is a generative model: it models how the data is generated in each class, P(x | C) and P(C), and then uses Bayes' rule. Logistic regression is discriminative: it models P(C | x) directly and only cares about the boundary between classes. Generative models can learn from fewer examples and handle missing features naturally; discriminative models usually reach higher accuracy when data is plentiful, because they do not depend on assumptions about how features are distributed. This distinction is explored more in Pattern Recognition (cse-6-12).

Strengths and weaknesses: Naive Bayes trains in a single pass of counting, is extremely fast, works with very many features, needs relatively little data and is easy to update with new examples. It is a strong baseline for text. Weaknesses: the independence assumption makes its probabilities overconfident (often very close to 0 or 1), so they should not be trusted as calibrated values; strongly correlated features get double-counted; and on large datasets with complex patterns, other models usually win.

Real example 1, Bangla news categorisation: A news portal wants to tag articles as politics, sports, economy or entertainment. Each article becomes word counts after splitting Bangla text into words. A multinomial naive Bayes with smoothing is trained on a few thousand labelled articles in seconds. Words like 'উইকেট' and 'গোল' push towards sports, 'বাজেট' and 'মূল্যস্ফীতি' towards economy. It gives a solid baseline that more complex models must beat, and it can be retrained nightly with new articles.

Real example 2, quick triage from symptoms: A rural health worker app suggests whether a patient's fever is more likely to be dengue, typhoid or a common viral fever, using yes/no symptoms (rash, joint pain, abdominal pain, duration over a week). A naive Bayes model built from clinic records gives a ranked list, and smoothing prevents a single unusual symptom from ruling a disease out completely. Because its probabilities are overconfident, the app shows the ranking and advises tests rather than displaying exact percentages.

Common mistakes and exam questions: Forgetting the prior. Forgetting smoothing and getting zeros. Multiplying probabilities without logs on long documents. Treating naive Bayes probabilities as well calibrated. Saying naive Bayes requires features to be independent in order to work at all (it often works despite dependence). Exams ask: compute class scores and posteriors from a small table, apply Laplace smoothing, explain the naive assumption, explain why logs are used, and compare generative and discriminative models.

Recap: Naive Bayes applies Bayes' rule with the assumption that features are independent given the class, so the score is the prior times a product of per-feature likelihoods, all learned by counting. In our SMS example, 'offer' alone gave P(spam) = 0.75; adding 'meeting' gave zero without smoothing and 0.32 with Laplace smoothing. Use logs to avoid underflow, pick Bernoulli, multinomial or Gaussian variants to suit the features, and treat its probabilities as rankings. Next lesson builds classifiers in a completely different way: by asking a sequence of questions, in a decision tree. Keep the counting spirit of naive Bayes in mind, though: decision trees also learn by counting how classes are distributed, just organised as a flowchart instead of a product of probabilities.
key_points: Bayes' rule: posterior P(C | x) is proportional to likelihood P(x | C) times prior P(C).
The naive assumption: features are independent given the class, so the likelihood is a product of per-feature terms.
Training is counting: priors are class fractions; likelihoods are feature frequencies within each class.
Worked: P(spam) = 0.4, P(offer | spam) = 0.75, P(offer | ham) = 1/6 give P(spam | offer) = 0.75.
A single zero count wipes out a class; Laplace smoothing (count + 1) / (n + 2) fixes it (posterior 0.32 in the example).
Sum log probabilities instead of multiplying to avoid underflow.
Bernoulli, multinomial and Gaussian variants suit binary, count and numeric features.
Naive Bayes is generative and fast but overconfident; logistic regression is discriminative.
lessons.tip: When you build any text classifier, train a multinomial naive Bayes first. It takes seconds and gives you an honest baseline; if your fancy model cannot clearly beat it, look at your data before your algorithm.
lessons.task: Collect 10 SMS or messenger messages from your phone (no private details needed, just mark each as 'promo' or 'personal'). Pick two words, count how often each appears in each class, apply Laplace smoothing, and compute by hand which class naive Bayes would predict for a new message containing both words.

options: Features are independent of each other given the class
quiz.explain: Conditional independence lets the joint likelihood factorise into a product of single-feature likelihoods.

quiz.q: A word appears in 0 of 8 spam training messages. With Laplace smoothing (count + 1) / (n + 2), what is P(word | spam)?
Why do implementations add log probabilities instead of multiplying probabilities?
options: Logs make the model more accurate
Logs remove the need for priors
Multiplying many small numbers underflows to zero on a computer

quiz.q: Scores are spam 0.03 and ham 0.09. What is P(spam | x)?
Which statement about naive Bayes versus logistic regression is correct?
options: Naive Bayes is discriminative, logistic regression is generative
Logistic regression always needs less data
Naive Bayes is generative (models P(x | C) and P(C)); logistic regression models P(C | x) directly

lessons.title: Decision Trees: Entropy, Information Gain and Gini
lessons.content:
Think of the game where one friend thinks of a cricketer and the others guess by asking yes/no questions: 'Is he Bangladeshi?', 'Is he a bowler?', 'Has he captained the team?'. Good players ask questions that split the possibilities roughly in half, so they reach the answer quickly. A decision tree is a machine learning model that plays this game with data. It learns a flowchart of questions about the features, and each path from the top to the bottom ends in a prediction. Trees are easy to read, need little data preparation, and are the building blocks of the powerful ensemble methods in the next lesson. The AI course introduced the idea; here we work through the maths properly.

The structure: A decision tree has a root node at the top, internal nodes that each test one feature (for example 'weather = cloudy?' or 'income above 30000?'), branches for the possible answers, and leaf nodes that give the prediction. To classify an example, start at the root, follow the branch that matches its feature value, and continue until you reach a leaf. The leaf predicts the majority class of the training examples that ended up there (or their average value, for regression).

How a tree is learned: The standard approach is greedy, top-down splitting. At the root, consider every feature and every possible split, and pick the one that makes the resulting groups as pure as possible, meaning each group is dominated by one class. Split the data accordingly. Then repeat the same process inside each branch, using only the examples that reached it. Stop when a node is pure, or other stopping rules apply. This is called recursive partitioning. It is greedy because it picks the best split right now without looking ahead, which is fast but not guaranteed to find the best possible tree.

Measuring impurity with entropy: Entropy measures how mixed a group is. For two classes with proportions p and 1 - p, entropy H = -p log2(p) - (1 - p) log2(1 - p), measured in bits (with 0 log 0 taken as 0). A pure group has entropy 0. A 50-50 mix has entropy 1 bit, the maximum for two classes. With more classes, sum -p log2(p) over all classes.

Worked example, the data: Ten afternoons were recorded for a class deciding whether to play football after school: 6 days yes and 4 days no. The parent entropy is H = -0.6 log2(0.6) - 0.4 log2(0.4) = 0.6 times 0.737 + 0.4 times 1.322 = 0.442 + 0.529 = 0.971 bits. Two candidate features: Weather (hot-sunny, cloudy, light rain) and Wind (weak, strong).

Worked example, splitting on Weather: Hot-sunny days: 4 days, 1 yes and 3 no. Cloudy: 3 days, 3 yes and 0 no. Light rain: 3 days, 2 yes and 1 no. Entropies: hot-sunny H(1/4) = 0.811; cloudy is pure, H = 0; light rain H(2/3) = 0.918. The weighted average entropy after splitting is (4/10) times 0.811 + (3/10) times 0 + (3/10) times 0.918 = 0.324 + 0 + 0.275 = 0.600.

Information gain: Information gain is the drop in entropy caused by a split: IG = parent entropy - weighted child entropy. For Weather, IG = 0.971 - 0.600 = 0.371 bits. Now Wind: weak wind on 5 days (4 yes, 1 no), strong wind on 5 days (2 yes, 3 no). Entropies 0.722 and 0.971, weighted (5/10) times 0.722 + (5/10) times 0.971 = 0.846. IG(Wind) = 0.971 - 0.846 = 0.125 bits. Weather gives much more information, so the tree's root question is 'What is the weather?'. The cloudy branch is already pure (predict yes); the other two branches are split further using the remaining features.

Gini impurity: An alternative measure, used by the CART algorithm, is Gini impurity: G = 1 - sum of p_k squared. It is the probability that two examples drawn at random (with replacement) from the group have different classes. Pure groups have G = 0; a 50-50 two-class group has G = 0.5. For the parent: G = 1 - 0.6^2 - 0.4^2 = 1 - 0.36 - 0.16 = 0.48.

Worked example, Gini for both features: Weather: hot-sunny G = 1 - (1/4)^2 - (3/4)^2 = 1 - 0.0625 - 0.5625 = 0.375; cloudy G = 0; light rain G = 1 - (2/3)^2 - (1/3)^2 = 1 - 0.444 - 0.111 = 0.444. Weighted: 0.4 times 0.375 + 0.3 times 0 + 0.3 times 0.444 = 0.150 + 0.133 = 0.283, a drop of 0.48 - 0.283 = 0.197. Wind: weak G = 1 - 0.64 - 0.04 = 0.32, strong G = 1 - 0.16 - 0.36 = 0.48, weighted 0.5 times 0.32 + 0.5 times 0.48 = 0.40, a drop of only 0.08. Gini also picks Weather. In practice entropy and Gini usually choose the same or very similar splits; Gini is slightly cheaper because it needs no logarithms.

The bias of information gain: Information gain favours features with many distinct values. A 'date' or 'student ID' feature splits every example into its own pure leaf, giving maximum gain while being useless for prediction. The C4.5 algorithm corrects for this with the gain ratio, which divides information gain by the entropy of the split itself. The older ID3 algorithm uses plain information gain; CART uses Gini and makes only binary (two-way) splits.

Numeric features: For a numeric feature, the tree chooses a threshold: 'temperature at most t?' versus 'above t?'. Sort the values and try thresholds halfway between neighbouring values. Example: temperatures 25, 28, 31 and 34 with labels yes, yes, no, no. Candidate thresholds are 26.5, 29.5 and 32.5. The split at 29.5 gives two pure groups (25 and 28 yes; 31 and 34 no), so it has the best gain. The same feature can be split again lower in the tree with a different threshold, letting trees model non-linear patterns without any feature engineering.

When to stop and overfitting: If we keep splitting until every leaf is pure, the tree can memorise the training data, including noise, ending with one example per leaf: low bias, very high variance. Common stopping rules (pre-pruning): a maximum depth, a minimum number of samples needed to split a node, a minimum number of samples per leaf, or a minimum impurity decrease. These are hyperparameters, tuned with cross-validation. A tree of depth 3 might underfit; depth 20 might badly overfit.

Pruning: Another approach is to grow a large tree and then cut back branches that do not help on validation data (post-pruning). Cost-complexity pruning, used in CART, adds a penalty per leaf, similar in spirit to regularisation: a branch is kept only if it reduces the error by more than the penalty. Pruned trees are smaller, easier to read and usually generalise better.

Trees as rules, and how big they get: Every root-to-leaf path is an if-then rule: 'IF weather = cloudy THEN play = yes'; a deeper rule might read 'IF weather = hot-sunny AND wind = strong THEN play = no'. A binary tree of depth d has at most 2^d leaves, so depth 3 means at most 8 rules and depth 10 up to 1024. That is why a depth limit is such an effective complexity dial: each extra level can double the number of regions the tree carves the feature space into, and with it the risk of fitting noise.

Missing values and categories in trees: Trees cope with messy data better than most models. Categorical features can be split directly by grouping categories, without one-hot encoding in implementations that support it. For missing values, some implementations learn which branch missing values should follow, while others use surrogate splits on correlated features; simpler libraries still require you to impute first. Because only the ordering of values matters for numeric splits, monotonic changes such as scaling or taking logarithms leave the learned tree unchanged.

Regression trees: Trees can predict numbers too. Each leaf predicts the average target of its training examples, and splits are chosen to reduce variance (the spread of targets) or squared error, instead of entropy. A regression tree predicting rent might first split on 'size at most 900 square feet', then on 'area = Gulshan or not', producing a step-shaped prediction function. It cannot extrapolate beyond the largest values seen in a leaf.

Strengths: Trees are interpretable: a short tree can be drawn and explained to a manager or a doctor. They handle numeric and categorical features, need no scaling, capture interactions between features naturally (a split on one feature, then another inside it), and are fast to predict. Feature importance can be measured by how much each feature reduces impurity across the tree.

Weaknesses: Single trees are unstable: small changes in the data can produce a completely different tree, which is high variance. Their predictions are piecewise constant, with axis-parallel boundaries, so a simple diagonal boundary needs many steps. Greedy learning can miss good combinations of splits. And an unpruned tree overfits easily. The next lesson shows how combining many trees fixes most of these problems.

Real example 1, a loan officer's checklist: A cooperative bank in Bogura builds a depth-3 tree to decide which small business loan applications need a field visit. The root splits on 'months of regular income at least 12', then on 'existing loans' and 'business type'. The tree's leaves come with counts, such as '84 past applicants, 91 percent repaid', so officers can see and question the logic, which matters for fairness and regulation.

Real example 2, diagnosing crop problems: An agriculture extension app asks farmers a few questions: Are the leaves yellow at the tips? Is the field waterlogged? Are there spots on the leaves? Behind the screen is a decision tree learned from expert-labelled cases, pruned so that it asks at most four questions. It is easy to translate into Bangla and voice prompts, and agronomists can check each path for sense.

Common mistakes and exam questions: Using log base e and calling the result bits. Forgetting to weight child entropies by group size. Choosing splits by training accuracy alone. Letting the tree grow fully without pruning. Including ID-like features. Exams love: compute entropy and Gini for a node, compute information gain for two candidate features and pick the root, compute a numeric threshold, explain pruning, and list advantages and disadvantages of trees.

Recap: A decision tree is a flowchart of feature tests learned by greedy recursive splitting. Entropy (0.971 bits for 6 yes and 4 no) and Gini (0.48) measure impurity; information gain picks the split that reduces impurity most: Weather gained 0.371 bits against Wind's 0.125, and Gini agreed (0.197 versus 0.08). Numeric features use thresholds, regression trees predict leaf averages, and depth limits or pruning control overfitting. Trees are readable but unstable, which leads directly to the next lesson: ensembles.
key_points: A decision tree is a flowchart: internal nodes test features, leaves give predictions; it is learned by greedy top-down splitting.
Entropy H = -sum p log2 p; for 6 yes and 4 no it is 0.971 bits; pure nodes have 0.
Information gain = parent entropy - weighted child entropy; Weather gave 0.371 bits, Wind 0.125, so Weather is the root.
Gini = 1 - sum p^2; parent 0.48, Weather split 0.283, Wind split 0.40; Gini also picks Weather.
Information gain favours many-valued features such as IDs; C4.5 uses gain ratio, CART uses Gini with binary splits.
Numeric features split at thresholds between sorted values (29.5 in the example).
Depth limits, minimum leaf sizes and pruning prevent overfitting; regression trees predict leaf averages.
Trees are interpretable and need no scaling but are unstable (high variance).
lessons.tip: When computing information gain by hand, make a small table for each candidate feature with columns: branch, count, yes, no, entropy, weight times entropy. It prevents the most common slip: forgetting to weight by branch size.
lessons.task: Record 8 to 10 days of your own life with two features (for example 'had a test that day: yes/no' and 'slept less than 6 hours: yes/no') and a label ('felt tired: yes/no'). Compute the information gain of each feature by hand and draw the one-level tree it suggests.

quiz.q: What is the entropy of a node with 4 yes and 4 no examples?
quiz.explain: A 50-50 mix of two classes has the maximum entropy of 1 bit.

quiz.q: What is the Gini impurity of a node with 3 examples of class A and 1 of class B?
Parent entropy is 1.0; after a split the weighted child entropy is 0.7. What is the information gain?
Why can plain information gain be misleading with a 'student ID' feature?
options: IDs split data into tiny pure groups, giving high gain but no predictive value
quiz.explain: Each ID gets its own pure leaf, maximising gain while generalising to nothing; gain ratio corrects this bias.

quiz.q: Which is a common way to stop a decision tree from overfitting?
options: Limiting maximum depth or pruning branches
quiz.explain: Depth limits, minimum samples per leaf and pruning reduce the tree's variance.

lessons.title: Ensemble Methods: Bagging, Random Forests and Boosting
lessons.content:
On the TV quiz show 'Who Wants to Be a Millionaire', contestants can ask the audience. Each audience member alone may be unsure or wrong, yet the most popular answer is right remarkably often, because individual mistakes point in different directions and partly cancel out. That is the wisdom of crowds, and it is the idea behind ensemble methods: instead of trusting one model, train many and combine their predictions. Ensembles of decision trees, in particular random forests and gradient boosting, are among the most successful methods for tabular data, the kind of spreadsheet-style data that most businesses have.

Why combining helps: In lesson 09 we saw that error comes from bias and variance. Averaging several models whose errors are not identical reduces variance, because random mistakes cancel. A single decision tree has high variance: small changes in the data give a different tree. That makes trees perfect candidates for averaging. A different strategy, boosting, builds models one after another, each fixing the previous ones' mistakes, which mainly reduces bias. Both rely on one condition: the models must make different errors. Ten identical models voting give exactly the same answer as one.

Worked example, majority vote: Suppose three classifiers are each correct 70 percent of the time, and their errors are independent. A majority vote is right when at least two of the three are right. The probability that all three are right is 0.7^3 = 0.343. The probability that exactly two are right is 3 times 0.7^2 times 0.3 = 3 times 0.49 times 0.3 = 0.441 (three ways to choose which one is wrong). Total: 0.343 + 0.441 = 0.784. The ensemble jumps from 70 to 78.4 percent. With five such voters, the majority (at least 3 of 5) is right with probability about 0.837. In reality errors are correlated, so gains are smaller, which is why ensemble methods work hard to make their members different.

Bootstrap sampling: How do we get different models from one dataset? One way is to train each on a different random sample. A bootstrap sample is drawn from the n training rows with replacement, also n rows in size. Some rows appear twice or more, others not at all. The probability that a particular row is picked at least once is 1 - (1 - 1/n)^n. For n = 10, that is 1 - 0.9^10 = 1 - 0.349 = 0.651. For large n it approaches 1 - 1/e, about 0.632. So each bootstrap sample contains about 63.2 percent of the distinct rows, and the remaining 36.8 percent are left out.

Bagging: Bagging stands for bootstrap aggregating. Draw B bootstrap samples, train one model on each (usually a deep, unpruned decision tree, which has low bias and high variance), and combine them: majority vote for classification, average for regression. Each tree overfits its own sample in its own way; averaging cancels much of that variance while keeping the low bias. In pseudo-code: for b in 1..B: sample = bootstrap(data); tree[b] = grow_tree(sample); predict(x) = majority or mean of tree[b](x) over all b. The trees can be trained in parallel.

Out-of-bag error: Since each tree never saw about 36.8 percent of the rows, those out-of-bag (OOB) rows can serve as a free validation set. For each training row, collect predictions only from the trees that did not see it, combine them, and compare with the true label. The resulting OOB error is a good estimate of test error without a separate validation split, which is handy when data is limited.

Random forests: Bagged trees are still correlated: if one feature is very strong, almost every tree splits on it at the top, and the trees look alike. Random forests, introduced by Leo Breiman in 2001, add a second source of randomness: at each split, the tree may only consider a random subset of the features. A common default for classification is the square root of the number of features: with 16 features, each split chooses among a random 4. For regression, a common default is about one third of the features. This decorrelates the trees, so averaging removes more variance. Random forests are robust, need little tuning, handle many features, and rarely overfit badly as more trees are added; more trees mainly cost time.

Random forest hyperparameters and importance: The main settings are the number of trees (hundreds is common; performance usually levels off rather than getting worse), the number of features per split, and tree size limits such as minimum samples per leaf. Random forests also report feature importance, for example the total impurity decrease each feature provides across all trees, or the drop in accuracy when a feature's values are randomly shuffled (permutation importance). Impurity-based importance can be biased towards features with many distinct values, so permutation importance is often more trustworthy.

Boosting, the idea: Boosting builds an ensemble sequentially. Start with a weak model, one only a bit better than guessing, such as a decision stump (a tree with a single split). Look at where it makes mistakes. Train the next weak model to focus on those mistakes. Keep adding models, each correcting the errors of the ensemble so far, and combine them with weights. Many weak learners become one strong learner. Because each new model targets remaining errors, boosting mainly reduces bias, and it can overfit if run too long, so the number of rounds is tuned with validation data.

AdaBoost: AdaBoost (adaptive boosting) keeps a weight on every training example. Initially all weights are equal. After training a weak learner, compute its weighted error e and give it a say alpha = 0.5 times ln((1 - e) / e). Then increase the weights of misclassified examples and decrease the others, so the next learner pays more attention to the hard cases. The final prediction is the sign of the alpha-weighted vote of all learners.

Worked example, one AdaBoost round: Ten examples each start with weight 0.1. A stump misclassifies 2 of them, so e = 0.2. Its say is alpha = 0.5 times ln(0.8 / 0.2) = 0.5 times ln 4 = 0.693. Misclassified weights are multiplied by e^alpha = 2, becoming 0.2 each; correct ones are multiplied by e^(-alpha) = 0.5, becoming 0.05 each. The new total is 2 times 0.2 + 8 times 0.05 = 0.4 + 0.4 = 0.8, so after normalising (dividing by 0.8), each misclassified example has weight 0.25 and each correct one 0.0625. The two hard examples now carry half of the total weight, so the next stump is forced to focus on them. A learner with error 0.5 would get alpha = 0: no better than a coin, no say.

Gradient boosting: Gradient boosting generalises the idea. Each new tree is trained to predict the residual errors (more precisely, the negative gradient of the loss) of the current ensemble, and its predictions are added with a small learning rate. Example: the true value is 20 and the first model predicts 15, leaving a residual of 5. The next tree learns to predict residuals and outputs 4 for this example; with learning rate 0.5, the ensemble's new prediction is 15 + 0.5 times 4 = 17. Step by step, predictions move towards the truth, very much like gradient descent but in the space of functions. Popular, highly optimised implementations include XGBoost, LightGBM and CatBoost; gradient boosted trees often give top results on tabular data, but need careful tuning of the learning rate, number of trees and tree depth, usually with early stopping.

Bagging versus boosting: Bagging trains models independently and in parallel, on bootstrap samples, and averages them; it mainly reduces variance and works best with strong, unstable learners such as deep trees. Boosting trains models sequentially, each depending on the previous ones, and combines them with weights; it mainly reduces bias, works with weak learners such as shallow trees, and is more sensitive to noisy labels and to the number of rounds. Random forests are the easy, robust default; gradient boosting often wins with tuning.

Stacking: Stacking combines different kinds of models, for example a logistic regression, a k-NN and a random forest. Their predictions (made out-of-fold, so no leakage) become input features for a final meta-model that learns how much to trust each one. It can squeeze out extra accuracy, and it appears often in competitions, at the cost of complexity and interpretability.

Costs of ensembles: Hundreds of trees are slower to predict and need more memory than one model, and they are much harder to explain than a single small tree or a logistic regression. Tools for explaining ensembles exist, such as feature importance and per-prediction explanation methods, but a bank or hospital that needs a simple, auditable rule may still prefer a simpler model with slightly lower accuracy.

Real example 1, predicting garment order delays: An export garments factory in Gazipur predicts which orders will ship late, from features such as order size, fabric type, number of style changes, line efficiency and supplier history. A single tree reaches an F1 of around 0.6 and changes a lot with each month's data. A random forest with 300 trees is more stable and more accurate, and its permutation importance shows that late fabric arrival and style changes matter most, guiding management action.

Real example 2, credit scoring with gradient boosting: A fintech lender in Dhaka compares logistic regression with gradient boosted trees on past loan data. Boosting achieves a noticeably higher AUC on a time-based test set. Because regulators and customers need explanations, the lender uses per-applicant explanation tools and also checks that the model behaves sensibly, for example that higher income never lowers the predicted repayment probability, before deployment.

Common mistakes and exam questions: Believing more trees in a random forest causes overfitting (it mostly just costs time; overfitting comes from other settings). Running boosting for too many rounds without early stopping. Using impurity importance as if it were causal. Forgetting that ensemble members must be diverse. Exams ask: compute the accuracy of a majority vote of independent classifiers, explain the 63.2 percent bootstrap fact, describe bagging and random forests and how they differ, perform one AdaBoost weight update, and compare bagging with boosting.

Recap: Ensembles combine many models whose errors differ. Majority voting of three independent 70 percent classifiers gives 78.4 percent. Bagging trains trees on bootstrap samples, each containing about 63.2 percent of distinct rows, and averages them; out-of-bag rows give a free error estimate. Random forests add random feature subsets at each split to decorrelate trees. Boosting builds models sequentially to fix earlier errors: AdaBoost reweights examples (alpha = 0.693 for error 0.2), and gradient boosting fits residuals with a learning rate. Next lesson introduces support vector machines, which seek the safest possible boundary between classes. Where ensembles win by combining many imperfect opinions, SVMs win by choosing one boundary very carefully.
key_points: Ensembles combine models with different errors; averaging reduces variance, boosting reduces bias.
Three independent 70 percent classifiers voting are right with probability 0.343 + 0.441 = 0.784.
A bootstrap sample of size n contains each row with probability 1 - (1 - 1/n)^n, about 63.2 percent for large n.
Bagging trains deep trees on bootstrap samples and votes or averages; out-of-bag rows give a free error estimate.
Random forests also pick a random subset of features at each split (for example 4 of 16) to decorrelate trees.
AdaBoost: alpha = 0.5 ln((1 - e) / e); with e = 0.2, alpha = 0.693 and misclassified weights rise to 0.25 each.
Gradient boosting adds trees that fit residuals with a learning rate (15 + 0.5 x 4 = 17 in the example).
Random forests are robust defaults; boosting often wins with careful tuning and early stopping.
lessons.tip: For any tabular prediction problem, train three models before anything fancy: a regularised linear or logistic model, a random forest with default settings, and a gradient boosted model with early stopping. Their comparison tells you a lot about how much non-linear structure your data has.
lessons.task: Ask five friends independently to guess the weight of a bag of rice or a jackfruit (in kg) without a scale, then weigh it. Compare each person's error with the error of the average guess. Then compute, for three independent voters who are each right 60 percent of the time, the probability that the majority is right.

quiz.q: Three independent classifiers are each 70 percent accurate. What is the accuracy of their majority vote?
For a large dataset, about what fraction of distinct rows appears in one bootstrap sample?
quiz.explain: The chance a row is picked at least once approaches 1 - 1/e, about 0.632.

quiz.q: What extra randomness does a random forest add compared with plain bagging of trees?
options: Each split considers only a random subset of features
Each tree uses a random loss function
Trees are trained in random order
quiz.explain: Random feature subsets at each split decorrelate the trees, making averaging more effective.

quiz.q: In AdaBoost, a weak learner has weighted error 0.2. What is its say alpha = 0.5 ln((1 - e) / e)?
Which statement best contrasts bagging and boosting?
options: Bagging trains models in parallel to reduce variance; boosting trains them sequentially to reduce bias
Bagging trains sequentially; boosting in parallel
Both only work with linear models
Boosting uses bootstrap samples; bagging reweights errors
quiz.explain: Bagging averages independent models; boosting adds models that fix previous errors.

lessons.title: Support Vector Machines: Maximum Margin and Kernels
lessons.content:
Imagine you must draw a boundary line between two villages' fields so that farmers from both sides are least likely to argue. Many lines would technically separate the fields. The wisest choice is the line that stays as far as possible from the nearest field on each side, leaving a wide no-man's-land. A small mistake in surveying will not push anyone onto the wrong side. Support vector machines (SVMs) choose a classification boundary in exactly this spirit: among all boundaries that separate the classes, they pick the one with the widest safety margin. Add the clever 'kernel trick' for curved boundaries, and you have one of the most elegant classic ML methods.

The setting: SVMs are mainly used for binary classification, with labels written as +1 and -1. Like logistic regression, a linear SVM uses a linear score s = w dot x + b and predicts +1 if s is positive and -1 otherwise. The boundary is the hyperplane w dot x + b = 0: a line in 2D, a plane in 3D. The difference lies in how w and b are chosen. Logistic regression maximises the likelihood of all training points; an SVM focuses on the points closest to the boundary.

Many boundaries, one best: If two classes can be separated by a straight line, there are usually infinitely many such lines. Some pass very close to a training point; a new point slightly different from it could easily fall on the wrong side. Intuition says the line in the 'middle of the gap' should generalise best. Statistical learning theory supports this: a larger margin is linked to better generalisation guarantees.

The margin: The distance from a point x to the hyperplane w dot x + b = 0 is |w dot x + b| divided by the length of w, written ||w||. The margin is the distance from the boundary to the closest training points. An SVM scales w and b so that the closest points satisfy |w dot x + b| = 1, which places them on two parallel 'gutter' lines, w dot x + b = +1 and w dot x + b = -1. The distance between these gutters, the full margin width, is 2 / ||w||. So maximising the margin is the same as minimising ||w||, subject to every training point being on its correct side of its gutter: y times (w dot x + b) at least 1.

Worked example, distances: Take w = (1, 1) and b = -3, so the boundary is x1 + x2 = 3. The length of w is the square root of (1 + 1) = 1.414. For the point (3, 2): w dot x + b = 3 + 2 - 3 = 2, positive, so it is classified +1, and its distance to the boundary is 2 / 1.414 = 1.414. For the point (1, 1): 1 + 1 - 3 = -1, so it is classified -1 and lies exactly on the negative gutter. For (2, 2): 2 + 2 - 3 = 1, exactly on the positive gutter. The margin width is 2 / ||w|| = 2 / 1.414 = 1.414. Check: the distance between (1, 1) and (2, 2) is the square root of (1 + 1) = 1.414, matching, because these two points face each other straight across the margin.

Support vectors: The training points lying exactly on the gutters, like (1, 1) and (2, 2) above, are called support vectors. They alone determine the boundary: move or delete any other point that is safely beyond its gutter, and the solution does not change. This makes SVMs memory-efficient at prediction time (the model can be written in terms of the support vectors) and explains the name. It also means SVMs focus on the hard, borderline examples rather than the easy ones far away.

Hard margin and its problem: The version above, where every point must be on the correct side outside the margin, is the hard-margin SVM. It only works if the data is perfectly linearly separable. Real data has overlaps and mislabelled points; a single outlier can make separation impossible or force a very narrow, fragile margin.

Soft margin and the C parameter: The soft-margin SVM allows some points to violate the margin, or even be misclassified, at a cost. Each point gets a slack value measuring how far it is on the wrong side of its gutter. The objective becomes: minimise (1/2) ||w||^2 + C times the sum of slacks. Equivalently, it minimises the hinge loss max(0, 1 - y times s) from lesson 07 plus an L2 penalty on w. The hyperparameter C controls the trade-off. Large C punishes violations heavily: a narrow margin that tries to classify every training point correctly (low bias, high variance, risk of overfitting). Small C tolerates violations for a wider margin (more regularisation, smoother boundary). C is tuned by cross-validation, usually over values like 0.01, 0.1, 1, 10, 100.

SVM versus logistic regression: Both are linear classifiers with a regularised loss; the difference is the loss shape. Log loss never becomes exactly zero, so every training point keeps pulling the boundary a little, even ones far on the correct side. Hinge loss becomes exactly zero once a point is beyond its gutter, so such points stop mattering entirely. In practice, on many datasets the two give similar accuracy. Logistic regression gives natural probabilities; the SVM gives a sparser solution that depends only on borderline points, and pairs naturally with kernels.

When a straight line is not enough: Imagine one-dimensional data where class A sits at x = -1, 0 and 1, and class B at x = -3 and 3. No single threshold separates them: B is on both sides of A. Now add a feature x squared, mapping each point to (x, x^2). Class A becomes (-1, 1), (0, 0), (1, 1), and class B becomes (-3, 9) and (3, 9). In this 2D space, the horizontal line x^2 = 5 separates them perfectly. A linear boundary in the new space corresponds to a non-linear boundary (here |x| less than about 2.24) in the original space. This is the same feature-mapping trick as polynomial regression.

The kernel trick: Mapping to many new features can be very expensive: a degree 3 polynomial expansion of 100 features creates well over a hundred thousand new features. The beautiful fact about SVMs is that the training and prediction can be written using only dot products between pairs of points. A kernel function K(x, z) computes the dot product of the mapped points directly from the original points, without ever building the new features. This is the kernel trick: we get the power of a huge feature space at the cost of computing K.

Worked example, a polynomial kernel: The polynomial kernel of degree 2 is K(x, z) = (x dot z + 1)^2. For x = (1, 2) and z = (3, 1): x dot z = 1 times 3 + 2 times 1 = 5, so K = (5 + 1)^2 = 36. This single number equals the dot product of x and z after mapping each into a 6-dimensional space containing a constant, scaled linear terms, squares and the cross term x1 x2. We computed it with one dot product and one squaring.
