The RBF kernel: The most popular kernel is the radial basis function (Gaussian) kernel: K(x, z) = e^(-gamma ||x - z||^2). It measures similarity: 1 for identical points, close to 0 for distant ones. For x = (1, 2) and z = (3, 1), ||x - z||^2 = 4 + 1 = 5; with gamma = 0.1, K = e^(-0.5) = 0.607; with gamma = 1, K = e^(-5) = 0.0067. The gamma hyperparameter sets how far each point's influence reaches: large gamma means very local influence and wiggly boundaries (overfitting risk); small gamma means smooth boundaries. C and gamma are usually tuned together with a grid or random search.

Practical points: Always scale features before using SVMs, since both margins and RBF distances depend on scale. SVMs are naturally binary; multi-class problems are handled by one-versus-rest or one-versus-one combinations, which libraries do automatically. Standard SVMs output scores, not probabilities; calibrated probabilities need an extra step. Training kernel SVMs becomes slow for very large datasets (roughly between quadratic and cubic in the number of examples), so for millions of rows, linear SVMs or other models are preferred. There is also a regression version, support vector regression, which ignores errors smaller than a tube width epsilon.

When to use SVMs: They shine on small to medium datasets with many features, such as text classification with thousands of word features, or certain bioinformatics and image feature problems, where a large margin gives good generalisation. Before deep learning dominated vision, kernel SVMs on hand-crafted image features were among the strongest classifiers. Today, for big tabular data, gradient boosting usually wins, and for raw images, sound and text, neural networks do.

Real example 1, classifying Bangla handwritten characters with features: A university project extracts simple features from scanned Bangla characters, such as stroke direction histograms. With a few thousand labelled samples and hundreds of features, an RBF SVM tuned over C and gamma with cross-validation outperforms k-NN and logistic regression. Inspection shows that the support vectors are mostly the ambiguous, sloppily written characters, exactly the borderline cases.

Real example 2, filtering abusive comments: A Bangladeshi news site wants to flag abusive comments for moderators. Each comment is turned into thousands of word and character-pattern features. A linear SVM, fast even with many features and robust thanks to its margin, ranks comments by score; moderators review the top-scoring ones. The value of C is tuned to balance catching abuse against flagging normal criticism.

Common mistakes and exam questions: Forgetting that only support vectors matter. Mixing up C (large C = less regularisation) with lambda (large lambda = more regularisation). Not scaling features. Using a huge gamma and overfitting. Thinking kernels are only for SVMs (the idea appears in other methods too). Exams ask: define margin and support vectors, compute the distance from a point to a hyperplane and the margin 2 / ||w||, explain hard versus soft margin and the role of C, show how a mapping like x to (x, x^2) makes data separable, and compute a polynomial or RBF kernel value.

Recap: An SVM finds the separating hyperplane with the largest margin. With w = (1, 1), b = -3, the point (3, 2) is 1.414 from the boundary, (1, 1) and (2, 2) are support vectors on the gutters, and the margin is 2 / ||w|| = 1.414. Soft margins allow violations, controlled by C, and are equivalent to hinge loss plus L2 regularisation. Kernels such as (x dot z + 1)^2 (36 in our example) and the RBF kernel give curved boundaries without building new features. Next lesson moves to neural networks, which learn their own features in layers.
key_points: A linear SVM predicts with the sign of w dot x + b and chooses the separating hyperplane with the largest margin.
Distance from x to the hyperplane is |w dot x + b| / ||w||; the margin width is 2 / ||w||.
Worked: w = (1, 1), b = -3; (3, 2) is 1.414 away; (1, 1) and (2, 2) lie on the gutters; margin 1.414.
Support vectors are the points on or inside the margin; they alone determine the boundary.
Soft margin trades margin width against violations with C; it equals hinge loss plus L2 regularisation.
Mapping x to (x, x^2) can make data linearly separable; the kernel trick computes such dot products directly.
Polynomial kernel (x dot z + 1)^2 gives 36 for (1, 2) and (3, 1); RBF kernel e^(-gamma ||x - z||^2) gives 0.607 with gamma 0.1.
Scale features, tune C and gamma together, and prefer other models for very large datasets.
lessons.tip: Remember the opposite directions of the knobs: in SVMs, larger C means less regularisation (tighter fit), while in ridge regression larger lambda means more. Write 'C up = fit harder' on your formula sheet.
lessons.task: On graph paper, plot class +1 points (3, 3), (4, 3), (3, 4) and class -1 points (1, 1), (1, 2), (2, 1). Draw the line x1 + x2 = 4.5, compute each point's value of x1 + x2 - 4.5 and its distance to the line, and identify which points would be support vectors.

quiz.q: What does an SVM maximise when choosing its separating hyperplane?
quiz.explain: It picks the boundary that is as far as possible from the closest training points of each class.

quiz.q: If w = (3, 4), what is the margin width 2 / ||w||?
quiz.explain: ||w|| = sqrt(9 + 16) = 5, so the margin is 2 / 5 = 0.4.

quiz.q: In a soft-margin SVM, what does a very large C tend to do?
options: Widen the margin and allow many violations
Narrow the margin to fit training points more strictly, risking overfitting
quiz.explain: Large C makes violations expensive, so the model fits training data tightly; small C regularises more.

quiz.q: What is the polynomial kernel K(x, z) = (x dot z + 1)^2 for x = (2, 0) and z = (1, 3)?
Which training points determine the final SVM boundary?
options: Only the support vectors on or inside the margin
Only the points farthest from the boundary
quiz.explain: Points safely beyond the margin can move or disappear without changing the solution.

lessons.title: Neural Networks: Perceptrons, Layers and Backpropagation
lessons.content:
When you look at a photo of a rickshaw, you do not consciously check 'three wheels, a hood, a seat, decorated panels'. Your brain combines simple signals from millions of neurons, layer upon layer, into the recognition 'rickshaw' in a fraction of a second. Artificial neural networks borrow this loose idea: many simple units, each doing a tiny calculation, connected in layers, with connection strengths learned from data. They power face unlock, speech recognition and machine translation. This lesson builds a small network by hand, runs it forward, and computes one step of learning by backpropagation. The full story of deep networks, convolution, sequence models and modern training tricks belongs to the Deep Learning course (cse-8-1) and the Neural Networks and Fuzzy Systems course (cse-7-8); here we lay the foundation.

The artificial neuron: A single artificial neuron takes inputs x1, x2 and so on, multiplies each by a weight, adds a bias, and passes the total through an activation function: output = f(w1 x1 + w2 x2 + ... + b). If f is the sigmoid, this is exactly logistic regression from lesson 11. So a neuron is not mysterious: it is a linear score followed by a non-linear squashing or clipping step. The weights say how much each input matters, and the bias shifts the threshold.

The perceptron: The earliest neural model, the perceptron, studied by Frank Rosenblatt in the late 1950s, used a step function: output 1 if the score is at least 0, else 0. Its learning rule is simple: for each misclassified example, add (learning rate times error times input) to the weights. If the data is linearly separable, this rule is guaranteed to find a separating line in a finite number of steps. But a single perceptron can only draw straight-line boundaries, which leads to a famous limitation.

The XOR problem: XOR outputs 1 when exactly one of two binary inputs is 1: (0,0) gives 0, (0,1) gives 1, (1,0) gives 1, (1,1) gives 0. Plot these four points and try to separate the 1s from the 0s with one straight line: it is impossible, because the 1s sit on one diagonal and the 0s on the other. A single neuron cannot learn XOR. The fix is to add a hidden layer: one hidden neuron can compute OR, another AND, and the output neuron combines them as 'OR but not AND', which is XOR. Stacking neurons creates new features that make the problem linearly separable, the same idea as feature mapping in SVMs, but learned.

Multi-layer networks: A multi-layer perceptron (MLP), also called a feedforward network, has an input layer (the features), one or more hidden layers, and an output layer. Every neuron in one layer connects to every neuron in the next (fully connected or dense layers). Information flows forward from inputs to outputs. Each hidden layer transforms its input into a new representation; the output layer makes the final prediction from the last representation. With enough hidden units, even one hidden layer can approximate any reasonable continuous function closely (the universal approximation theorem), although that says nothing about how many units are needed or whether training will find good weights.

Why activation functions must be non-linear: If every neuron used a linear activation, stacking layers would be pointless: a linear function of a linear function is still linear, so a 10-layer linear network equals one linear model. Non-linear activations give networks their power. Common choices: sigmoid, 1 / (1 + e^(-z)), squashes to between 0 and 1 and is used for binary outputs; tanh squashes to between -1 and 1; ReLU, max(0, z), passes positives unchanged and zeroes negatives. ReLU is the usual default for hidden layers because it is cheap and its gradient does not shrink for positive inputs, which helps deep networks train. For multi-class outputs, softmax turns a vector of scores into probabilities that sum to 1.

Worked example, the network: Take a tiny network with 2 inputs, 2 hidden ReLU neurons and 1 sigmoid output. Hidden neuron 1 has weights (0.5, -0.2) and bias 0.1; hidden neuron 2 has weights (0.3, 0.4) and bias -0.5. The output neuron has weights v1 = 2.0, v2 = 1.0 and bias -0.2. The input is x = (1, 2) with true label y = 1.

Worked example, forward pass: Hidden neuron 1: score 0.5 times 1 + (-0.2) times 2 + 0.1 = 0.5 - 0.4 + 0.1 = 0.2; ReLU(0.2) = 0.2, so h1 = 0.2. Hidden neuron 2: 0.3 times 1 + 0.4 times 2 - 0.5 = 0.3 + 0.8 - 0.5 = 0.6; h2 = 0.6. Output score z = 2.0 times 0.2 + 1.0 times 0.6 - 0.2 = 0.4 + 0.6 - 0.2 = 0.8. Prediction p = sigmoid(0.8) = 1 / (1 + e^(-0.8)) = 0.690. The network says 69 percent chance of class 1. The log loss for y = 1 is -ln(0.690) = 0.371.

Counting parameters: Our tiny network has 2 times 2 weights plus 2 biases in the hidden layer (6) and 2 weights plus 1 bias in the output (3): 9 parameters. A network for 28 by 28 pixel digit images (784 inputs), with 128 hidden units and 10 outputs, has 784 times 128 + 128 = 100480 parameters in the first layer and 128 times 10 + 10 = 1290 in the second: 101770 in total. Even small networks have many parameters, which is why they need plenty of data and regularisation.

Training: what we need: Training means adjusting all weights to reduce the average loss over the training data, using gradient descent from lesson 06. For that we need the derivative of the loss with respect to every weight. Computing each derivative separately would be hopelessly slow for networks with millions of weights. Backpropagation computes all of them efficiently in one backward sweep using the chain rule.

The chain rule idea: If the loss L depends on z, and z depends on a weight v, then dL/dv = dL/dz times dz/dv. In a network, the loss depends on the output, which depends on the last hidden layer, which depends on the layer before, and so on. Backpropagation starts at the loss, computes how the loss changes with the output score, then passes this 'error signal' backwards, layer by layer, multiplying by local derivatives. Every intermediate value from the forward pass is reused, so the backward pass costs about as much as the forward pass.

Worked example, backward pass at the output: A neat fact: for a sigmoid output with log loss, the derivative of the loss with respect to the output score is simply dL/dz = p - y = 0.690 - 1 = -0.310. Since z = v1 h1 + v2 h2 + c, we have dz/dv1 = h1 and dz/dv2 = h2. So dL/dv1 = -0.310 times 0.2 = -0.062, and dL/dv2 = -0.310 times 0.6 = -0.186. With learning rate 0.5, gradient descent updates v1 to 2.0 - 0.5 times (-0.062) = 2.031 and v2 to 1.0 - 0.5 times (-0.186) = 1.093. Both weights grow, increasing z and pushing p towards the correct answer 1. Notice v2 changes more because h2 was more active: weights attached to more active neurons get bigger updates.

Worked example, one layer deeper: The error signal for hidden unit 1 is dL/dh1 = dL/dz times v1 = -0.310 times 2.0 = -0.620. Because h1 = ReLU(score) and its score 0.2 was positive, the ReLU derivative is 1, so the error passes through unchanged. The gradient for hidden weight w11 (from x1 = 1) is -0.620 times 1 = -0.620, and for w12 (from x2 = 2) it is -0.620 times 2 = -1.240. Had the score been negative, ReLU would have output 0 and blocked the gradient completely; that neuron's incoming weights would not change for this example.

Mini-batches and epochs: In practice, gradients are averaged over a mini-batch of examples (for example 32 or 128), and the weights are updated after each mini-batch. One pass over the whole training set is an epoch; training usually runs many epochs, while watching the validation loss. Weights must start with small random values, not all zeros: if all weights were equal, every hidden neuron would compute the same thing and receive the same update forever, so the network would never learn different features.

Overfitting and regularisation in networks: Networks are flexible, so they overfit easily on small datasets. Standard remedies, which Deep Learning covers in depth, include L2 weight decay (the ridge penalty of lesson 10), early stopping when validation loss stops improving, dropout (randomly switching off neurons during training) and simply collecting more data. Input features should be scaled, as with any gradient-based method, or training becomes slow and unstable.

When to use neural networks: For images, audio and text, deep networks that learn their own features from raw data are now the standard approach. For small tabular datasets, a plain MLP is often beaten by gradient boosted trees and is harder to tune, so try the simpler models first. Neural networks also need more computation, and are hard to interpret, which matters in regulated decisions.

Real example 1, recognising Bangla digits: A student project trains an MLP on images of handwritten Bangla digits (০ to ৯), 28 by 28 pixels each, flattened to 784 inputs, with one hidden layer of 128 ReLU units and a 10-way softmax output, the 101770 parameter network above. After a few epochs it beats logistic regression clearly. A convolutional network, studied in the Deep Learning course, does better still, because it uses the 2D structure of images.

Real example 2, predicting electricity demand: A distribution company in Chattogram experiments with a small neural network that predicts the next day's hourly demand from temperature, humidity, day of week, holidays and recent demand. Compared with gradient boosting on the same features, the network gives similar accuracy but needs more tuning. The team keeps the boosting model in production and continues the network experiment for longer sequences, which recurrent and attention-based models handle well.

Common mistakes and exam questions: Using linear activations in hidden layers. Initialising all weights to zero. Forgetting to scale inputs. Training too long without watching validation loss. Confusing the forward pass (compute predictions) with backpropagation (compute gradients) and gradient descent (update weights). Exams ask: why a perceptron cannot learn XOR, compute a forward pass through a small network, compute output-layer gradients using p - y, count parameters, explain the role of activations, and outline backpropagation.

Recap: A neuron computes an activation of a weighted sum plus bias; a single one draws only linear boundaries, so it fails on XOR. Layers of neurons with non-linear activations such as ReLU learn new features. In our worked network, x = (1, 2) gave h = (0.2, 0.6), z = 0.8, p = 0.690 and loss 0.371. Backpropagation applies the chain rule backwards: dL/dz = p - y = -0.310, giving gradients -0.062 and -0.186, and v1 moved from 2.0 to 2.031. The next lesson leaves labels behind entirely, with k-means clustering.
key_points: A neuron computes f(w dot x + b); with a sigmoid it is logistic regression.
A single perceptron draws only straight boundaries, so it cannot learn XOR; a hidden layer fixes this.
Hidden layers need non-linear activations (ReLU, sigmoid, tanh); stacked linear layers collapse to one linear model.
Worked forward pass: x = (1, 2) gives h1 = 0.2, h2 = 0.6, z = 0.8, p = 0.690, loss 0.371.
Backpropagation uses the chain rule backwards; for sigmoid with log loss, dL/dz = p - y.
Worked gradients: dL/dv1 = -0.062, dL/dv2 = -0.186; with learning rate 0.5, v1 becomes 2.031.
A 784-128-10 network has 101770 parameters; weights must start small and random, not zero.
Networks excel on images, audio and text; on small tabular data, try boosting and simpler models first.
lessons.tip: When doing backpropagation by hand, write the forward pass values in a table first (every score and every activation). The backward pass reuses every one of them, and most exam errors come from recomputing them wrongly.
lessons.task: Using the worked network in this lesson, run the forward pass for x = (2, 1) and y = 0. Compute h1, h2, z, p and the log loss, then compute dL/dv1 and dL/dv2 using dL/dz = p - y. Check whether the updates push p in the right direction.

quiz.q: Why can a single perceptron not learn the XOR function?
options: The XOR classes cannot be separated by one straight line
quiz.explain: The 1s and 0s of XOR lie on opposite diagonals; a hidden layer is needed to create separable features.

quiz.q: What happens if all hidden layers use linear activations?
options: The network trains faster and better
The whole network collapses to a single linear model
quiz.explain: A composition of linear functions is linear, so the extra layers add no expressive power.

quiz.q: A hidden ReLU neuron receives score -0.4. What is its output?
quiz.explain: ReLU(z) = max(0, z), so a negative score gives 0 (and blocks the gradient).

quiz.q: For a sigmoid output with log loss, p = 0.8 and y = 1. What is dL/dz?
How many parameters does a dense network with 4 inputs, 3 hidden units and 1 output have (including biases)?
quiz.explain: Hidden: 4 x 3 + 3 = 15; output: 3 x 1 + 1 = 4; total 19.

lessons.title: Clustering with k-Means
lessons.content:
A new supershop chain in Dhaka has records of 200000 customers: how often they visit, how much they spend, what they buy, what time of day they come. Nobody has labelled these customers as 'office worker', 'family shopper' or 'student'. Yet the marketing team would love to know which natural groups exist, so they can design different offers for each. This is unsupervised learning: finding structure in data without labels. The most widely used tool for it is k-means clustering, simple enough to run by hand on six points and fast enough to group millions. This lesson works through k-means step by step, explains how to choose the number of clusters, and lists the traps.

What clustering is: Clustering groups examples so that examples in the same group (cluster) are similar to each other and different from those in other groups. Unlike classification, there are no right answers to learn from; the algorithm decides the groups from the structure of the data, and humans then interpret them. Similarity is usually measured by distance, typically Euclidean distance, so everything from lesson 15 about feature scaling applies here too. Clustering is used for customer segmentation, grouping news articles by topic, compressing images by reducing colours, finding regions with similar crop patterns, and as an exploratory first look at a new dataset.

The k-means idea: k-means represents each of k clusters by its centre, called the centroid, which is the mean of the points in the cluster. It looks for the centroids and assignments that minimise the within-cluster sum of squared distances (SSE, also called inertia): the total, over all points, of the squared distance from each point to its own cluster's centroid. Small SSE means tight, compact clusters.

The algorithm (Lloyd's algorithm): Step 1: choose k and pick k initial centroids, for example k random data points. Step 2, assignment: assign each point to its nearest centroid. Step 3, update: move each centroid to the mean of the points assigned to it. Repeat steps 2 and 3 until the assignments stop changing. Each step can only lower (or keep) the SSE: assigning points to the nearest centroid cannot increase their distances, and the mean is exactly the point that minimises the sum of squared distances to a group. Since there are finitely many possible assignments and the SSE never increases, the algorithm always stops, usually after a handful of iterations.

Worked example, the data: Six shops are described by two scaled features: points A (1, 2), B (2, 1), C (2, 3), D (6, 5), E (7, 7) and F (8, 6). Take k = 2, with initial centroids c1 = (1, 2) and c2 = (2, 3), which are the points A and C. This is a deliberately poor start: both centroids lie in the lower-left group.

Worked example, iteration 1 assignment: A is distance 0 from c1, so cluster 1. B: distance to c1 is the square root of (1 + 1) = 1.414, to c2 the square root of (0 + 4) = 2.0, so cluster 1. C is distance 0 from c2, so cluster 2. D (6, 5): to c1 the square root of (25 + 9) = 5.831, to c2 the square root of (16 + 4) = 4.472, so cluster 2. E and F are also closer to c2. Clusters: {A, B} and {C, D, E, F}.

Worked example, iteration 1 update: c1 = mean of (1, 2) and (2, 1) = (1.5, 1.5). c2 = mean of (2, 3), (6, 5), (7, 7), (8, 6) = (23/4, 21/4) = (5.75, 5.25). The SSE at this point is 30.5. Notice that c2 has been dragged towards the upper-right group, but C still pulls it down.

Worked example, iteration 2: Reassign with the new centroids. C (2, 3): distance to c1 (1.5, 1.5) is the square root of (0.25 + 2.25) = 1.581; to c2 (5.75, 5.25) it is about 4.373. C moves to cluster 1. A and B stay in cluster 1; D, E and F stay in cluster 2 (D is only 0.354 from c2). Update: c1 = mean of A, B, C = (5/3, 6/3) = (1.667, 2); c2 = mean of D, E, F = (21/3, 18/3) = (7, 6). Iteration 3 changes no assignments, so the algorithm has converged.

Worked example, final SSE: Cluster 1: A (1, 2) to (1.667, 2): 0.444; B (2, 1): 0.111 + 1 = 1.111; C (2, 3): 0.111 + 1 = 1.111; subtotal 2.667. Cluster 2: D (6, 5) to (7, 6): 1 + 1 = 2; E (7, 7): 0 + 1 = 1; F (8, 6): 1 + 0 = 1; subtotal 4. Total SSE = 6.667, down from 30.5 after the first update. For comparison, putting all six points in a single cluster (centroid (4.333, 4)) gives SSE 73.33. Two clusters explain most of the spread.

Initialisation matters: k-means finds a local minimum, not necessarily the best one. A bad start can leave two centroids sharing one natural group while another group is split or merged. Our poor start recovered, but that is not guaranteed. Two standard remedies: run k-means several times with different random starts and keep the solution with the lowest SSE (libraries do this by default), and use k-means++ initialisation, which picks the first centroid at random and each next one with probability proportional to its squared distance from the nearest centroid already chosen, so starting centroids are spread out.

Choosing k, the elbow method: k must be chosen in advance, and SSE always decreases as k grows (with k equal to the number of points, SSE is 0), so we cannot simply minimise SSE. The elbow method plots SSE against k = 1, 2, 3 and so on, and looks for the 'elbow' where adding clusters stops giving big improvements. In our example SSE falls from 73.3 at k = 1 to 6.7 at k = 2; further clusters would shave off much less, suggesting k = 2. Real elbows are often blurry.

Choosing k, the silhouette score: For each point, let a be its average distance to other points in its own cluster and b its average distance to points in the nearest other cluster. Its silhouette is (b - a) / max(a, b), between -1 and 1: near 1 means well inside its cluster, near 0 means on a border, negative means probably in the wrong cluster. The average silhouette over all points can be compared for different k; higher is better. Most importantly, check that clusters are meaningful and useful for the business question; a statistically neat k may not match how the marketing team can act.

Assumptions and limitations: k-means works best when clusters are roughly round (spherical), similar in size and similar in spread, because it uses distance to a single centre. It struggles with elongated or curved clusters (two interlocking half-moons), with clusters of very different density, and with outliers, since one extreme point can drag a mean far away. It needs numeric features with meaningful averages; for categorical data, variants such as k-modes exist. It always produces k clusters, even if the data has no real cluster structure. The next lesson covers hierarchical clustering and density-based clustering, which handle some of these cases better.

Relatives of k-means: k-medoids requires each centre to be an actual data point (a medoid) and can use any distance, which makes it more robust to outliers and usable when averages make no sense, at a higher computational cost. Gaussian mixture models, met in Pattern Recognition (cse-6-12), replace hard assignments with probabilities and allow elliptical clusters of different sizes; k-means can be seen as a simplified special case. Clustering at scale and its use in business analytics returns in Data Mining (cse-7-6).

Scaling and preparation: Since k-means is distance-based, scale features first. If one feature is monthly spending in taka (thousands) and another is visits per month (single digits), spending alone will decide the clusters. Remove or cap obvious outliers, and consider reducing many correlated features with PCA (lesson 23) first. Computation is cheap: each iteration costs roughly n times k times d operations for n points, k clusters and d features, so k-means scales to very large datasets, and mini-batch versions go further.

Interpreting clusters: After clustering, describe each cluster by its centroid and by summary statistics of its members, in original units. 'Cluster 3: average spend 18000 taka per month, visits 2 times, mostly weekends, large baskets with rice and oil' reads like a family monthly-shopping segment. Naming clusters is a human task, and it is good practice to check whether clusters stay stable when you rerun with a different random seed or a different sample.

k-means for vector quantisation: k-means also compresses data. An image with millions of colours can be redrawn with only 16 colours by clustering pixel colours into k = 16 clusters and replacing each pixel with its centroid colour. Each pixel then needs only 4 bits instead of 24. The same idea underlies some speech and image coding methods.

Real example 1, mobile financial service users: A mobile wallet company clusters active users on scaled features such as number of cash-in and cash-out transactions, bill payments, merchant payments, average transaction size and share of transactions at night. Five clusters emerge, roughly: salary receivers who cash out quickly, small merchants, bill payers, remittance receivers in rural areas, and heavy app shoppers. Each gets a different education campaign and offer. The team rechecks the clusters every quarter because behaviour shifts.

Real example 2, grouping upazilas by agricultural profile: A research group describes upazilas by scaled shares of land under Aman, Boro, jute, vegetables and fish ponds, plus average rainfall. k-means with k chosen by silhouette and expert judgement produces groups such as 'Boro-dominant irrigated plains' and 'mixed fish and rice wetlands'. Extension programmes then design region-specific advice for each group instead of one national message.

Common mistakes and exam questions: Forgetting to scale features. Treating cluster numbers as meaningful labels (cluster 1 is not 'better' than cluster 2). Assuming k-means finds the global optimum. Choosing k by minimising SSE. Applying k-means to clearly non-spherical shapes. Exams ask: run two iterations of k-means by hand on a small dataset, compute SSE, explain why the algorithm converges, describe k-means++, and explain the elbow and silhouette methods and the limitations of k-means.

Recap: k-means alternates between assigning points to the nearest centroid and moving centroids to the mean of their points, lowering the SSE each time until nothing changes. On our six points, a poor start of (1, 2) and (2, 3) still converged in two iterations to centroids (1.667, 2) and (7, 6), with SSE 6.667 versus 73.33 for one cluster. Use k-means++ and multiple restarts, scale features, choose k with the elbow, silhouette and business sense, and remember that k-means prefers round, similar-sized clusters.
key_points: Clustering finds groups in unlabelled data; k-means represents each cluster by the mean (centroid) of its points.
k-means minimises SSE, the total squared distance from points to their own centroid.
Lloyd's algorithm alternates assignment to the nearest centroid and centroid update; SSE never increases, so it converges.
Worked: six points from start (1, 2), (2, 3) converge to centroids (1.667, 2) and (7, 6) with SSE 6.667.
k-means finds a local minimum; use k-means++ initialisation and several restarts.
Choose k with the elbow plot, the silhouette score (b - a) / max(a, b) and business sense, not by minimising SSE.
k-means assumes roughly round, similar-sized clusters and is sensitive to outliers and feature scale.
Interpret clusters by their centroids in original units and check stability across runs.
lessons.tip: When running k-means by hand, make a table with one row per point and columns for the distance to each centroid. Circle the smallest distance in each row; the circles are your new assignments, and the column-wise averages of the circled points' coordinates are the new centroids.
lessons.task: Take the six points of this lesson and run k-means with k = 2 again, but start with centroids (2, 1) and (8, 6). Record the assignments and centroids at each iteration and the final SSE. Do you reach the same answer as the lesson, and in how many iterations?

quiz.q: In k-means, what is the centroid of a cluster?
options: The point closest to the origin
The mean of the points assigned to the cluster
The first point placed in the cluster
The median distance in the cluster
quiz.explain: The update step moves each centroid to the mean of its assigned points, which minimises the cluster's squared distances.

quiz.q: Why should you not choose k simply by picking the value with the lowest SSE?
options: SSE is undefined for k above 3
SSE always decreases as k increases, reaching 0 when k equals the number of points
SSE does not depend on k
quiz.explain: More clusters always fit at least as tightly, so minimising SSE would choose one cluster per point.

quiz.q: Points (0, 0) and (2, 2) are in one cluster. Where is the new centroid?
quiz.explain: The centroid is the mean: ((0 + 2) / 2, (0 + 2) / 2) = (1, 1).

quiz.q: What does k-means++ improve?
options: It removes the need for scaling
It spreads out the initial centroids to give better starting points
quiz.explain: It chooses each new initial centroid with probability proportional to squared distance from those already chosen.

quiz.q: For which data is plain k-means likely to perform poorly?
quiz.explain: k-means uses distance to a single centre, so it splits curved or elongated clusters incorrectly.

lessons.title: Hierarchical and Density-Based Clustering
lessons.content:
A family tree shows how people are related at every level: siblings, then cousins, then the wider gusthi, all the way up to a common ancestor. You can read it at whatever level you need. Hierarchical clustering builds exactly this kind of tree for data, so you do not have to choose the number of clusters in advance. A different idea, density-based clustering, asks where points are crowded together, the way you would spot the busy bazaars on a night-time satellite photo of Bangladesh, and treats lonely points as noise. Both fix weaknesses of k-means from the previous lesson. This lesson works through hierarchical clustering by hand with three linkage rules, then runs DBSCAN on the same data.

Agglomerative clustering: The most common hierarchical method is agglomerative, or bottom-up. Start with every point as its own cluster. Repeatedly find the two closest clusters and merge them. Continue until everything is one cluster. Record each merge and the distance at which it happened. The opposite, divisive (top-down) clustering, starts with one big cluster and splits it repeatedly; it is less common because choosing good splits is expensive.

Linkage, the key choice: Distance between two points is clear, but what is the distance between two clusters? The linkage rule decides. Single linkage uses the closest pair of points, one from each cluster. Complete linkage uses the farthest pair. Average linkage uses the average of all pairwise distances between the two clusters. Ward's method merges the pair of clusters whose merge increases the total within-cluster SSE the least, the same quantity k-means minimises. Different linkages can give very different trees.

Worked example, the data: To keep the arithmetic visible, use one-dimensional data: six points at positions 1, 2, 4, 8, 9 and 15. Think of them as the distance in kilometres of six shops along a highway from a town centre.

Worked example, single linkage: The closest pairs are (1, 2) and (8, 9), each at distance 1, so merge {1, 2} at height 1 and {8, 9} at height 1. Next, the distance from {1, 2} to 4 is the closest pair, 4 - 2 = 2; from {8, 9} to 4 it is 4; from {8, 9} to 15 it is 6. The smallest is 2: merge {1, 2, 4} at height 2. Now from {1, 2, 4} to {8, 9}, single linkage is 8 - 4 = 4, and from {8, 9} to 15 it is 6. Merge at height 4 to get {1, 2, 4, 8, 9}. Finally 15 joins at height 15 - 9 = 6. Merge heights: 1, 1, 2, 4, 6.

Worked example, complete linkage: The first two merges are the same, at height 1. Then from {1, 2} to 4 the farthest pair is 4 - 1 = 3; from 4 to {8, 9} it is 9 - 4 = 5; from {8, 9} to 15 it is 15 - 8 = 7; from {1, 2} to {8, 9} it is 8. The smallest is 3: merge {1, 2, 4} at height 3. Next, {1, 2, 4} to {8, 9} is 9 - 1 = 8, while {8, 9} to 15 is 7, so this time 15 joins {8, 9} at height 7. The last merge, {1, 2, 4} with {8, 9, 15}, happens at height 15 - 1 = 14. Merge heights: 1, 1, 3, 7, 14. Notice the different shape: complete linkage made two balanced groups, while single linkage left 15 as a late loner.

Worked example, average linkage: After the two height-1 merges, {1, 2} to 4 averages (3 + 2) / 2 = 2.5, the smallest, so {1, 2, 4} forms at 2.5. Then {1, 2, 4} to {8, 9}: the six pairwise distances are 7, 8, 6, 7, 4 and 5, averaging 37 / 6 = 6.167; {8, 9} to 15 averages (7 + 6) / 2 = 6.5. So {1, 2, 4} and {8, 9} merge at 6.167. Finally 15 joins at the average of 14, 13, 11, 7 and 6, which is 51 / 5 = 10.2. Merge heights: 1, 1, 2.5, 6.167, 10.2.

The dendrogram: The result is drawn as a dendrogram: points along the bottom, and a horizontal bar joining two clusters at the height of their merge. To get clusters, cut the tree with a horizontal line. In the single-linkage tree, a cut at height 3 crosses three vertical lines, giving {1, 2, 4}, {8, 9} and {15}; a cut at 5 gives {1, 2, 4, 8, 9} and {15}. A long vertical gap between successive merges suggests a natural number of clusters: in the complete-linkage tree, the jump from 7 to 14 strongly suggests two clusters. One run of the algorithm thus gives a whole family of clusterings.

What linkage does to cluster shapes: Single linkage can follow long, thin, curved shapes, because chains of nearby points merge one by one; but it suffers from chaining, where a few bridge points can join two clearly separate groups into one long straggly cluster. Complete linkage prefers compact clusters of similar diameter and is less prone to chaining but sensitive to outliers. Average linkage is a compromise. Ward's method tends to produce round, similar-sized clusters, much like k-means, and is a popular default for numeric data.

Cost and practicality: A naive agglomerative algorithm stores all pairwise distances: n squared numbers. For 10000 points that is 100 million distances, already heavy, and the time grows at least as fast. So hierarchical clustering suits small to medium datasets, or a sample of a large one. Merges are greedy and never undone, so an early bad merge stays. Its big advantages: no need to choose k in advance, any distance measure works, and the dendrogram itself is an informative picture, widely used in biology to show how gene expression profiles or species relate.

Density-based clustering, the idea: Think of clusters as regions where points are packed densely, separated by sparse regions. A point in a dense region belongs to a cluster; a point in empty space is noise. This lets clusters take any shape, finds the number of clusters automatically, and labels outliers instead of forcing them into a cluster.

DBSCAN definitions: DBSCAN has two parameters: a radius eps and a count minPts. The eps-neighbourhood of a point is all points within distance eps of it, including the point itself. A core point has at least minPts points in its neighbourhood. A border point is not core but lies within eps of a core point. A noise point is neither. Clusters are built by starting from a core point and adding every point reachable through chains of core points within eps of each other, plus the border points around them.

Worked example, DBSCAN: Use the same six points, with eps = 2 and minPts = 2. Neighbourhoods: 1 has {1, 2}; 2 has {1, 2, 4}; 4 has {2, 4}; 8 has {8, 9}; 9 has {8, 9}; 15 has only {15}. So 1, 2, 4, 8 and 9 are core points and 15 is noise. Points 1, 2 and 4 link through chains (1 to 2, 2 to 4), forming cluster A = {1, 2, 4}; 8 and 9 form cluster B = {8, 9}; 15 is labelled noise. Now raise minPts to 3: only point 2 is core. Points 1 and 4 become border points of its cluster, and 8, 9 and 15 all become noise. The parameters matter a lot.

Choosing DBSCAN's parameters: A common heuristic is to set minPts to at least the number of dimensions plus one (often 4 or more for real data), then compute for each point the distance to its k-th nearest neighbour with k = minPts - 1, sort these distances, and plot them. The 'knee' of the curve, where distances suddenly rise, suggests eps. Features must be scaled, as always with distances.

Strengths and weaknesses of DBSCAN: It finds arbitrarily shaped clusters, such as two interlocking half-moons where k-means fails, does not need k, and explicitly marks noise. But it struggles when clusters have very different densities, since one eps cannot suit both a crowded city and a sparse village; it is sensitive to eps; and in high dimensions distances become less meaningful, so density is hard to define. Extensions such as OPTICS and HDBSCAN handle varying density better; they are worth knowing by name.

Comparing the three families: k-means: fast, needs k, round clusters, every point assigned. Hierarchical: no k needed, a full tree, flexible distances, but slow on large data. DBSCAN: any shape, finds noise, needs eps and minPts, struggles with varying densities. In practice, try more than one, scale your features, and judge results by whether the clusters make sense and help the task, since there is no single correct clustering.

Real example 1, hotspots of road accidents: A transport research team plots the GPS coordinates of reported road accidents on the Dhaka-Chattogram highway. DBSCAN, with eps of a few hundred metres and minPts chosen from the k-distance plot, finds dense accident hotspots near particular bazaars, bridges and bends, while isolated accidents are labelled noise. Engineers then inspect each hotspot for road design problems. k-means would have forced every accident into some cluster and split the long, thin highway awkwardly.

Real example 2, relating rice varieties: An agricultural research institute measures traits of 40 rice varieties: grain length, plant height, days to maturity, yield and tolerance scores. Agglomerative clustering with Ward's method on scaled traits produces a dendrogram that breeders read directly: varieties that merge early are similar and may share ancestry, while a deep split separates short-duration varieties from long-duration ones. The tree guides which varieties to cross.

Common mistakes and exam questions: Forgetting to scale features. Confusing single linkage (closest pair) with complete linkage (farthest pair). Reading cluster labels from a dendrogram without stating the cut height. Running hierarchical clustering on huge datasets. Using one eps for clusters of very different density. Exams ask: perform agglomerative clustering by hand with single and complete linkage and draw the dendrogram, cut a dendrogram to get k clusters, define core, border and noise points and run DBSCAN on a small dataset, and compare k-means, hierarchical and DBSCAN.

Recap: Agglomerative clustering repeatedly merges the closest clusters, producing a dendrogram you can cut at any height. On points 1, 2, 4, 8, 9, 15, single linkage merged at 1, 1, 2, 4, 6; complete linkage at 1, 1, 3, 7, 14; average linkage at 1, 1, 2.5, 6.167, 10.2. DBSCAN with eps = 2 and minPts = 2 found {1, 2, 4} and {8, 9} with 15 as noise. Hierarchical methods avoid choosing k; DBSCAN finds any shape and flags outliers. Whichever method you use, scale the features first and judge the clusters by whether they are meaningful and useful. Next we turn to reducing the number of features with PCA.
key_points: Agglomerative clustering starts with single points and repeatedly merges the two closest clusters.
Linkage defines cluster distance: single (closest pair), complete (farthest pair), average, or Ward (smallest SSE increase).
On 1, 2, 4, 8, 9, 15: single linkage merges at 1, 1, 2, 4, 6; complete at 1, 1, 3, 7, 14; average at 1, 1, 2.5, 6.167, 10.2.
A dendrogram is cut at a chosen height to give clusters; long gaps between merges suggest a natural k.
Single linkage follows long shapes but suffers chaining; complete and Ward prefer compact clusters.
DBSCAN: core points have at least minPts neighbours within eps; border points are near a core; the rest is noise.
Worked DBSCAN (eps 2, minPts 2): clusters {1, 2, 4} and {8, 9}, noise 15; with minPts 3, only {1, 2, 4} remains.
Hierarchical clustering needs no k but is slow on big data; DBSCAN finds any shape but struggles with varying density.
lessons.tip: When doing hierarchical clustering by hand, keep a distance matrix and update it after every merge using the linkage rule (min for single, max for complete). Cross out the merged rows and write the new row; it keeps the bookkeeping honest.
lessons.task: Take the points 2, 3, 7, 8, 9 and 20. Perform agglomerative clustering with single linkage and with complete linkage, writing every merge height, and sketch both dendrograms. Then run DBSCAN with eps = 1.5 and minPts = 2 and list the clusters and noise.

quiz.q: In single linkage, how is the distance between two clusters defined?
options: Farthest pair of points, one from each cluster
Closest pair of points, one from each cluster
quiz.explain: Single linkage uses the minimum pairwise distance, which allows chain-like clusters.

quiz.q: Clusters {1, 2} and {6} are compared with complete linkage. What is their distance?
quiz.explain: The farthest pair is 1 and 6, at distance 5.

quiz.q: What is a key advantage of hierarchical clustering over k-means?
options: It is much faster on millions of points
It does not require choosing the number of clusters in advance
quiz.explain: The dendrogram can be cut at any height after the fact to give different numbers of clusters.

quiz.q: In DBSCAN, a point with fewer than minPts neighbours that is not within eps of any core point is a:
quiz.explain: Points that are neither core nor near a core point are labelled noise.

quiz.q: Which situation is hardest for a single DBSCAN run?
options: Not knowing the number of clusters
quiz.explain: One eps value cannot suit both dense and sparse clusters; variants like HDBSCAN address this.

lessons.title: Dimensionality Reduction with PCA
lessons.content:
Photograph a bamboo pole lying on a field from directly above and you see its full length. Photograph it end-on and you see only a small circle. Both photos are 2D shadows of a 3D object, but one keeps far more information than the other. Principal component analysis (PCA) solves the same problem for data: given many features, find the few directions along which the data varies the most, and describe each example by its position along those directions. You keep most of the information with far fewer numbers. This lesson builds PCA from variance and covariance, computes it by hand for five points, and explains when and how to use it.

Why reduce dimensions: Datasets often have dozens or hundreds of features, many of them correlated: height and arm length, total marks and average marks, rainfall in June and July. More features mean slower training, more risk of overfitting, and the curse of dimensionality from lesson 15, where distances lose meaning. You also cannot plot 50 dimensions. Dimensionality reduction finds a smaller set of new features that keeps most of the useful structure. Feature selection keeps some original features and drops others; feature extraction, like PCA, builds new features as combinations of the old ones.

Variance and covariance refresher: The variance of a feature measures its spread: the average squared distance from its mean (dividing by n - 1 for a sample). Covariance between two features measures whether they move together: positive if they tend to be above their means together, negative if one is high when the other is low, near zero if unrelated. For d features, the covariance matrix is a d by d table whose diagonal holds the variances and off-diagonal entries hold the covariances. It is symmetric.

The PCA idea: The first principal component (PC1) is the direction (a unit-length vector) along which the projected data has the largest possible variance. The second principal component (PC2) is the direction of largest remaining variance that is perpendicular to PC1, and so on. With d features there are d components, ordered from most to least variance. Keeping the first k components and dropping the rest gives a k-dimensional summary. Equivalently, PC1 is the line that minimises the total squared perpendicular distance from the points to the line, so maximising the variance kept and minimising the information lost are the same goal.

How it is computed: Step 1: centre the data by subtracting each feature's mean (and usually standardise to unit variance if features have different units). Step 2: compute the covariance matrix. Step 3: find its eigenvectors and eigenvalues. The eigenvectors are the principal component directions; each eigenvalue equals the variance of the data along its eigenvector. Step 4: sort by eigenvalue, keep the top k eigenvectors, and project each centred example onto them: its new coordinate on component j is the dot product of the example with eigenvector j. In practice, libraries compute PCA through the singular value decomposition (SVD) of the centred data matrix, which gives the same components more stably.

Worked example, the data: Five students' scores on two tests, already centred so each column has mean zero: (-2, -1), (-1, -1), (0, 0), (1, 1) and (2, 1). The x values have squared deviations 4, 1, 0, 1, 4, summing to 10; dividing by n - 1 = 4 gives variance 2.5. The y values give 1, 1, 0, 1, 1, sum 4, variance 1.0. The products x times y are 2, 1, 0, 1, 2, sum 6, covariance 6 / 4 = 1.5. Covariance matrix: first row (2.5, 1.5), second row (1.5, 1.0). The positive covariance shows the two scores rise together.

Worked example, eigenvalues: For a 2 by 2 matrix, eigenvalues solve lambda squared - (trace) lambda + (determinant) = 0. Trace = 2.5 + 1.0 = 3.5. Determinant = 2.5 times 1.0 - 1.5 times 1.5 = 2.5 - 2.25 = 0.25. So lambda = (3.5 plus or minus the square root of (12.25 - 1)) / 2 = (3.5 plus or minus 3.354) / 2, giving lambda1 = 3.427 and lambda2 = 0.073. Their sum, 3.5, equals the total variance 2.5 + 1.0: PCA redistributes the variance, it does not create or destroy it.

Worked example, explained variance: The share of variance explained by PC1 is 3.427 / 3.5 = 0.979, about 97.9 percent. PC2 explains only 2.1 percent. So one number per student, the PC1 score, captures almost everything these two tests say. This explained variance ratio is the main tool for choosing k.

Worked example, the direction and projections: For lambda1 = 3.427, the eigenvector satisfies (2.5 - 3.427) v1 + 1.5 v2 = 0, so v2 = 0.618 v1. Normalising to length 1 gives PC1 = (0.851, 0.526), a direction about 31.7 degrees above the x axis, leaning towards x because x has more variance. Projecting: for (-2, -1), the PC1 score is -2 times 0.851 + (-1) times 0.526 = -2.227; for (-1, -1) it is -1.376; for (0, 0) it is 0; and by symmetry 1.376 and 2.227 for the last two. Check: the variance of these scores, (2.227^2 + 1.376^2 + 0 + 1.376^2 + 2.227^2) / 4, is 3.427, exactly lambda1.

Reconstruction: From a PC1 score z we can map back to an approximation of the original point: z times PC1. For (-2, -1), z = -2.227 gives (-1.894, -1.171), close to the original. The average squared reconstruction error, computed with the same n - 1 divisor, is 0.073, exactly the dropped eigenvalue lambda2. This is a general fact: the information lost equals the sum of the eigenvalues you drop.

A geometric picture: Imagine the five points as beads scattered around a tilted stick. PCA first finds the angle of the stick: PC1, at about 31.7 degrees. The PC1 score of each bead is how far along the stick it sits from the centre; PC2 measures how far each bead sticks out sideways. Because the beads hug the stick tightly, the sideways distances are tiny, and dropping them changes little. In higher dimensions, the same picture becomes an ellipsoid-shaped cloud whose longest axes are the leading components.

PCA in pseudo-code: X = training features; mu = mean of each column; s = standard deviation of each column; Z = (X - mu) / s; C = covariance matrix of Z; eigenvalues and eigenvectors of C sorted from largest; W = first k eigenvectors as columns; scores = Z times W. For new data, reuse the same mu, s and W: scores_new = ((X_new - mu) / s) times W. Storing mu, s and W is all that is needed to apply PCA in production.

Choosing the number of components: Common approaches: keep enough components to explain a target share of variance, such as 90 or 95 percent; look for an elbow in a scree plot of eigenvalues; or choose k by cross-validating the downstream model's performance. With standardised features, a rough rule keeps components with eigenvalue above 1, but it is only a heuristic.

Standardise first: PCA is driven by variance, so units matter. If one feature is income in taka (variance in the millions) and another is family size (variance about 2), PC1 will simply be 'income'. Standardising each feature to mean 0 and standard deviation 1 (equivalent to PCA on the correlation matrix) puts features on equal footing. As always, compute the means and standard deviations, and the PCA itself, on training data only, then apply to validation and test data.

Interpreting components: Each component is a weighted combination of original features; the weights are called loadings. In a dataset of district statistics, PC1 might have positive loadings on literacy, electricity access and income and negative loading on child mortality, so it reads as a 'development' axis. Interpretation is useful but subjective, and later components are often hard to name. Remember that components are new features, not original ones, which can make models harder to explain to stakeholders.

Uses of PCA: Visualisation: project high-dimensional data onto PC1 and PC2 and plot it to see groups and outliers. Preprocessing: reduce features before k-means, k-NN or regression, removing noise and correlation and speeding up training. Compression: store k scores instead of d values. Noise reduction: reconstruct from the top components to smooth away small noisy variations. Handling multicollinearity: principal components are uncorrelated with each other, which stabilises regression.

Limitations: PCA finds only linear directions; data on a curved surface (a rolled-up sheet) is not summarised well. High variance does not always mean useful for prediction: a direction with small variance can be the one that separates classes, and PCA, being unsupervised, ignores labels. Methods such as linear discriminant analysis (in Pattern Recognition, cse-6-12) use labels, and non-linear methods such as kernel PCA, t-SNE and UMAP, and autoencoders (in Deep Learning, cse-8-1) handle curved structure, though t-SNE and UMAP are mainly for visualisation.

Real example 1, summarising school performance: An education researcher has, for each of 500 secondary schools, pass rates in 12 SSC subjects. Subject pass rates are strongly correlated. After standardising, PCA shows PC1 explains most of the variance with roughly equal loadings on all subjects, an overall performance score, while PC2 contrasts science subjects with humanities. Plotting schools on PC1 and PC2 reveals clusters by region and school type, and the researcher uses the two scores instead of 12 numbers in further analysis.

Real example 2, sensor data in a textile mill: A spinning mill records 40 sensor readings per machine every minute: temperatures, vibrations, speeds and humidity. Many are correlated. PCA on normal-operation data finds that 6 components explain about 95 percent of the variance. For each new reading, the mill computes the reconstruction error from those 6 components; a sudden jump signals behaviour that normal patterns cannot explain, and maintenance staff inspect the machine. This is a simple, effective anomaly detector.

Common mistakes and exam questions: Forgetting to centre or standardise. Fitting PCA on the whole dataset before splitting (leakage). Assuming high-variance components are the most predictive. Treating component signs as meaningful (an eigenvector multiplied by -1 is equally valid). Over-interpreting later components. Exams ask: compute a 2 by 2 covariance matrix, find its eigenvalues and the explained variance ratio, find PC1, project points, explain the relation between eigenvalues and variance, and discuss limitations.

Recap: PCA finds perpendicular directions of maximal variance: the eigenvectors of the covariance matrix, with eigenvalues equal to the variance along each. For our five points, the covariance matrix with rows (2.5, 1.5) and (1.5, 1.0) has eigenvalues 3.427 and 0.073; PC1 = (0.851, 0.526) explains 97.9 percent of the variance, and the scores run from -2.227 to 2.227. Dropping PC2 loses exactly 0.073 of variance. Standardise first, fit on training data only, and choose k by explained variance or downstream performance. The capstone and the production lesson will show where PCA fits in a full pipeline.
key_points: PCA finds perpendicular directions (principal components) along which the data has the most variance.
Steps: centre (and usually standardise), compute the covariance matrix, take its eigenvectors, sort by eigenvalue, project.
Each eigenvalue is the variance along its component; eigenvalues sum to the total variance.
Worked: covariance rows (2.5, 1.5) and (1.5, 1.0) give eigenvalues 3.427 and 0.073; PC1 explains 97.9 percent.
PC1 = (0.851, 0.526); point (-2, -1) projects to -2.227; the reconstruction error equals the dropped eigenvalue 0.073.
Choose k by explained variance (for example 95 percent), a scree plot, or downstream validation.
Standardise features and fit PCA on training data only to avoid leakage.
PCA is linear and unsupervised: high variance is not always what predicts the label.
lessons.tip: For a 2 by 2 covariance matrix, remember the shortcut: eigenvalues are (trace plus or minus the square root of (trace^2 - 4 det)) / 2. Check your answer: the two eigenvalues must add up to the trace and multiply to the determinant.
lessons.task: Take five centred points (-2, 0), (-1, -1), (0, 0), (1, 1), (2, 0). Compute the covariance matrix (dividing by 4), its eigenvalues, and the share of variance explained by PC1. Then explain in one sentence why PC1 here points along the x axis or not.

quiz.q: What does the first principal component represent?
options: The direction along which the projected data has the largest variance
The feature with the largest mean
The direction that best separates the classes
quiz.explain: PC1 maximises the variance of the projected data; PCA ignores class labels.

quiz.q: A covariance matrix has eigenvalues 6 and 2. What share of variance does PC1 explain?
Why should features usually be standardised before PCA?
options: PCA only works on binary data
Otherwise features with large units dominate the components
quiz.explain: PCA follows variance, so a feature measured in large units would dominate PC1 simply because of its scale.

quiz.q: For the covariance matrix with rows (2.5, 1.5) and (1.5, 1.0), what is the sum of its eigenvalues?
quiz.explain: Eigenvalues sum to the trace: 2.5 + 1.0 = 3.5 (they are 3.427 and 0.073).

quiz.q: Which statement about PCA is true?
options: Dropping components loses variance equal to the sum of their eigenvalues
PCA uses labels to choose directions
PCA can capture any curved structure
Components are always easy to interpret
quiz.explain: The reconstruction error equals the total variance of the dropped components.

lessons.title: The ML Toolkit and Machine Learning in Production
lessons.content:
A cook who makes a wonderful biryani once at home has not yet run a restaurant. A restaurant must make the same biryani every day, for hundreds of people, with ingredients that change from season to season, and someone must notice when the taste starts to slip. Machine learning is similar. Training a model with good test scores in a notebook is the home-cooking part. Putting it into a real product, where it serves predictions reliably, is watched, and is retrained when the world changes, is the restaurant part, and it is where many ML projects fail. This lesson tours the standard Python toolkit, shows how pipelines prevent leakage, and explains deployment, monitoring and drift.

The Python toolkit: Most ML work today uses Python. NumPy provides fast arrays and linear algebra; pandas provides data frames for loading, cleaning and joining tabular data; matplotlib and similar libraries draw plots; scikit-learn provides consistent implementations of almost every classic algorithm in this course: linear and logistic regression, k-NN, Naive Bayes, trees, random forests, gradient boosting, SVMs, k-means, DBSCAN, hierarchical clustering, PCA, plus scaling, encoding, cross-validation and metrics. XGBoost, LightGBM and CatBoost provide fast gradient boosting; PyTorch and TensorFlow are the main deep learning frameworks. Jupyter notebooks are popular for exploration. This lesson avoids version-specific details, since APIs change; always check the documentation of the version you install.

The fit, transform, predict pattern: scikit-learn uses one simple interface. A model object is created with its hyperparameters, learns from data with fit(X_train, y_train), and makes predictions with predict(X_new); classifiers often also have predict_proba. Preprocessing objects such as a standard scaler, an imputer or PCA learn with fit(X_train) and apply with transform(X). This uniformity means you can swap a logistic regression for a random forest by changing one line, which makes comparing models cheap.

Pipelines prevent leakage: Lessons 03, 04 and 13 warned that scaling, imputation and PCA must be fitted on training data only, and inside cross-validation must be refitted on each training fold. Doing this by hand is error-prone. A pipeline chains steps, for example imputer, then scaler, then PCA, then logistic regression, into one object. Calling fit on the pipeline fits each step on the training data in order; calling predict applies the same learned transformations to new data. When the whole pipeline is passed to cross-validation or grid search, every fold refits every step correctly, so leakage is avoided automatically. Column transformers let numeric and categorical columns get different preprocessing inside the same pipeline.

Reproducibility: Results should be repeatable. Fix random seeds for data splitting, model initialisation and algorithms such as random forests and k-means. Record the exact data snapshot, the code version (use git), library versions, hyperparameters and metrics for every experiment. Experiment-tracking tools help, but even a careful spreadsheet is better than nothing. Six months later, someone will ask why the model approved a loan, and you must be able to recreate exactly the model that made the decision.

Testing ML code: Software testing ideas from the Software Testing and QA course apply here too. Write unit tests for feature functions (does 'days since last purchase' handle a customer with no purchases?), data validation checks that reject rows with impossible values, and a small regression test that the saved pipeline still produces the expected predictions on a fixed set of examples. A model that silently receives a column in the wrong order can still output plausible-looking numbers, so automated checks matter more than in ordinary code.

Saving and loading models: After training, the fitted pipeline is serialised (saved to a file) so it can be loaded elsewhere without retraining. Python commonly uses pickle-based tools for scikit-learn models; deep learning frameworks have their own formats, and portable formats such as ONNX exist for moving models between frameworks. Two warnings: loading a pickled file can execute code, so never load model files from untrusted sources; and the loading environment should use compatible library versions.

Ways to serve predictions: Batch prediction runs the model periodically on many records, for example every night scoring all customers for churn risk and writing results to a database; it is simple and cheap. Online (real-time) prediction wraps the model in a web API: an app sends features and gets a prediction back within milliseconds, as in fraud checks during payment. Edge or on-device prediction runs the model on a phone or embedded device, useful when connectivity is poor, as in rural Bangladesh, or when privacy matters; models must then be small and fast, a topic that connects to Mobile App Development and Embedded Systems.

Worked example, sizing an online service: A mobile financial service expects 3 million fraud checks per day. On average that is 3000000 / 86400 seconds = 34.7 requests per second. If one prediction takes 20 milliseconds on one CPU core, one core handles 1000 / 20 = 50 predictions per second, enough for the average. But traffic peaks around salary days and Eid can be several times the average, so the team plans capacity for the peak, not the mean, and keeps the model fast, for example by preferring a compact gradient boosted model over a huge ensemble.

Training-serving skew: A classic production bug: features are computed one way during training and a different way in the live system. For example, training used 'average transaction amount over the last 30 days' computed from a clean warehouse table, while the live app computes it from the last 30 transactions. The model then sees inputs it was not trained on, and accuracy silently drops. The fix is to share one feature-computation code path between training and serving, and to compare the distributions of live features with training features.

Why models decay, data drift: The world changes after deployment. Data drift (covariate shift) means the distribution of inputs changes: new phone models, a new customer segment after a marketing campaign, different prices after inflation. A model trained on last year's customers may face this year's very different ones. Drift does not always hurt, but it is a warning sign.

Concept drift: Concept drift means the relationship between inputs and the target changes. Fraudsters change tactics once old patterns are blocked; buying behaviour shifted sharply during the COVID-19 lockdowns; a disease's symptom pattern can differ in a new season. Even if inputs look the same, yesterday's rules no longer predict today's outcomes. Concept drift is the more dangerous kind, and it is only fully visible when true labels arrive, which may take weeks (for example, whether a loan is repaid).

Worked example, measuring drift with PSI: The population stability index (PSI), widely used in credit scoring, compares a feature's distribution in production with training. Split the feature into bins; for each bin, with expected training share e and actual share a, add (a - e) times ln(a / e). Suppose four income bins each held 25 percent of training customers, but this month's applicants fall 10, 20, 30 and 40 percent into them. The terms are (0.10 - 0.25) ln(0.4) = 0.137, (0.20 - 0.25) ln(0.8) = 0.011, (0.30 - 0.25) ln(1.2) = 0.009 and (0.40 - 0.25) ln(1.6) = 0.071, totalling 0.228. A common rule of thumb treats PSI below 0.1 as stable, 0.1 to 0.25 as a moderate shift worth investigating, and above 0.25 as a major shift; these cut-offs are conventions, not laws. Here the shift is moderate and worth a closer look.

Monitoring: A production model needs a dashboard and alerts, just like a server. Monitor system health (latency, errors, throughput), input data (missing values, out-of-range values, drift statistics such as PSI), predictions (the share of positive predictions, the average score), and, when labels arrive, real performance (accuracy, precision, recall, MAE) overall and for important subgroups. A sudden jump in predicted fraud rate from 1 to 8 percent overnight usually means a broken data pipeline, not a fraud wave.

Retraining and safe rollout: Models are retrained on a schedule (for example monthly) or when monitoring shows decay. A new model should beat the current one on a recent, time-based holdout set before it replaces it. Safe rollout strategies include shadow mode, where the new model makes predictions that are logged but not used, and A/B tests or canary releases, where a small share of traffic uses the new model first. Keep the old model ready for quick rollback. The practices of automating training, testing, deployment and monitoring are known as MLOps.

Humans in the loop and feedback loops: Many systems keep humans in charge of uncertain or high-stakes cases: the model handles clear cases and passes borderline ones to a person. Beware feedback loops: if a loan model rejects certain applicants, you never learn whether they would have repaid, so future training data reflects past model decisions. Recommendation systems can narrow what users see and then learn from that narrowed behaviour. Some random exploration or careful study design can help, which links to the reinforcement learning course (cse-8-4).

Real example 1, nightly churn scoring at a telecom: A mobile operator in Bangladesh runs a batch pipeline every night: extract yesterday's usage, compute features with the same code used in training, load the saved pipeline (imputer, scaler, gradient boosted model), score all prepaid subscribers, and send the top-risk list to the retention team's system. A monitoring job computes PSI for key features and tracks weekly churn precision once true churn becomes known. After a major tariff change, PSI on data usage jumps above 0.25, triggering an early retraining.

Real example 2, an on-device crop disease app: An agri-tech startup's app identifies rice leaf diseases from photos taken in the field, often without internet. The team compresses the model to run on low-cost Android phones in under a second. Photos and predictions are uploaded when the phone reconnects, with farmers' consent; agronomists label a sample each month, revealing that accuracy drops on photos from a new phone brand with different colour processing. They add such photos to training data and release an updated model.

Common mistakes and exam questions: Preprocessing outside the pipeline and leaking information. No fixed seeds or records, so results cannot be reproduced. Computing features differently in training and serving. Deploying and never monitoring. Retraining blindly on data that the model itself shaped. Loading untrusted pickle files. Exams ask: explain the fit and transform pattern and why pipelines prevent leakage, compare batch, online and edge serving, define data drift and concept drift with examples, compute a simple drift measure, and describe a monitoring and retraining plan.

Recap: The Python toolkit (NumPy, pandas, scikit-learn, boosting libraries, deep learning frameworks) shares a fit, transform, predict pattern, and pipelines chain preprocessing with models so that cross-validation never leaks. A pipeline of imputer, scaler, PCA from lesson 23, and model is a typical example. Production adds new duties: reproducibility, saving models safely, choosing batch, online or edge serving (3 million daily checks average 34.7 per second), avoiding training-serving skew, and monitoring for data and concept drift (PSI 0.228 in our example signalled a moderate shift). Retrain carefully and roll out safely. The next lesson asks a deeper question: even when a model works, is it fair?
key_points: The standard toolkit is NumPy, pandas, scikit-learn, boosting libraries and deep learning frameworks; check docs for your version.
scikit-learn uses fit, transform and predict; models are swappable with one line.
Pipelines chain preprocessing and model so cross-validation refits every step per fold, preventing leakage.
Reproducibility needs fixed seeds and records of data, code, library versions, hyperparameters and metrics.
Serving options: batch, online API and on-device; size for peak load (3 million per day averages 34.7 per second).
Training-serving skew happens when features are computed differently in training and production.
Data drift changes inputs; concept drift changes the input-target relationship; PSI 0.228 in the example signals a moderate shift.
Monitor health, inputs, predictions and real performance; retrain with time-based checks and roll out with shadow or canary releases.
lessons.tip: From your very first ML project, put every preprocessing step inside a pipeline and save the whole pipeline, not just the model. It is the single habit that prevents the most common leakage bugs and the most common deployment bugs.
lessons.task: Pick any model you trained earlier in this course. Write a one-page production plan: how predictions will be served (batch, online or on-device), how many predictions per second at peak, which three input features you would monitor for drift, what performance metric you would track once labels arrive, and what would trigger retraining.

quiz.q: Why does putting the scaler inside a pipeline help during cross-validation?
options: It makes the model more accurate on training data
It removes the need for a test set
It scales the labels as well
The scaler is refitted on each training fold only, preventing leakage
quiz.explain: The pipeline refits every step on each fold's training part, so validation folds never influence preprocessing.

quiz.q: A model scores all customers every night and stores the results. This is:
quiz.explain: Periodic scoring of many records at once is batch prediction.

quiz.q: Fraudsters change tactics so that old patterns no longer indicate fraud. This is an example of:
quiz.explain: The relationship between inputs and the target has changed, which is concept drift.

quiz.q: Features were computed from a clean warehouse table during training but from raw app logs in production. What problem is this?
quiz.explain: The same feature computed differently in training and serving gives the model unfamiliar inputs.

quiz.q: Why should you never load a pickled model file from an untrusted source?
options: Loading it can execute arbitrary code
It will always have lower accuracy
quiz.explain: Unpickling can run code embedded in the file, which is a security risk.

lessons.title: Fairness, Bias and Privacy in Machine Learning
lessons.content:
Imagine a lending app that approves 62 percent of applicants from cities but only 46 percent from villages. Is the model unfair, or are village applicants genuinely riskier according to the data? Does the answer change if you learn that the model wrongly rejects far more good village borrowers than good city borrowers? Questions like these are not side issues. ML models now help decide who gets loans, jobs, medical attention and government support, and they are trained on personal data. A model can be accurate overall and still harm particular groups, or leak private information. This lesson gives you the vocabulary, a worked fairness calculation, and practical habits. It builds on the ethics discussion in the AI course and goes deeper into measurement.

Where bias comes from: Bias in ML usually comes from the data and the problem setup, not from malicious programmers. Historical bias: the data reflects past discrimination, so a model trained on past hiring decisions learns past preferences. Representation bias: some groups are under-represented, for example a speech model trained mostly on Dhaka accents performs worse on Sylheti or Chittagonian speakers. Measurement bias: the label or a feature is a poor proxy, such as using 'arrests' as a proxy for 'crime', when policing intensity differs between areas. Aggregation bias: one model for everyone when relationships differ between groups. And deployment bias: a model used for a different purpose or population than intended.

Proxies and why removing a column is not enough: A common first idea is to delete sensitive attributes such as gender, religion or ethnicity from the features. This rarely guarantees fairness, because other features act as proxies: mobile number patterns, name, area code, school, shopping patterns or district can correlate strongly with the removed attribute. The model can reconstruct the information indirectly. Worse, without the sensitive attribute you cannot even measure whether outcomes differ between groups. Fairness work usually needs the sensitive attribute for auditing, kept under strict access controls, even if it is not used for prediction.

Worked example, the data: A loan model is tested on 1000 urban and 1000 rural applicants. In each group, 600 later turned out to be good borrowers (would repay) and 400 would default. 'Positive' means the model approves. Urban group: true positives 540, false negatives 60, false positives 80, true negatives 320. Rural group: true positives 420, false negatives 180, false positives 40, true negatives 360.

Worked example, overall accuracy: Urban accuracy is (540 + 320) / 1000 = 86 percent. Rural accuracy is (420 + 360) / 1000 = 78 percent. Overall accuracy is 82 percent, a figure that hides an 8-point gap between groups. Always break metrics down by relevant subgroups.

Fairness metric 1, demographic parity: Demographic parity (statistical parity) asks whether the approval rate is the same across groups. Urban approval is (540 + 80) / 1000 = 62 percent; rural approval is (420 + 40) / 1000 = 46 percent. The ratio is 0.46 / 0.62 = 0.74. A heuristic from US employment guidelines, the four-fifths rule, flags ratios below 0.8 as possible adverse impact; it is a screening rule, not a definition of fairness, and laws differ by country. Demographic parity ignores whether the groups differ in true repayment rates; here they are the same (60 percent good borrowers in each), so the gap is a real concern.

Fairness metric 2, equal opportunity: Equal opportunity asks whether qualified people have the same chance of approval: equal true positive rates. Urban TPR is 540 / 600 = 0.90; rural TPR is 420 / 600 = 0.70. A good rural borrower is rejected 30 percent of the time, against 10 percent for a good urban borrower, a gap of 0.20. Equalised odds is stricter: equal TPR and equal false positive rates. Urban FPR is 80 / 400 = 0.20 and rural FPR is 40 / 400 = 0.10, so the model is also more lenient with risky urban applicants.

Fairness metric 3, predictive parity: Predictive parity asks whether an approval means the same thing for each group: equal precision. Urban precision is 540 / 620 = 0.871; rural precision is 420 / 460 = 0.913. Approved rural applicants are actually more reliable, consistent with the model setting a tougher bar for them. A related idea, calibration within groups, asks that a predicted 70 percent repayment chance means about 70 percent in every group.

Reading the worked example together: The rural group has the same share of good borrowers as the urban group, yet good rural borrowers are rejected three times as often (30 versus 10 percent). The higher rural precision is not a sign of fairness; it is the side effect of an unusually strict bar. A plausible cause is that rural applicants have thinner records (fewer transactions, less formal income data), so the model is less confident about them and more often says no. That points to a data fix, not just a threshold fix.

You cannot have everything: A well-known mathematical result says that when groups have different base rates (different true proportions of positives), a classifier that is not perfect cannot satisfy calibration (or predictive parity) and equal false positive and false negative rates at the same time. So choosing a fairness definition is a value judgement about which errors matter most, made with stakeholders, domain experts and legal advisers, not a purely technical choice. Document which metric you chose and why.

Mitigation options: Pre-processing: collect more representative data, fix biased labels, or reweight examples so under-represented groups count more. In-processing: train with a fairness constraint or penalty added to the loss. Post-processing: adjust decision thresholds per group to equalise a chosen metric (this may be legally restricted in some settings, so seek advice). Often the most effective step is non-technical: improve data collection in under-served areas, or change how the model's output is used, for example routing borderline rural applicants to a human officer rather than auto-rejecting them.

Transparency and explanation: People affected by automated decisions increasingly expect, and in some jurisdictions are legally entitled to, meaningful information about them. Interpretable models (small trees, logistic regression with clear features), global feature importance and per-decision explanations help.
