Model cards (short documents describing a model's purpose, training data, performance by subgroup and limitations) and datasheets for datasets are good practice. Explanations should be honest about uncertainty and not give false confidence.

Privacy risks: ML depends on personal data: call records, mobile money transactions, health records, locations. Risks include collecting more than needed, using data for purposes people did not agree to, data breaches, and re-identification: removing names is not anonymisation, because combinations such as birth date, area and gender can single out individuals. Models themselves can leak information: membership inference attacks try to tell whether a person's record was in the training set, and very large models can sometimes reproduce memorised training text.

Privacy protections: Data minimisation (collect only what you need and delete it when no longer needed), informed consent, access control, encryption, and pseudonymisation are basics. Aggregating data before analysis helps. Differential privacy adds carefully calibrated noise so that results barely change whether any one person is included, giving a mathematical privacy guarantee at some cost in accuracy. Federated learning trains models across many devices while raw data stays on each device, sharing only model updates. Laws such as the EU's GDPR set rules on consent, purpose limitation and automated decisions; check the current law in Bangladesh and any country where your users live, since data protection legislation is evolving in many places.

Security of ML systems: Models can also be attacked. Adversarial examples are inputs changed in tiny, deliberate ways that flip a model's prediction, such as stickers that fool an image classifier. Data poisoning inserts crafted examples into training data, for example fake reviews designed to teach a spam filter that certain spam is normal. Model stealing queries a public API many times to copy its behaviour. Defences include validating and monitoring training data, rate-limiting APIs, and testing models against known attacks.

Accountability: Every deployed model should have a named owner responsible for its behaviour, a record of the decisions made while building it, and a process for people to question its outcomes. 'The algorithm decided' is never an acceptable answer to a person who was harmed.

Other harms to consider: Fairness and privacy are not the only issues. Automation can remove human judgement from cases that need it. Models can be gamed by people who learn their rules. Surveillance applications such as face recognition raise civil-liberty concerns. Environmental costs of training very large models are real. A useful practice is a short impact assessment before deployment: who benefits, who could be harmed, how errors will be noticed and corrected, and who is accountable.

Real example 1, credit scoring with phone data: Fintech lenders in several countries, including Bangladesh, have explored credit scoring from mobile phone usage for people without bank history. This can expand access for the unbanked, a real benefit. But it raises questions: are women, who in many households may share or have less access to phones, scored unfairly? Do users understand what data is used? A responsible lender audits approval rates and TPR by gender and region, limits data collection to what is necessary with clear consent, and offers a human review route.

Real example 2, allocating social support: A government agency considers ranking households for a cash support programme using a model trained on survey data. If remote char areas were under-sampled in the survey, the model may systematically under-score them. The team checks performance by division and area type, adds a field-verification step for low-confidence cases, publishes a plain-language description of the criteria, and creates a grievance process so excluded households can appeal.

Common mistakes and exam questions: Assuming removing sensitive attributes makes a model fair. Reporting only overall accuracy. Picking a fairness metric without discussing its trade-offs. Treating pseudonymised data as anonymous. Forgetting that bias can enter at problem definition, data collection, labelling, modelling and deployment. Exams ask: list sources of bias with examples, compute demographic parity, TPR and FPR gaps from confusion matrices, explain why fairness definitions conflict, describe mitigation strategies, and explain privacy techniques such as differential privacy and federated learning.

Recap: Bias enters through historical, representation, measurement, aggregation and deployment issues, and proxies make simply dropping sensitive columns ineffective. In our loan example, approval rates were 62 versus 46 percent (ratio 0.74), TPRs 0.90 versus 0.70, FPRs 0.20 versus 0.10, and precision 0.871 versus 0.913: different fairness metrics tell different stories, and they cannot all be equalised when base rates differ. Mitigate through better data, constraints, thresholds and human review; protect privacy with minimisation, consent, differential privacy and federated learning. Responsible ML is part of the engineering, not an afterthought. The final lesson brings the whole course together in a capstone project.
key_points: Bias usually comes from data and setup: historical, representation, measurement, aggregation and deployment bias.
Dropping sensitive attributes does not ensure fairness because proxies remain; auditing needs the attribute.
Always report metrics by subgroup: 86 versus 78 percent accuracy was hidden inside an 82 percent overall figure.
Demographic parity compares approval rates: 62 versus 46 percent, ratio 0.74.
Equal opportunity compares TPR (0.90 versus 0.70); equalised odds also compares FPR (0.20 versus 0.10).
Predictive parity compares precision (0.871 versus 0.913); with different base rates, these criteria cannot all hold at once.
Mitigation: better data, reweighting, fairness constraints, threshold adjustment and human review.
Privacy: minimise data, get consent, beware re-identification; differential privacy and federated learning add protection.
lessons.tip: Whenever you report a model's performance, add a small table with the same metrics broken down by the groups that matter for the application (gender, region, age band). Gaps that are invisible in the overall number are often obvious in that table.
lessons.task: Take any classifier you built in this course, or the loan example in this lesson with your own numbers. Choose two groups, write their confusion matrices, and compute approval rate, TPR, FPR and precision for each. Write a paragraph explaining which gap you think matters most for this application, and why.

quiz.q: Why does removing the 'gender' column not guarantee a fair model?
options: Models always need gender to work
Other features can act as proxies for gender
Gender cannot be stored in a data frame
quiz.explain: Correlated features such as name or shopping patterns can let the model reconstruct the removed attribute.

quiz.q: Group A has approval rate 50 percent and group B 40 percent. What is the demographic parity ratio B / A?
Equal opportunity requires equal values of which metric across groups?
quiz.explain: Equal opportunity asks that qualified individuals in each group have the same chance of a positive decision.

quiz.q: A speech recogniser trained mostly on one regional accent performs poorly on others. Which type of bias is this?
quiz.explain: Some groups are under-represented in the training data, so the model serves them worse.

quiz.q: What does differential privacy do?
options: Adds calibrated noise so results barely depend on any single person's data
Deletes all personal data before training
Trains a separate model per person
quiz.explain: It gives a mathematical guarantee that including or excluding one person changes outputs very little.

lessons.title: Capstone: Predicting Boro Rice Yield, End to End
lessons.content:
Boro rice, grown in the dry season with irrigation, supplies a large share of Bangladesh's rice. An agricultural extension office wants a simple tool: given a few facts about a farm, predict its Boro yield in tonnes per hectare, so field officers can spot farms likely to fall short and visit them early with advice. This capstone walks through the whole machine learning workflow from lesson 02 on a small dataset, with every number checked: framing the problem, preparing data, splitting, building a baseline, fitting and comparing models, choosing honestly, and thinking about deployment and fairness. The data is invented for teaching and kept tiny so you can redo every step with a calculator; real projects would use hundreds or thousands of farms.

Step 1, frame the problem: The target is yield in tonnes per hectare, a number, so this is supervised regression. The users are field officers; the decision is which farms to visit. Errors in both directions cost something: over-predicting a struggling farm means a missed visit, under-predicting means a wasted trip. Mean absolute error (MAE), in tonnes per hectare, is easy to explain to officers ('on average the prediction is off by 0.3 tonnes'), so we choose MAE as the main metric. We also agree on a success bar: the model must clearly beat a naive baseline and be simple enough to explain.

Step 2, the features: For each farm we have three candidate features: the number of irrigations during the season, whether an improved seed variety was used (1 for yes, 0 for no), and fertiliser applied in kg per hectare. All three are known before harvest, so using them involves no leakage. A feature such as 'harvested grain sold in the market' would leak the answer and is excluded.

Step 3, the data: Ten farms, as (irrigations, improved seed, fertiliser, yield): farm 1 (10, 1, 200, 5.8); farm 2 (6, 0, 150, 4.1); farm 3 (8, 1, missing, 5.2); farm 4 (12, 1, 220, 6.3); farm 5 (5, 0, 120, 3.6); farm 6 (9, 0, 180, 4.9); farm 7 (7, 1, 160, 5.0); farm 8 (11, 0, 210, 5.3); farm 9 (8, 0, 170, 4.6); farm 10 (10, 1, 190, 5.9). Farm 3's fertiliser value is missing because the farmer was not sure.

Step 4, split before anything else: We hold out farms 9 and 10 as the test set and use farms 1 to 8 for training. In a real project the test set should be larger, perhaps 20 percent of many farms, and if data spans several seasons, the test set should be the latest season, to mimic predicting the future. The test set is locked away until the very end. Every decision below uses training data only.

Step 5, handle the missing value using training data only: The known fertiliser values among training farms are 200, 150, 220, 120, 180, 160 and 210. Sorted: 120, 150, 160, 180, 200, 210, 220; the median is 180. So we fill farm 3's fertiliser with 180. The median is preferred to the mean because it resists outliers. Crucially, the test farms' values were not used to compute it; if a test farm had a missing value, we would fill it with the same training median, 180.

Step 6, explore: With only eight rows, a quick look already shows patterns. Farms with more irrigations tend to yield more: the three farms with 10 or more irrigations yield 5.3 to 6.3, while the two with 6 or fewer yield 3.6 and 4.1. Improved-seed farms average (5.8 + 5.2 + 6.3 + 5.0) / 4 = 5.575 tonnes, against (4.1 + 3.6 + 4.9 + 5.3) / 4 = 4.475 for traditional seed. Fertiliser rises along with irrigation, so the two are correlated, a warning that their separate effects will be hard to untangle.

Step 7, the baseline: The simplest model predicts the training mean for every farm: (5.8 + 4.1 + 5.2 + 6.3 + 3.6 + 4.9 + 5.0 + 5.3) / 8 = 40.2 / 8 = 5.025. On the test farms, errors are |4.6 - 5.025| = 0.425 and |5.9 - 5.025| = 0.875, so test MAE = 0.65. Any useful model must beat 0.65.

Step 8, model A, irrigation only: Least squares on the eight training farms gives yield = 2.2929 + 0.3214 times irrigations: each extra irrigation adds about 0.32 tonnes per hectare in this data. Training MAE is 0.309. Test predictions: farm 9 (8 irrigations) gives 2.2929 + 0.3214 times 8 = 4.864, error 0.264; farm 10 (10 irrigations) gives 5.507, error 0.393. Test MAE = 0.329, about half the baseline's error.

Step 9, model B, irrigation plus improved seed: Adding the seed indicator gives yield = 2.367 + 0.272 times irrigations + 0.692 times seed. Holding irrigation fixed, improved seed adds about 0.69 tonnes per hectare. Training MAE drops to 0.061. Test predictions: farm 9 (8 irrigations, traditional seed) gives 2.367 + 0.272 times 8 = 4.543, error 0.057; farm 10 (10 irrigations, improved seed) gives 2.367 + 2.72 + 0.692 = 5.779, error 0.121. Test MAE = 0.089, a large improvement.

Step 10, model C, adding fertiliser: With all three features: yield = 1.917 + 0.182 times irrigations + 0.653 times seed + 0.007 times fertiliser. Training MAE falls slightly to 0.055, as it always can when you add a feature. But test predictions 4.555 and 5.712 give errors 0.045 and 0.188, and test MAE rises to 0.117. The irrigation coefficient also shrank from 0.272 to 0.182, because fertiliser and irrigation are correlated and now share the credit: the multicollinearity warned about in step 6.

Step 11, interpret the comparison honestly: The pattern is the classic one from lessons 08 and 09: more features lowered training error but not test error. Model B looks best. However, with only two test farms, the difference between 0.089 and 0.117 is far too small to trust; one unusual farm could flip it. In a real project you would use k-fold cross-validation on the training data (lesson 13) to compare models A, B and C, perhaps with ridge regression to handle the correlated features (lesson 10), and only then confirm the chosen model once on a larger test set. The honest conclusion here: irrigation and improved seed clearly help prediction; fertiliser's extra value is unproven with this data.

Step 12, choose and finalise: We choose model B: it beats the baseline by a wide margin, uses two features officers can collect easily, and its coefficients are easy to explain: 'each extra irrigation is worth about a quarter tonne per hectare; improved seed is worth about 0.7 tonnes'. Before deployment, refit model B on all ten farms (training plus test), since more data gives better estimates, and record that the final test estimate comes from the earlier held-out evaluation.

Step 13, caution about causation: The coefficients describe associations in this data, not proven causal effects. Farms using improved seed may also have better land, more experienced farmers, or easier access to credit. Advising every farmer that improved seed will add 0.7 tonnes would overstate what the model knows. Controlled field trials, run by agronomists, are the right way to measure causal effects. The model's job is to flag farms likely to fall short, which it can do from associations alone.

Step 14, deploy simply: The model is just two coefficients and an intercept, so it can run in a spreadsheet or a small offline mobile app, important where field connectivity is weak. Officers enter irrigations and seed type; the app shows the predicted yield and flags farms predicted below, say, 4.8 tonnes per hectare for a visit. The threshold is set with the extension office according to how many visits staff can make, a business decision informed by the model, as in lesson 12.

Step 15, monitor and maintain: Each season, compare predictions with actual harvests, tracking MAE overall and by upazila. Watch for drift (lesson 24): new seed varieties, a drought year or changes in irrigation costs can change the relationships. Retrain each season with the new data, check performance on the latest season before adopting the update, and keep a record of every model version.

Step 16, fairness and data checks: Ask who might be served badly. If the training farms came mostly from well-connected areas near roads, predictions for remote char or haor farms may be less accurate. Report MAE by area type and farm size, as in lesson 25. Also consider how the tool is used: it should direct extra help towards struggling farms, not be repurposed to deny credit to them without review. Farmers' data should be collected with consent and kept no longer than needed.

What this capstone used: Problem framing and metrics (lessons 01, 02, 12), data cleaning and imputation (03), splitting and leakage (04), linear regression and least squares (05, 06), loss functions (07), overfitting and the bias-variance trade-off (08, 09), regularisation as the next step (10), cross-validation as the proper comparison tool (13), production and drift (24) and fairness (25). Tree ensembles (18) would be natural candidates with more data and non-linear effects, and clustering (21, 22) could group farms into types for targeted advice.

Real example 1, scaling up: A real version might combine thousands of farm survey records with satellite vegetation indices, rainfall and soil maps. Then gradient boosted trees might beat linear regression, cross-validation would be grouped by district to test generalisation to new areas, and the deployment would need data pipelines rather than a spreadsheet. The steps would be exactly the same as in this capstone.

Real example 2, the same workflow elsewhere: The identical steps apply to predicting HSC results from SSC marks and attendance, estimating garment line output from operator skill and order complexity, or forecasting rickshaw-van freight demand from market days. Frame, split, baseline, model, validate, interpret honestly, deploy simply, monitor and check fairness.

Common mistakes and exam questions: Imputing with statistics computed on all data, including test rows. Skipping the baseline. Choosing a model because its training error is lowest. Over-trusting differences on a tiny test set. Reading coefficients as causal effects. Forgetting monitoring and fairness. Exams and viva boards often ask you to describe an end-to-end ML project: be ready to state the target, features, metric, split, baseline, models compared, validation method, result and limitations, exactly as in this lesson.

Recap: On ten invented farms, the baseline mean 5.025 gave test MAE 0.65. Irrigation alone (yield = 2.2929 + 0.3214 irrigations) reduced it to 0.329. Adding improved seed (2.367 + 0.272 irrigations + 0.692 seed) brought it to 0.089. Adding fertiliser lowered training MAE to 0.055 but raised test MAE to 0.117, and the tiny test set means the comparison needs cross-validation before we trust it. We chose the simple, explainable model, planned simple deployment, monitoring and fairness checks, and kept causation claims modest. That is the whole course in one project. Congratulations on completing Machine Learning; Deep Learning (cse-8-1), Data Mining (cse-7-6), Pattern Recognition (cse-6-12), Reinforcement Learning (cse-8-4) and Data Science (cse-6-14) are natural next steps.
key_points: Frame first: Boro yield in t/ha is a regression target; MAE is chosen because officers can understand it.
Split before anything else: farms 1 to 8 train, farms 9 and 10 test; real projects need larger, time-based test sets.
Impute with the training median only: known training fertiliser values give a median of 180.
Baseline (training mean 5.025) has test MAE 0.65; every model must beat it.
Irrigation only: yield = 2.2929 + 0.3214 irrigations, test MAE 0.329.
Irrigation plus improved seed: 2.367 + 0.272 irrigations + 0.692 seed, test MAE 0.089.
Adding fertiliser lowers training MAE to 0.055 but raises test MAE to 0.117; with two test farms, confirm with cross-validation.
Coefficients are associations, not causes; deploy simply, monitor drift by season, and check accuracy across areas.
lessons.tip: Turn this capstone into a template: for any ML project, write one line each for target, users and decision, metric, features, split, baseline, models, validation, result, limitations, deployment and monitoring. If you cannot fill a line, that is the next thing to work on.
lessons.task: Redo the capstone with a calculator or a short Python script: recompute the training median, the baseline test MAE, and model A's test predictions from the given coefficients. Then hold out farms 1 and 2 instead of 9 and 10, refit model A by least squares on the other eight farms, and report how the test MAE changes. What does this tell you about tiny test sets?

quiz.q: Why is the missing fertiliser value filled with the median of the training farms only?
options: The median is always equal to the mean
Test farms have no fertiliser values
Using test rows to compute it would leak test information into training
The mean cannot be computed with missing values
quiz.explain: All preprocessing statistics must come from training data so the test set stays an honest estimate.

quiz.q: The baseline predicts 5.025 for both test farms with true yields 4.6 and 5.9. What is its MAE?
Model B is yield = 2.367 + 0.272 irrigations + 0.692 seed. What does it predict for a farm with 10 irrigations and improved seed?
Adding fertiliser lowered training MAE but raised test MAE. What is the most appropriate next step?
options: Report model C because training error is lowest
Add more features until test MAE falls
Compare the models with cross-validation, possibly using ridge regression
quiz.explain: Two test farms are too few to decide; cross-validation on training data gives a more reliable comparison.

quiz.q: Why should the seed coefficient 0.692 not be told to farmers as a guaranteed gain?
options: Because seed is a categorical feature
Because it describes an association that may reflect other differences between farms
Because linear regression cannot use binary features
quiz.explain: Farms using improved seed may differ in other ways; causal effects need controlled trials.
